01436bcc-073d-529a-9751-7349d0fd45fc.name: Wooden Qur’an Stand
01436bcc-073d-529a-9751-7349d0fd45fc.short_description: Items like this Qur’an stand were popular props in Orientalist painting. On the inside, this hard wood Qur’an stand, which is inlaid with ebony, bone and mother-of-pearl, is decorated with two large square geometric panels, surrounded by a wide zig-zag border. The two squares are in turn subdivided into four small squares, filled with abstract star motifs. On the underside, the stand has two large geometric roundels. Two narrow, rectangular mashrabiyyah panels occupy the upper part of the feet. The remaining surfaces surrounding them are filled with chequerboard designs.

019b1d84-e6f3-5e53-a049-f7191924c562.name: Ottoman wooden spoons
019b1d84-e6f3-5e53-a049-f7191924c562.short_description: The Kunstkammer at Ambras contains a number of wooden Ottoman spoons. One such spoon is recorded in the Kunstkammer at Munich as early as AD 1596, suggesting that the ones at Ambras also date from the 16th century, despite only being listed on a later inventory. The spoons feature floral motifs such as tulips, carnations and hyacinths in gold paint. Their backs and part of the handles are decorated with wave-band motifs.

01c7dad2-5f26-5c46-9416-87c4c613cb64.name: Table and two chairs (*Peškuns*)
01c7dad2-5f26-5c46-9416-87c4c613cb64.description:
Interested in woodcut and its application on both profane and sacral objects, artist Branko Šotra (1906–1960) created several ensembles of *peškuns* during the 1930s. In interwar Yugoslavia, *peškun* (Tr. *peşkun*), a richly decorated (with carving, mother-of-pearl, and other) circular or polygonal low table/chair of Oriental origin, was an indispensable element of the so-called *Bosnian room* that was popular in homes in Belgrade, as an emulation of the royal family’s furnishings. They were made and decorated by skilled craftsmen, the most appreciated being those from Konjic.  
However, Šotra combined the traditional form of the *peškun* with the motifs he was personally interested in and treated them using the contemporary language of Art Deco. On the top hexagonal table and chair tops of the *peškuns*, he carved relief scenes of rural life, while the lower, supporting, parts with ogee arches are decorated with geometric ornaments, motifs of grain ears, flowers, affronted doves and parrots. On the tabletop, there is a representation of a kitchen where a mother is nursing a child, a father is sitting and smoking next to the table with a *fildžan* – a Turkish coffee cup (Tr. *kahve fıncanı*) – and a *džezva* – coffee pot (Tr. *cezve*) – while a cat is drinking milk from a bowl. On the chair-tops are depictions of a shepherdess spinning wool in a meadow under a tree, surrounded by sheep and a stack of hay, and, on another chair, a woman reaping grain, a tree, a water gourd, and, in the background, a road leading to the village.  
The introduction of contemporary features into tradition was not Šotra’s exclusive approach. As a contributor to the journal *Primenjena umetnost* (*The Applied Art*), he published, in 1937, a pattern and instruction for the woodcuts for peškun, with geometric and floral ornaments inspired by folk art. After graduating from The Royal Art School in Belgrade in 1929, Branko Šotra taught drawing in Sarajevo, Loznica, and Vršac, and woodcut in Ohrid. At the same time, he dealt with painting, fresco painting, icon painting, and woodcarving. After World War II, he dedicated himself to the art of printing and pedagogical work. He served as the rector and professor at The Academy of Applied Arts from 1948 to 1956.

01c7dad2-5f26-5c46-9416-87c4c613cb64.obtention: Given in 2006 by the author's niece, Ksenija Gaćinović from Belgrade.

0283d533-1980-536d-937a-06e5a3d00c92.name: Corbel.
0283d533-1980-536d-937a-06e5a3d00c92.description: The sides of this corbel are painted with a simplified floral decoration of blue and yellow foliate scrolls ending in tri-lobed or four-lobed palm-leaf motifs on a bright red background. The edges of the corbel are decorated with yellow dots within blue circles. These floral motifs are perfectly typical of the Ifriqiyan decorative repertoire of the AH 3rd and 4th century (AD 9th and 10th century). The front projection of the corbel is carved in the shape of a grasshopper's head with curved grooves. Although the Orient has not left to us any other comparable wooden corbels, Ifriqiyan architecture does feature similar stone models as early as the AH 3rd century (AD 9th century), for example at the Mosque of the Three Doors. This corbel was part of the wooden roof of the prayer hall of the Great Mosque of Kairouan and served to support one of the ceiling beams. It is probably derived from an ancient design. However, one is struck by the consummate skill of the woodcarver's simple, rough-hewn, linear treatment of the surfaces, so appropriate for the decoration of a protruding architectural element.
0283d533-1980-536d-937a-06e5a3d00c92.short_description: This corbel was part of the wooden ceiling of the prayer room of the Great Mosque of Kairouan, acting as a joist for the ceiling beams. Its floral motifs belonged to the Ifriqiyan decorative repertoire from the AH 3rd–5th / AD 9th–11th centuries.
0283d533-1980-536d-937a-06e5a3d00c92.dates: Hegira, end of 3rd–beginning of 5th century / AH 9th–11th century.
0283d533-1980-536d-937a-06e5a3d00c92.dimensions: Length 62 cm, width 16 cm, thickness 10 cm.
0283d533-1980-536d-937a-06e5a3d00c92.method_for_datation: The motifs decorating this corbel are found on some carved panels of the *minbar* and on the painted wooden semi-dome of the *mihrab* of the Great Mosque of Kairouan, which dates to the middle of the 3rd / 9th century. These motifs are also found in the Umayyad art in Syria. All these allow us to date this corbel to the end of the 3rd / 9th century, certainly to the renovation work ordered and commissioned by the Aghlabid prince Ibrahim II (261-289 / 875-902).
0283d533-1980-536d-937a-06e5a3d00c92.method_for_provenance: The motifs decorating this corbel are found on some carved panels of the *minbar* and on the painted wooden semi-dome of the *mihrab* of the Great Mosque of Kairouan.
0283d533-1980-536d-937a-06e5a3d00c92.obtention: After the restoration of the Great Mosque of Kairouan, between 1962 and 1972, some beams, boards and joists were taken out and completely refurbished. This piece was placed along with thousands of other fragments in the storerooms of the National Institute of the Patrimony of Kairouan. It was selected for display when the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada was extended.

040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.name: Pieces from the Nur al-Din Zangi *minbar*.
040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.description:
A collection of panels formed from small and medium-sized pieces of interlocking pinewood representing all that remains of the Minbar of Nur al-Din Zangi, which was crafted in Aleppo as a good omen for the conquest of Jerusalem. The *minbar* was destroyed in a fire of 1969 which damaged some of the sections of al-Aqsa Mosque, especially the southern, *qibla*, wall. Nur al-Din Zangi ordered the production of the *minbar* while preparing for the conquest of Jerusalem but he died before he could retake the city, and Salah al-Din (Saladin) undertook the transportation of the *minbar* from Aleppo to Jerusalem in AH 583 / AD 1187.  
The *minbar* was made from interlocking pine and inlaid with mother-of-pearl, ivory and pearls. The different components that constitute it are attached to each other by means of wooden nails and, in addition, the interlocking technique (*ta'sheeq*) is employed. The *minbar* was made up of three sections: the entrance, which faced *muqarnas* tiers, a staircase and a podium, which was covered by a kiosk. The door was composed of two leafs, important sections of which remain. The entrance opened onto the staircase with a wooden enclosure on both sides, crafted in the *mashrabiyya* technique. The staircase leads to the podium where the *khatib* would deliver the sermon.  
The *minbar* is rich in vegetal and geometric decorations as well as an arrangement of star-shaped medallions, each of which forms a complete decorative unit which, with the surrounding units, forms beautiful latticework (*mashrabiyya)*. The *minbar* also has a collection of epigraphic inscriptions that contain Qur'anic verses and an endowment (*waqf*) inscription of Nur al-Din Zangi and his son al-Salih, who accomplished what his father began. This is in addition to the inscriptions which bear the name of the craftsmen who made the *minbar*. The *minbar* of Nur al-Din is considered to be one of the most beautiful of the Islamic wooden *minbar*s.
040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.short_description: The remains of a *minbar* destroyed in 1969 in a fire that damaged al-Aqsa Mosque. The minbar was commissioned by Nur al-Din Zangi in Aleppo as a good omen for the conquest of Jerusalem. Salah al-Din (Saladin) undertook its transportation to Jerusalem. The pieces have rich vegetal and geometric decoration, interlocking and star-shaped panels and names of the craftsmen.
040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.initial_owner: Nur al-Din Zangi (ruled in Syria AH 541–69 / AD 1146–74) and Salih bin Nur al-Din Zangi, Salah al-Din Ayyubi (known as Saladin, r. AH 564–89 / AD 1169–93).
040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.dates: Construction of the *minbar* began in hegira 564 / AD 1169, and was completed in AH 570 / AD 1174.
040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.method_for_datation: The *minbar* is dated by the epigraphic inscriptions it bears, and a number of historical sources, some of the most important being those of Abu Shama (d. 665 / 1267) and Ibn al-Athir (d. 630 / 1223) and Mujir al-Din al-Hanbali (d. 927 / 1520).
040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.method_for_provenance: Aleppo was narrowed down as the place of production for the *minbar*, supported by both the epigraphic inscriptions on it and by historical sources.
040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.provenance: Custom-made in Aleppo, Syria for al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem.
040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.obtention: The *minbar* was transferred from al-Aqsa Mosque to the Islamic Museum after the fire of 1969.

0440ce02-52d9-59e9-9d80-0b24ab6725f0.name: Table.
0440ce02-52d9-59e9-9d80-0b24ab6725f0.description:
A low table made of wood inlaid with cloud-bands and simple arabesque compositions in ebony and mother-of-pearl; set into the top is an underglaze painted ceramic tile with a centralised design featuring flowers on an arabesque framework, surrounded by a border with cloud-bands on a turquoise background. The table has 12 sides, to match the 12 sides of the ceramic top, but it is constructed with spandrel-like joins between the legs so that it stands on six legs.  
  
This table is a rare example of furniture from the Ottoman imperial court, as well as a most unusual use of Iznik tilework. The beautiful, bright colours of the tile make a striking contrast to the subdued tones of the inlaid wood. It seems unlikely that such a fine piece of furniture would have been intended for everyday use; more likely, it was used as part of the elaborate ceremonials which defined Ottoman court protocol and impressed foreign ambassadors.
0440ce02-52d9-59e9-9d80-0b24ab6725f0.short_description: A table made of wood inlaid with ivory and mother-of-pearl, with a 12-sided Iznik tile serving as the top. A rare example of furniture from the Ottoman court, this splendid table may have been used in the elaborate ceremonials which defined court protocol and impressed visiting ambassadors.
0440ce02-52d9-59e9-9d80-0b24ab6725f0.type: Woodwork, mother of pearl, painted, glazed ceramic
0440ce02-52d9-59e9-9d80-0b24ab6725f0.method_for_datation: The technique, materials and style of the woodwork are similar to those found on the throne of Sultan Süleyman in the Topkapı Palace Museum in Istanbul. The tile, too, is similar to those found in Sultan Süleyman's mosque (completed in 963 / 1557), though its size and distinct shape mean it must have been made specifically as a table-top.
0440ce02-52d9-59e9-9d80-0b24ab6725f0.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period; Istanbul, as home to the imperial ateliers, may be where the wood was inlaid and the final product assembled.
0440ce02-52d9-59e9-9d80-0b24ab6725f0.bibliography:
Mitter, P. and Clunas, C., "The Empire of Things: The Engagement with the Orient", A Grand Design: The Art of the Victoria and Albert Museum (eds. M. Baker and B. Richardson), London, 1997, p.255.  
  
Stanley, T., with Rosser-Owen, M. and Vernoit, S., Palace and Mosque: Islamic Art from the Middle East, London, 2004, p.103.
0440ce02-52d9-59e9-9d80-0b24ab6725f0.author: Barry Wood

04d27671-b1ac-5ad5-85cb-254ee0e80def.name: Bridal cushion
04d27671-b1ac-5ad5-85cb-254ee0e80def.description: This bridal cushion from Ma’an, Jordan, traditionally prepared by a bride as part of her trousseau for her new home, is among the most distinctive examples of Jordanian domestic textiles. They feature embroidery patterns that are believed to reflect connections with the Caucasus, whether through historical travel, trade, or settlement. These motifs stand as a testament to Ma'an's role as a crossroads of cultural exchange, where influences from distant regions were absorbed into local artistic traditions.

06a3bee7-1756-596e-90e4-49becb64c66e.name: Royal Brigantine
06a3bee7-1756-596e-90e4-49becb64c66e.description:
Responsible for the construction and design, Torquato José Clavina was the foreman ship's carpenter at the Naval Arsenal, much admired for his skill and competence. The brigantine is a magnificent work in gilded wood, crafted by the artist Manuel Vieira, while on the broadside is a panel of zoomorphic elements over darkened gold. In the Queen Maria I style, the barge is painstakingly decorated with pinnacles, friezes, caryatides, flower-like ornaments and tile panels depicting vases of flowers in frames. On the posterior panel of the quarterdeck cabin, there is a painting of Pedro Alexandrino de Carvalho, who was responsible for painting the sovereign's private cabin. The quarterdeck cabin stands out from all the others for its richness and beauty, notably for the framed Venetian mirrors. The lower poop panel has complex and beautiful ornamentation: Amphitrite and Neptune are represented in two bas-reliefs surrounded by gilded-wood floral borders.  
On board were 78 paddlers with 40 oars, which made the barge glide through the water with the help of the boss and the bow oarsman. Throughout its history, the barge transported several monarchs and heads of state.  
With the first French invasion of November of 1807, the barge was assigned to take Queen Maria I and the rest of the royal family to the *Príncipe Real*, the ship on which they would escape to Brazil. Likewise, it was from this galley that King João VI disembarked in Lisbon following this turbulent period.  
Later, on his first State visit in 1903, King Edward VII of England chose his oldest ally: Portugal. The Royal Brigantine headed for the British ship HMS *Victoria and Albert* to receive the monarch. This visit was followed by series of other State visits, amongst which were the visits of Kaiser William II of Germany, Émille Loubet, President of the Republic of France, and King Albert I of Belgium. The brigantine was always present.  
During the Republic, the brigantine was neglected and did not glide over the river for 40 years. In 1957, on the occasion of the official visit of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, the barge crossed the waters of the Tagus for the last time.  
In 1963 it became part of the collection of the Museu de Marinha (Naval Museum) where it underwent restoration. The quality of the restoration saw the museum receive several honourable distinctions including that given by the World Ship Trust.
06a3bee7-1756-596e-90e4-49becb64c66e.short_description:
In 1780 Queen Maria I ordered the construction of a grand royal barge: the Royal Brigantine of Queen Maria I. Its construction was destined to celebrate the betrothal of Prince João (future King João VI) to the Spanish Princess Carlota Joaquina, in 1784.  
Symbol of power and a jewel of naval archeology, the brigantine represents more than 200 years of historical pageantry.
06a3bee7-1756-596e-90e4-49becb64c66e.method_for_datation: Technical and historical royal documentation in the Portuguese Naval Archives.
06a3bee7-1756-596e-90e4-49becb64c66e.obtention: In 1963 the Royal Brigantine and other royal barges were taken to the Naval Museum by order of the Naval Ministry of the time.

Silva, G. C., “A última missão do Bergantim Real”, *Revista da Armada*, Nos. 405 and 406 de Fevereiro e Março, 2007.

0703f771-513c-549f-8e72-02d81616e8d9.name: Captain's Pearl Chest containing his most precious possessions, including folding pearl gauges with 44 grades, knife for opening oysters, weight set and hand compass
0703f771-513c-549f-8e72-02d81616e8d9.short_description: This pearl merchant's chest, known in the region as bishtakha, was an indispensable item of a pearl merchant's profession, as it contained not only all his equipment, but also his valuable bags of pearls. Made of hardwood and often elaborately decorated, these chests could come in different sizes and were designed to hold pearling scales with their agate weights, scoops, graded sieves, small discrete boxes for cash - often hidden in secret compartments - bags of pearls and the so-called chao book, used to calculate - by means of detailed tables - the value of specific pearls on the basis of their weight.

07cfbb4a-25e5-5ae3-a64e-9de990ccf477.name: Bridal cushion
07cfbb4a-25e5-5ae3-a64e-9de990ccf477.description: This bridal cushion from Ma'an, traditionally prepared by a bride as part of her trousseau for her new home, reflects the town’s position as a crossroads of cultural exchange. Its embroidered designs and use of ikat textiles reveal connections with wider textile traditions from Central Asia, Turkey, and Syria, where ikat weaving was historically widespread and highly developed. These influences reached Ma'an through networks of travel, trade, pilgrimage, and migration, becoming integrated into local practices.

0a76c8b6-966d-5ed5-a3d7-707a07c8ea48.short_description: This storage chest is the finest one that has been preserved of a small group of pieces of furniture with mother-of-pearl inlays in lacquer - all from Gujarat. The lid is decorated with a spiral ornamentation that helps us date it. An identical mother-of-pearl decoration is found on a canopy made in 1608-1609 for the grave of the Sufi sheikh Nizam al-Din Awliya in Delhi.

0b5ea864-f20c-51f8-b510-3ee37516c735.name: Door lintel.
0b5ea864-f20c-51f8-b510-3ee37516c735.description:
A door lintel, decorated with a very deep, undercut floral pattern comprising a central rosette flanked by intertwined foliage, scrolls filled with palmettes, pines and grapes, all arranged in a panel surrounded by pearling.  
  
This type of floral pattern was very common during the Umayyad period and is seen throughout the decorative arts. Similar carved patterns adorned the Qasr al-Mushatta (now at the Pergamon Museum, Berlin).  
  
The function of this lintel is purely aesthetic; it would reside on the upper part of a decorated doorway.
0b5ea864-f20c-51f8-b510-3ee37516c735.short_description: Door lintel from Qasr al-Tuba bearing a very deep, undercut floral pattern with a central rosette that was common during the Umayyad period and is seen throughout the decorative arts. Such elaborate lintels would have been positioned on the upper parts of decorated doorways.
0b5ea864-f20c-51f8-b510-3ee37516c735.dimensions: Height 44 cm, length 2.18 m, depth 42.5 cm.
0b5ea864-f20c-51f8-b510-3ee37516c735.method_for_datation: The lintel was a part of a building, dated approximately to the 2nd / 8th century; the date has also been established through historical inferences.

0b61c9ae-ef04-5d1e-af0b-b7e4ab248173.name: Type-writing machine
0b61c9ae-ef04-5d1e-af0b-b7e4ab248173.short_description: Dimitrija Chupovski (1878-1940) was born in Papradishte near Veles, R. Macedonia in 1878. He lived in Krushevo and acquired his education in Belgrade and St. Petersburg. He was a renowned Macedonian lexicographer, textbook writer and philologist who prepared the modern grammar of Macedonian language. Chupovski also worked out the first Macedonian-Russian dictionary.

0be609b8-eaa5-59f2-a721-5797ecc66645.name: Silver-inlaid brass Qur’an stand
0be609b8-eaa5-59f2-a721-5797ecc66645.short_description: This stand is an example of Mamluk revivalist work, made during an age that encouraged the nationalistic reappraisal of indigenous heritage. It copies a famous Mamluk Qur’an stand in the Museum of Arab Art in Cairo, inscribed with the name of the Mamluk Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun (r. AD 1294-1340) and made by Muhammad ibn Sunqur al-Baghdadi.
0be609b8-eaa5-59f2-a721-5797ecc66645.dates: Hegira late 13th century / AD late 19th century
keywords: Qur'an stand; Neo Mamluk; Mamluk Revival; silver; metalwork; inlay; furnishing; revivalism

0c359028-43e3-559c-a7ca-c955341c48c8.name: Wood panels (walls and ceiling) of Syrian Room
0c359028-43e3-559c-a7ca-c955341c48c8.short_description: In the late 1970s, Doris Duke acquired a variety of components that were said to have come from a house owned by the Quwatlis, a prominent merchant family of Damascus. Combining historic elements with new pieces made in Hawai‘i by local craftsmen, Duke and her staff created an interior that conveys the spatial layout and multi-media, multi-sensory experience of the Syrian *qa‘a* (Arabic: hall), a reception room found in affluent courtyard homes of the late Ottoman period (in Syria: 1516–1918).

0c62c358-069e-5101-ad0e-063173c5eefc.name: Chair
0c62c358-069e-5101-ad0e-063173c5eefc.description: This chair, known as *jamuga* in the Spanish tradition, is most certainly a Moresque European piece designed from a combination of pattern books. The chair consists of a great widely decorated back and a curved seat with two arms. The four legs are delicately ornamented. The inscriptions probably have been taken from a design book or other visual model too, rather than being designed by an Arab master calligrapher. The decorated panels, aesthetically pleasing, are imprecise in terms of execution and calligraphic style.
0c62c358-069e-5101-ad0e-063173c5eefc.author: Cecilia Casas Desantes, Cristina Giménez
keywords: Production of applied arts in Europe in the Islamic mode; Orientalism

0e4a2c60-95e1-53b1-b364-83013292b0c9.name: Qur’an Stand
0e4a2c60-95e1-53b1-b364-83013292b0c9.short_description:
This Qur’an stand would elevate larger holy books to prevent direct contact with the unclean surface of the ground. The pigmented wood structure from India features deep floral carvings.  
  
Mughal-style carvings with rows of florals and vines adorn the Qur’an stand in geometric precision. While Islamic woodwork in India remains widely understudied, the lobed arches of the legs remind of Mughal architecture. Furthermore, the woodwork of the Mughal Empire rarely bears inscriptions, hindering an accurate dating and study of clusters of pieces.  
  
These stands still cradle Qur’ans in affluent homes, mosques, Islamic schools (*madrasa*), and in tombs for recitation and display purposes.
0e4a2c60-95e1-53b1-b364-83013292b0c9.owner: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani
0e4a2c60-95e1-53b1-b364-83013292b0c9.method_for_datation: The date and origin were established in research-based comparison from an examination of material, colour, engraving and pattern.

0e56903a-9b5a-5b71-84c1-c4e82186198b.name: Yoke (*nīr*)
0e56903a-9b5a-5b71-84c1-c4e82186198b.description: This yoke was used for animals to raise water from a *zājrah* well. Donkeys and bullocks typically work side-by-side to pull together against the weight of the water.

0e93c801-4f27-5f79-b617-0e699aabf827.name: Wooden panel
0e93c801-4f27-5f79-b617-0e699aabf827.short_description: Wooden panel from a door with vegetal decoration, in high relief, forming a calyx-shaped ornament from which spring spiralling leaves. The panel is representative of the transitional stage characterised by the bevelled technique to the next phase of which a distinctive example is the door presented by Caliph al-Hakim to the mosque of Al-Azhar in 1010.
keywords: Panel; Wood

0ed94ac3-d966-5b35-beee-4763d3799155.name: Table clock
0ed94ac3-d966-5b35-beee-4763d3799155.description: An example of a richly decorated table clock decorated with alabaster columns, the popularity for which spread at the end of the 18th century in Pest, Buda and Óbuda. Richly decorated table clocks such as this one were common in the late 18th century and this type with a column decoration shows the stylistic change that took place at the end of the century, marking a transition towards Neo-Classicism. Architectural elements such as this were often used instead of ornate decoration once the Neo-Classical style took hold. From among similar clocks preserved in the collection at the Budapest History  Museum, this example is one of the most characteristic and richly decorated. It is signed by the clockmaker, Johann Kerbacher.
0ed94ac3-d966-5b35-beee-4763d3799155.short_description: This richly decorated table clock is a rare example documenting the mastery of Johan Kerbacher, whose signed clocks made in his workshop in Óbuda (Old Buda) are known from the second half of the 18th century. The alabaster-column decoration was a frequently used motif in the period, which popularity spread at the end of the 18th century in Pest, Buda and Óbuda, and marked the transition to Neo-Classicism.
0ed94ac3-d966-5b35-beee-4763d3799155.method_for_datation: on the basis of the signature on the clock
0ed94ac3-d966-5b35-beee-4763d3799155.bibliography: *Budapest az Újkorban* (*Budapest in the Modern Times*), (ed. G. Szvoboda Dománszky), Budapest, 1995, p. 22.
0ed94ac3-d966-5b35-beee-4763d3799155.author: Terézia Bardi, Beatrix Basics
keywords: Applied art; timekeeping; Neo-Classicism; enamel; alabaster; gilding; silver; gold; metalwork; Johann Kerbacher; Óbuda; furnishing; workshop

0fca5a3a-17d8-542b-bada-abe14d89b5ed.name: Carved wooden chest
0fca5a3a-17d8-542b-bada-abe14d89b5ed.description: A carved wooden chest with painted geometric and floral decoration, it illustrates the decorative styles that began to appear in the 19th century and also how industrial colours, imported from Europe, were being used.
keywords: Craftsmanship; traditional craftsmanship; Moroccan craftsmen; woodwork; carving; trade; raw material; industrial colours; geometric decoration; floral decoration; geometric motifs; floral motifs; vegetal decoration; vegetal motifs; furniture

1028751a-07f0-53c2-8d14-e1b298d6e008.name: Board
1028751a-07f0-53c2-8d14-e1b298d6e008.description: Qur'anic board used in the African *madrasas* (schools), places where the first verses of the Qur'an are learned, under the direction of the *marabout* (teacher). The learning method consists of copying and reciting the different verses of the Qur'an, in a process of memorisation, which allows the students to erase them and then to write the following verses. The *alluha* (table of wood), the reed, and the ink are the only available pedagogic materials of the Qur'anic schools in the rural areas. The Qur'anic boards turn into documents that preserve the written personality of those who used them, the irregularity of the letter, the crooked lines, the hesitations, the corrected mistakes, the erased lines that refuse to disappear, as a register of a period of effort and domain of skills typical of the school stage.
keywords: Wood; education; Qur´an

112c53a7-9492-5a54-9745-591f4c96202c.name: Hand-held plough (*haīs*)
112c53a7-9492-5a54-9745-591f4c96202c.description: Ploughing with a *haīs* is the first stage in the traditional cultivation process. The *haīs* is drawn by a draft animal, usually a bullock. A ploughman walks along behind, using a sturdy guide rope and verbal commands to steer the animal while directing the path of the *haīs* by means of a tall wooden handle.

114c06c2-280f-51d2-a9f9-1733b739488a.name: *Kuttab* (Qur'an school).
114c06c2-280f-51d2-a9f9-1733b739488a.description: A *kuttab* is an educational establishment where children are taught to memorise the Holy Qur'an, the rudiments of the Arabic language and arithmetic. The *kuttab,* seen here is made up of two sides (forming an L-shape) and a ceiling. One side (facing) is composed of a door decorated with geometric designs, and assembled in parts. Towards the left of it, are four storage areas or cupboards, two on each side, separated by a deep niche where the teacher would sit. The cupboard doors are ornamented with geometric designs composed of star-shaped medallions executed in the same manner as that used to embellish the door. On the two sides of the niche, and above it, are 29 small compartments framed within lobed arches which were used to store educational equipment. The lower area of this side of the *kuttab* is adorned with an assemblage of various decorations. Above this whole area, at the top, there is a rectangle with seven panels. Each is filled with various shapes of turned wooden elements and is separated from the neighbouring panels with balusters of turned wood. On the right-hand side of the *kuttab* there are two cupboards decorated in a similar fashion as the other storage areas. These two cupboards are surrounded by 12 small compartments with lobed niches; to the left of them there is a plain, undecorated door. The ceiling is ornamented with geometric designs made up of parts of star-like medallions executed by superimposing thin wooden bars. Below it is a frame composed of *muqarnas* pendentives. The *kuttab* also contains some recent decorative additions.
114c06c2-280f-51d2-a9f9-1733b739488a.short_description: A *kuttab* is an educational establishment for teaching children to memorise the Holy Qur'an, reading and writing. A *kuttab* was usually situated on the second floor of a *sabil* (water dispensary). This particular example was taken from a building in Rosetta, a city in the north of the Nile delta.
114c06c2-280f-51d2-a9f9-1733b739488a.dimensions: Height 340 cm, length 465 cm, width 215 cm.
114c06c2-280f-51d2-a9f9-1733b739488a.method_for_datation: The techniques of assemblage and superimposition of small wooden parts in the construction of wooden objects was widespread during the Ottoman period of the 16th and 17th centuries, and was used especially for the decoration of household objects and ceilings in the domestic context. Amongst the residences where this style of construction and decoration are utilised are the Bayt al-Suhaymi (1058 / 1648), and the residence of Waqf al-Sadat (1070 / 1659), both of which are in the city of Cairo. These techniques were also used in the construction of *minbars* (pulpits) and *dikkat al-muballigh* (recitation platforms) in mosques during the Ottoman era.
114c06c2-280f-51d2-a9f9-1733b739488a.method_for_provenance: Provenance is supported by information in the archives of the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo.
114c06c2-280f-51d2-a9f9-1733b739488a.obtention: The piece was transferred to the museum from the residence of al-Mazdini in Rashid, (Rosetta), Egypt, but the history of its transportation is not known.
114c06c2-280f-51d2-a9f9-1733b739488a.bibliography:
Khalifa, Rabi' H., *Funun al-Qahira fi al-'ahd al-Othmani \[Arts of Cairo during the Ottoman Era*\], Cairo, 1985.  
Mustafa, M., *Dalil Mathaf al-fan al-Islami \[Guide to the Museum of Islamic Art*\], Cairo, 1978.
114c06c2-280f-51d2-a9f9-1733b739488a.author: Salah Sayour
keywords: Furnishing; wood; turned wood; geometric decoration; kuttab; education; religious schools; architectural decoration
materials: Ornamental wooden decoration using assemblage, interlocking and superimposition of wooden bars; turned woodwork.

1182b4e7-198f-51a0-b819-4ec5360c27f8.name: Casket
1182b4e7-198f-51a0-b819-4ec5360c27f8.description: This casket was displayed in the exhibition about Islamic Art held in Munich in 1910. Afterwards it was acquired by Lázaro Galdiano, one of the most important Spanish art collectors. It is important to note Lazaro Galdiano's interest in and art appraisal of objects from the Spanish Muslim period. He was one of the earliest collectors of Arab art in Spain.

13838f38-9d4c-5ce5-b63d-fabe43b3504a.name: «Holbein table»
13838f38-9d4c-5ce5-b63d-fabe43b3504a.description: The table known as the «Holbein table« is one of the most important and most mysterious items in the furniture collection. Until 1965 it was attributed to the Basle painter Hans Holbein the Younger. It was only investigations by the Swiss National Museum in Zurich that revealed the true name of the artist as Hans Herbst. Painted table tops were a popular form of art in the Renaissance. They told stories, but above all represented the expert art knowledge and importance of the person who commissioned them, who has immortalised himself with a coat of arms and that of his wife in the middle of the table. They were Hans Bär and Katharina Brunner. Bär was a textile merchant in Basle and enlisted with foreign armies in the important function of standard bearer. He was killed at the battle of Marignano in 1515. The black background of the table imitates a slate on which various objects have been drawn, which, at a closer glance, turns out to be six allegorical scenes. To achieve as true-tolife an impression as possible, the artist used the trompel’oeil technique, creating an optical illusion, and distributed random objects across the table top such as playing cards, a pair of spectacles and a seal stamp bearing his name.
13838f38-9d4c-5ce5-b63d-fabe43b3504a.method_for_datation: Inscription on the painting on the surface of the table
keywords: Holbein Tisch; Hans Herbst; Basle; Basel; Furniture; Alegorien; Stadtbibliothek; Zentralbibliothek Zürich; Painting; Coat of Arms

1477ac86-b5c4-5cf6-bb7a-c80c93766095.name: Rosette from Ibn Tulun's Minbar at the mosque of Sultan Lagin
1477ac86-b5c4-5cf6-bb7a-c80c93766095.short_description: The Ibn Tulun Mosque in Cairo was erected in the late ninth century and renovated and remodelled under Sultan Lagin 1296. The *minbar* of the Ibn Tulun mosque is one of the most pre-eminent works of Egyptian applied arts.

148b5238-d0f6-5a73-ade6-65b1ffbc8ca4.name: Palanquin
148b5238-d0f6-5a73-ade6-65b1ffbc8ca4.short_description:
The palanquin from India, a symbol of royal power, is comprised of a wooden compartment with a woven floor and roof resembling an arch or two oyster halves seated on large poles. Engraved decorations, various shapes and motifs enhance the carriage. Thin drapes protect from prying eyes and cover the fortune carried inside the carriage. Only men of certain castes or elephants were allowed to bear the palanquin transporting royals on long journeys and brides to their wedding ceremony.  
  
Across the Arabian Peninsula, palanquins receive the name *howdah* (*hawdaj*,) and carried Bedouin women on a camel’s back, frequently appearing in the poetry of the Murrah tribe. Since 1266, another variation called *mahmal* ceremonially transferred the cover of the Kaaba with the Egyptian pilgrimage to Mecca. Today, palanquins might be represented as the predecessors of bullet-proof cars with tinted windows, escorting royals and their entourage.

14d23909-007c-5bfe-ba51-0f21c11eaef4.name: Namban Oratory
14d23909-007c-5bfe-ba51-0f21c11eaef4.description:
This rectangular oratory surmounted by a triangular pediment with the monogram *IHS* (the abbreviation of the Greek *IHSOUS*, or JESUS) located at the centre, has two side-panels enclosing a painting of the Virgin Mary holding the infant Jesus. Although the lacquer decoration presents a predominantly Japanese ornamental grammar – especially a floral one – both its form and the iconography embody Christian cultural references. The pictorial image is itself an example of the possible interaction between the Jesuit painting school – operating in Japan since the 1580s – and the Japanese pupils that quickly demonstrated skill in Western-style painting.  
As it is, such a hybrid object, that crosses different artistic backgrounds, could only have been made during the Portuguese presence in Japan, during the period spanning approximately 1549 to 1640.  
The oratory is mentioned in the *Inventário Artístico de Santarém* (Santarém Artistic Inventory) as Indo-Portuguese lacquer work. Such misinformation reveals how, in the middle of the 20th century, such an item was unfamiliar to the European public in general, but that was not the case in the late 16th and beginning of the 17th century, at least not for the Portuguese elite. Such a statement can only be based on the remaining objects – with or without associated painting – the number of which has expanded increasingly during the last three decades (this example did not come to light until 1985). A fact that also draws attention to the demands of the Iberian market for these objects at the time.  
The Sardoal Oratory has the particularity of being associated with a religious space, thanks to an inscription located on the altar of Nossa Senhora da Esperança in the Church of Nossa Senhora da Caridade. This text, dated 1670, is the earliest known reference in Portugal to a reminiscent *Namban* object.

153c5ddb-dd1d-5e3c-9e80-de0b66684f95.name: Parts of a *minbar*.
153c5ddb-dd1d-5e3c-9e80-de0b66684f95.description:
These elements of the facing of the *minbar* are formed by two distinctive parts. The first one consists of two longitudinal panels from the upper parts of the lateral faces of the *minbar*. Their surfaces, divided into sections and surmounted by an arch, are decorated with stacks of pinecones and acanthus rosettes borrowed from Abbasid flora. The panels are framed by a band bearing an inscription in angular *kufic* script also in an Eastern style. The inscription in the right panel, whose spandrels are adorned with half-sprays of acanthus, includes the date the Fatimids founded the *minbar*. The one in the left panel shows Qur'anic texts from verse 36 of Sura 24, 'The light'.  
The second part includes the three elements from the back.  
The top, arched panel is topped by an inscription in *kufic* script, which indicates the name of the Umayyad patron and the date the *minbar* was repaired. Its surface, framed by a border of small floral medallions, is decorated in two styles: the upper section is occupied in the centre by a rectangular panel with a poly-lobed arch with floral medallions and on the sides by festoon acanthus rosettes. The lower section is adorned with an acanthus rosette flanked by poly-lobed medallions containing polygonal knotwork based on an eight-pointed star.  
The rectangular middle part, bordered with a votive inscription, is adorned with a central motif of tiered chevrons with palm foliage and serrated acanthus rosettes inscribed in squares.  
The lower part is decorated with half-balusters in turned and painted wood, glued on a slab.  
These facings, which illustrate a historic period of Morocco when two political and religious movements fought for the hegemony of the country, play an important role in the history of Moroccan art, which, from that time forward, would be influenced both from the East and from Andalusia.
153c5ddb-dd1d-5e3c-9e80-de0b66684f95.short_description: These *minbar* parts illustrate a historical episode and the beginnings of Islamic art in Morocco, when Fatimids and Córdoban Umayyads were fighting for control of the country. The Fatimids incorporated Eastern decoration when making the *minbar*, and the Umayyads added Western elements when converting it.

155d1175-57c1-5993-9a33-680636e74497.name: Cosmetic case for a man
155d1175-57c1-5993-9a33-680636e74497.short_description: The craft of lacquer work was widely practised in Iran from the 16th to the 19th century. Master artists in Esfahan or Teheran supplied the lacquer work for the court and the upper circles of society. The main subjects illustrated are: life at court, the legendary history of Iran and religious themes based on the Qur'an and the Old and New Testaments. The mirror and cosmetic case is a nice example of the considerable influence European Baroque painting had on Iranian lacquer work particularly during the Qajar epoch.

178f74aa-fe42-524b-94f2-f5d4a1c1bd50.name: Processional Altar of St. John the Evangelist
178f74aa-fe42-524b-94f2-f5d4a1c1bd50.description:
A silver processional altar made at the beginning of the 18th century, which belonged to the Royal Monastery of Our Lady of Conception, and was used in the Procession of the Holy Sacrament in Beja. The social and religious significance of the Corpus Christi Day procession cannot be understated; it represents one of the greatest manifestations of the Portuguese Baroque, which once acknowledged, justifies the sumptuousness of some of the pieces used in these ceremonies. Traditionally, up until 1893, the altar was carried by farmers.  
Rectangular in shape, the *acroteria* (small bases placed at the four extremities) has a beaded edging, and four *albarradas* or ornamental vases, alternate with smaller jars in the middle. The entirety is covered with vegetable and scalloped-shell ornamentation, and St. James' crosses. The wooden carrying rods are also silver plated.  
The octagonal shaped pedestal stands over the main body, decorated with double scalloped-shell ornamentation, pear-shaped “tables” and St. James' crosses. There is also an octagonal platform with small jars placed at each corner of the pedestal.  
An iron column rises above the pedestal, covered with silk cloth embroidered with gold thread. It meets a gold and silver halo embellished with precious stones above which a gold and silver crown rests, also studded with precious stones. In the middle of the altarpiece, the Martyrdom of St. John the Evangelist is played out, the saint graphically shown immersed in boiling olive oil. The wooden effigy of the saint with clasped hands looks straight up at the sky. The silver boiler, standing on a silver tripod above the fire, is kept alight by two multicoloured wooden figures, kneeling at either side of the boiler. One of them is blowing and the other is using a solid-silver pitchfork.  
The patrons of the altarpiece were a group of nuns devoted to St. John the Evangelist. There was another group of nuns in the same convent that devoted themselves to St. John the Baptist and commissioned a similar processional altar in honour of the saint. In fact, both altarpieces date from the beginning of the 18th century and were made in the same workshop. They both show the same crowned stamps of the city of Lisbon and the same maker's letter “M”.
178f74aa-fe42-524b-94f2-f5d4a1c1bd50.short_description: A silver processional altar made at the beginning of the 18th century, it portrays features typical of the Portuguese Baroque at the time of King João V. Designed to represent the Martyrdom of St. John the Evangelist, the piece belonged to the Royal Monastery of Our Lady of Conception and was used in the procession of the Holy Sacrament in Beja, on Corpus Christi Day.

17a2e88a-66ac-57c9-918e-1dc52eb70372.name: Chest
17a2e88a-66ac-57c9-918e-1dc52eb70372.short_description: This large wood rectangular trunk with a back-hinged lid is supported on four legs joined by a scalloped apron. The trunk is extensively inlaid with mother-of-pearl on its top, front, sides, and base. On the front, a flower and vase motif and a floral spray flank a central lattice-filled roundel. A highly ornate trefoil and geometric band runs along the edges of the central panel. The interior is unornamented with one compartment at left and two small shelves at right.

19a79dbf-5845-53ed-a137-ee4c74fd1299.name: Inkpot and blotter
19a79dbf-5845-53ed-a137-ee4c74fd1299.short_description: Dimitrija Chupovski (1878-1940) devoted his life to raising the awareness of Macedonians about their national identity. He worked actively on the recognition of Macedonian as distinct Slavic language and prepared the grammar of the modern Macedonian language. He also contributed to opening schools for children in Macedonia to learn in their native language.

19c131a2-1764-5332-adc2-8dd10e15a0f0.name: Fragment of wooden ceiling.
19c131a2-1764-5332-adc2-8dd10e15a0f0.description: The ceiling, made of interlocking panels, is divided into geometric shapes by a frame with mouldings that intersect and intertwine with one another, creating squares or diamonds containing an eight-pointed star in their centre. The internal parts are carved richly and meticulously in arabesques, to form lace-like patterns. The decoration is made up of plant motifs and animals carved in full relief, including lions, gazelles, hares, birds of prey attacking their quarry and eagles with their wings outstretched. This type of decoration, with a highly worked background and the bands of the frame moulded with a simple geometric motif, is the same as is found in the more stylised stucco and plaster slabs from the medieval church of San Giuliano di Caltagirone, possibly used as decorative architectural dividers between the apse and the nave, or as an altar. The ceiling, which undoubtedly originated in a shared residence and may have come from the Royal Palace itself (suggested by the presence of figurative subjects as well as the traditional geometrical decorative motifs and arabesques) is an example of Fatimid ‘frozen realism’ (Scerrato 1979).
19c131a2-1764-5332-adc2-8dd10e15a0f0.short_description: Ceiling decorated with plant motifs and carved figures of common animals such as lions, gazelles and hares. Created by Fatimid craftsmen, this example almost certainly came from the Royal Palace.

1b9f2cfd-d948-5273-a47b-a0eb83cc7069.name: Qur'an stand (*kursi*)
1b9f2cfd-d948-5273-a47b-a0eb83cc7069.short_description: This tall, hexagonal brass side table has a flat top, six-sided body, and six baluster-shaped feet. The table is inlaid with inscriptional panels offset by engraved or pierced vegetal patterns. The sides are composed of several panels inset within a frame. This stand may originally have been used to support the Qur’an as it was read. For protection, the Qur’an could be stored inside the stand by opening the small doors and placing the text within.

1ca4ae5b-e753-59d1-a5de-423460efb5d1.name: Iconostasis in the Church of the Holy Saviour
1ca4ae5b-e753-59d1-a5de-423460efb5d1.short_description: This iconostasis was created by one of the greatest Macedonian masters of woodcarving, Petre Filipovski Garka, who formed his own group of artisans and developed his outstanding style of wood-carving, which was widely recognizable in the Balkans in the early 19th century. This exquisite piece of wood-carving was made from walnut in the technique of high relief. The iconostasis depicts scenes from the Old and the New Testament in which biblical figures are rendered wearing traditional costumes worn in Macedonia. The detail shows the self-portraits of Petre Filipovski and his associate artisans.

1cc24be1-3e5f-5a9b-babb-1317370820d2.name: Walls and ceiling of the Damascus Room
1cc24be1-3e5f-5a9b-babb-1317370820d2.short_description: The Damascus Room consists of eighteenth-century *‘ajami* wood panelling (four walls and a ceiling), which would have originally decorated a reception room (typically known as a *qa‘a*) of an affluent courtyard home in Syria. It is a quintessential example of late-Ottoman Syrian architectural decoration reconstituted to meet the needs of a twentieth-century environment and collector.

1d94b78b-1988-5dfa-9032-f8a590336d06.name: Chest from Palencia Cathedral.
1d94b78b-1988-5dfa-9032-f8a590336d06.description: Wood core and leather chest, covered with ivory plates and arrises (edges) reinforced with enamelled copper. It has a prismatic structure and a coffin-shaped lid. The fretwork ivory plates are finely decorated with chiaroscuro plant arabesques, formed by fan- and ring-shaped leaves and palmettes interspersed with peacocks, gazelles and griffins facing one another. The traditional themes of a lion attacking a deer and crossbowmen hunting also appear. The decoration is completed by an inscription in florid *kufic* characters that reads: 'In the name of God the Clement and the Merciful. Everlasting blessing, complete protection, constant peace, lasting fortune, renewed benefits, glory, wealth, constant favour and the hope to be heard, for its owner, may God prolong his life. Of that which was made in the city of Cuenca, under the orders of *hajib* Hisham al-Dawla Abu Muhammad son of al-Ma'mun Dhu'l-Majdayn, son of al-Zafir Dhu'l-Riyasatayn, Abi Muhammad son of Dhi'l-Nun, may Allah enlighten him! in the year one and forty and four hundred. The work of 'Abd al-Rahman bin Zaywan'. Although it would be inaccurate to speak of an ivory workshop in Cuenca, the creation of three 11th-century chests has nonetheless been documented: one from Silos (1026) which is now in the Museum of Burgos (Spain), this chest from Palencia (1049–50) and the box from Narbonne Cathedral (France), from a similar period as this one.
1d94b78b-1988-5dfa-9032-f8a590336d06.short_description: The work on the ivory plates that cover this wooden chest was taken from the Caliphate tradition, although the relief is lower and the interpretation of its decorative plant and hunting scenes more schematic. It was made in Cuenca for one of the sons of the king of Toledo.
1d94b78b-1988-5dfa-9032-f8a590336d06.dimensions: Height 23 cm, width 34 cm, depth 23 cm.
1d94b78b-1988-5dfa-9032-f8a590336d06.method_for_datation: The chest, signed by ‘Abd al-Rahman bin Zaywan, is dated 441 / 1049–50.
1d94b78b-1988-5dfa-9032-f8a590336d06.method_for_provenance: It takes its name from Palencia Cathedral where it was found in use as a reliquary. However, we know from the inscription that it was made in Cuenca, which at that time belonged to the Taifa of Toledo.
1d94b78b-1988-5dfa-9032-f8a590336d06.obtention: The chest was donated to the National Archaeological Museum by the Bishop and Chapter of Palencia Cathedral on 14 December 1911.

1e282c8c-3fed-5331-b88b-4c2782ff7968.name: Fragment of a painted wooden panel.
1e282c8c-3fed-5331-b88b-4c2782ff7968.description:
In Palace B in the Raqqa region, we find a group of applied ornamental techniques executed in various materials. These include the use of plaster frames for doors and windows as well as wooden panels to cover walls and ceilings of formal imperial halls. Similar forms and techniques existed in the Umayyad period and may be found in Qasr al-Hayr al-Gharbi. This indicates a continuation of this type of palatial decoration between the Umayyad and Abbasid periods.  
This rectangular fragment from a painted wooden panel is decorated with stylised floral and vegetal motifs bracketed by geometric designs. The decoration is executed in black, red, yellow and brown applied in gradual shades to make the drawings seem three-dimensional.
1e282c8c-3fed-5331-b88b-4c2782ff7968.short_description: A painted wooden panel that once decorated the reception hall of an 'Abbasid palace in Raqqa reveals a high degree of expertise in three-dimensional shading of floral motifs.
1e282c8c-3fed-5331-b88b-4c2782ff7968.method_for_datation: The object was found in Palace B in the Raqqa region. An inscription on plaster was found on one of the walls of the palace associating it with the Abbasid Caliph al-Mu'tasim Billah (r. 218–27/ 833–42). The palace is thought to have been built in around 220 (835).
1e282c8c-3fed-5331-b88b-4c2782ff7968.method_for_provenance: This piece of architectural ornamentation was found in palace B in the Raqqa region and was probably made *in situ*.
1e282c8c-3fed-5331-b88b-4c2782ff7968.obtention: The object was recovered during archaeological excavations carried out in 1952 by the Syrian General Directorate of Antiquities under the direction of Nasib Salibi.

1ea97525-6563-5427-9f6b-2069ec80926d.name: Pencase
1ea97525-6563-5427-9f6b-2069ec80926d.short_description:
Little is known of the painter Muhammad Yusuf. As his signature attests, he was the son of Muhammad Zaman (active Hegira ca. 1072-1105 / AD ca. 1662-1694). Besides the pencase presented here, only two others are known, both of which are in the Museum of Decorative Arts in Tehran. Like his better-known brother Muhammad ʿAli, he apparently specialised in lacquer paintings. A fourth work is part of the so-called Plovtsova Album in St. Petersburg (VP-7153); it is dated Hegira 1108 (AD 1696/97) and so far the oldest known and published work by Muhammad Yusuf.  
  
The pencase shows a sumptuously dressed young woman in a landscape on the front. With its many Europeanising motifs, it is typical of the landscapes of Muhammad Zaman and his brother Haji Muhammad (active Hegira 1084-1124 / AD 1673-1712). The young woman, on the other hand, goes back to a figure type that was popular in Safavid Persia from around 1660 to the late 1680s. "Invented" by Bahram Sofrakish (active Hegira 1030-1050s / AD 1621-1640s) probably in the Deccan in South India, he brought it to Isfahan around 1640, where it was further developed by Shaykh ʿAbbasi (active Hegira 1057-1094 / AD 1647-1683) and then taken up by other painters. The sides of the pencase are decorated with an array of different flowers. Such "flower portraits" are first found in the work of Shafiʿ Abbasi (active Hegira 1040-1066 / AD 1631-1656), and are later incorporated into the work of Muhammad Zaman and especially his brother.
1ea97525-6563-5427-9f6b-2069ec80926d.method_for_provenance: Information of previous owner was provided by Christie's, where the object was bought in 2017.

1f803c2c-5108-54ea-bfed-5c226d537a0e.name: Mirror
1f803c2c-5108-54ea-bfed-5c226d537a0e.description:
The mirror, which has a gilded wooden frame and ground-glass edges with flower and plant ornaments, is probably the work of one of the numerous glass workshops on the island of Murano, near Venice. Its form most probably suited the sophisticated taste of the European nobility. There are similar mirrors in many manors and museum collections today.  
Unfortunately, the original owner is unknown.  
Exhibited in the Baroque salon of the permanent collection of Varaždin’s Gothic-Renaissance castle, the mirror, together with other items of the collection, present the visitor with the most representative trends and refined atmosphere of the Baroque period in Varaždin.
1f803c2c-5108-54ea-bfed-5c226d537a0e.short_description: The mirror, which has a gilded wooden frame and ground-glass edges with flower and plant ornaments, is probably the work of one of the numerous glass workshops on the island of Murano, near Venice. It is representative of the trends and refined atmosphere of the Baroque period in Varaždin.

204c2ab2-db81-52a6-a76c-ac1ed90fe523.name: Window screen.
204c2ab2-db81-52a6-a76c-ac1ed90fe523.description:
A wooden panel consisting of a framed latticework is called a *mashrabiyya*. The area of this *mashrabiyya* is structured in three zones formed by carved frames of different sizes. Each zone is filled with a geometric design of woodwork. The vertical and horizontal bars of the outer area are combined with diagonals arranged in the same direction in each row giving the impression of a stem and leaf pattern. In contrast, the diagonal bars of the second zone lead away radially from an oval centre forming a pattern of abstract flowers. The hinged aperture situated in the upper part of the second zone is filled with a latticework consisting of round junctions, each with four diagonal bars leading away radially.  
The outer frame of the panel, assembled in a different way from the frame of the aperture, might be not original. The ledges are of various widths and are not carved like the two inner ones.  
Wooden latticework panels are intended to serve as windows onto the inner courtyard of a house or onto the street.
204c2ab2-db81-52a6-a76c-ac1ed90fe523.short_description: Wooden panel consisting of a framed latticework, called *mashrabiyya*. The latticework is formed by vertical, horizontal and diagonal bars arranged in geometrical patterns. *Mashrabiyyas* serve as windows onto the courtyard of the house or onto the street.
204c2ab2-db81-52a6-a76c-ac1ed90fe523.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
204c2ab2-db81-52a6-a76c-ac1ed90fe523.owner: National Museum of Fine Arts, Stockholm. In order to reorganise the expanding collections, the main part of the Islamic collection has been on permanent loan to the Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities since 1982.
204c2ab2-db81-52a6-a76c-ac1ed90fe523.method_for_datation: The dating of this object is difficult. The latticework shows no specific features. Since the acquisition is also unknown, there is no *terminus ante quem*. Furthermore, it lacks a comparative study of the decorative patterns to establish a certain dating. To date, the only feature is the rough surface that could be evidence of a dating earlier than the 13th / 19th century.
204c2ab2-db81-52a6-a76c-ac1ed90fe523.method_for_provenance: Window screens housed in the Louvre Museum, Paris, for which an Egyptian provenance seems to be proved, show a similar structure and design to this screen.
204c2ab2-db81-52a6-a76c-ac1ed90fe523.obtention: Gift to the National Museum of Fine Arts from the estate of Björkman, Paris.
204c2ab2-db81-52a6-a76c-ac1ed90fe523.bibliography:

Lane-Pool, S., *The Art of the Saracens in Egypt*, London, 1886.
204c2ab2-db81-52a6-a76c-ac1ed90fe523.author: Friederike Voigt
keywords: Mashrabiyya; architecture; woodwork; latticework; geometric design

20ddf7d0-c8c3-5985-8cd5-4be93c3b922b.name: Qur’an box.
20ddf7d0-c8c3-5985-8cd5-4be93c3b922b.description:
This Qur’an box was constructed to contain a Qur’an made of 30 fascicles. It was probably produced at the request of a Mamluk sultan or a high dignitary, in order for them to donate it to a religious foundation (mosque, *madrasa* or mausoleum).  
The box, which is supported on four legs, consists of a square wooden box covered in brass plates. The sloping, desk-like lid is attached on the back by two hinges and has a buckle on the front through which to put a lock. Each brass plate is decorated and features inscriptions in gold and silver inlay. The inside of the box is upholstered in fabric and has two compartments, each with 15 divisions, in which to put a Qur’an. The outer sides are covered in Arabic inscriptions, in *kufic* and *thuluth* script, that protrude from the surface; the calligraphy covers a backdrop composed of small-scale plants including lotus blossoms. Quotations from the Qur’an run along the length of the outer surfaces (Sura 24 verse 35 and Sura 2 verse 255 ‘Ayat al-Kursi’). More quotations are found on the desk-like lid and on the narrow inscription friezes (Sura 3 verses 26–7, Sura 26 verses 192–9, Sura 56 verses 76–89 and 92–5, and Sura 59 verses 22–4). The underside is decorated with geometric patterns.  
Both a name and the 30 Qur’an fascicles are missing. Two related Qur’an boxes from the same period, around AH 730 / AD 1330, have survived in Cairo. One of these displays the name of the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad and the date AH 723 / AD 1322. It now belongs to the library of al-Azhar mosque. The second, undated, box is housed in the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo.  
In Mamluk Egypt, Qur’ans were usually kept in boxes (*sunduq*) or in freestanding metal cabinets (*kursi*). Because they were used constantly, few of the actual Qur’ans survived.
20ddf7d0-c8c3-5985-8cd5-4be93c3b922b.short_description: This square box, supported on four legs, was made to hold a now missing Qur’an of 30 separate volumes, which were placed in two rows of 15 compartments. Magnificently executed Qur’anic inscriptions in different scripts lavishly decorate the exterior in gold and silver.
20ddf7d0-c8c3-5985-8cd5-4be93c3b922b.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
20ddf7d0-c8c3-5985-8cd5-4be93c3b922b.dimensions: Height 27 cm, width 42.5 cm, depth 42.5 cm.
20ddf7d0-c8c3-5985-8cd5-4be93c3b922b.method_for_datation: The name of the maker of this Qur’an box also appears on a tall *kursi* (an octagonal cabinet which houses a Qur’an) housed in the Museum of Islamic Art, Cairo, and dated to 727–8 / 1327–8. It is thought that the Berlin Qur’an box dates from the same period.
20ddf7d0-c8c3-5985-8cd5-4be93c3b922b.method_for_provenance: Inlaid Qur’an boxes such as this one were only known in Mamluk Egypt, and it was here where they were also made.
20ddf7d0-c8c3-5985-8cd5-4be93c3b922b.obtention: Acquired from a private art gallery in Cairo in 1904 through B. Moritz.

232d8890-0876-5479-966e-ac44c41896b0.name: Frieze panels.
232d8890-0876-5479-966e-ac44c41896b0.description:
Two panels made of pine, each carved with an inscription in deep relief and background decoration in lower relief. Both levels of carving are decorated with plaster and with green, red, and white paint. The inscriptions, done in a style of calligraphy known as foliated *kufic*, consist of verses from the Qur'an: the first panel has part of *sura* 2, verse 164, while the second has part of *sura* 3, verse 191. Clearly these panels were part of a much larger ensemble, one which probably decorated the upper level of a building intended for religious use, such as a *madrasa* or a mosque. Friezes of Qur'anic quotations were common in such settings in many parts of the Islamic world; one such frieze in the Mosque of Ibn Tulun in Cairo was originally over 2 km long.  
  
The style of the panels suggests an origin in Spain or North Africa under the Almohads. The Almohads are known to have had fairly ascetic views on art, yet it is worth noting that for them, a Berber dynasty with origins in the Sahara desert, wood would have been considered a luxury material.
232d8890-0876-5479-966e-ac44c41896b0.short_description: Two panels of pinewood carved in relief with inscriptions and (originally) decorated with paint and plaster. The inscriptions are Qur’anic verses, and the panels were probably once part of a frieze in a mosque. Wood was considered a luxury material in a desert environment like that of North Africa.
232d8890-0876-5479-966e-ac44c41896b0.dates: Hegira 6th / AD 12th or early AH 7th / AD 13th century.
232d8890-0876-5479-966e-ac44c41896b0.dimensions: 378B–1907: Height 16.8cm, width 101.4cm, depth 1.8cm; 378C–1907: Height 16.7cm, width 103cm, depth 2cm.
232d8890-0876-5479-966e-ac44c41896b0.method_for_datation: Both the style of calligraphy and the arabesque scrolls forming the background, are typical of Spanish and North African architectural decoration under the Almoravids (448–551 / 1056–1147) and Almohads (524–667 / 1130–1269).
232d8890-0876-5479-966e-ac44c41896b0.bibliography: Stanley, T., with Rosser-Owen, M. and Vernoit, S., *Palace and Mosque: Islamic Art from the Middle East*, London, 2004, p.27.
232d8890-0876-5479-966e-ac44c41896b0.author: Barry Wood
keywords: foliated; kufic; inscription; carving

24c4d60c-f039-586c-b878-b41f99dc6b12.name: Panel.
24c4d60c-f039-586c-b878-b41f99dc6b12.description:
The rectangular panel consists of an arch with small plain sections on each side. Its carved decoration shows a symmetrical floral composition. The centre forms a vase-like motif with a flower. Leaves of different sizes and shapes fill the space inside and outside the arch. The decoration consists of a variety of small elements, but the overall composition appears integrated since the curves form a relationship through all parts. The deep carved patterns are of charming clarity and possess sculptural depth.  
This type of decoration goes back to the stuccoes and wood carvings at Samarra. Samarra, situated some 60 miles up the Tigris from Baghdad, was the capital of the Abbasid caliphs from AH 224 / AD 838until AH 270 / AD 883. Ahmad ibn Tulun, the founder of the Tulunid dynasty in Egypt (AH 254–94 / AD 868–906) spent many years in Samarra and brought the Abbasid style of decoration and Abbasid craftsmen to his own capital, al-Qata'i. The so-called style C of the Samarra stuccoes is characterised by bevelling carved, symmetrical abstract patterns of leaf and vase motifs which match the shapes within the arch of the wooden panel. The wood carvings made in Tulunid Egypt at the end of the AH 3rd / AD 9th century represent the culmination of this style, although they have a tendency to break up the originally broad sculptured surface into smaller elements as in the case of this panel. The specific function of the panel is not known; it was possibly part of the architectural decoration.
24c4d60c-f039-586c-b878-b41f99dc6b12.short_description: The carved decoration on this rectangular wooden panel shows a vase-like motif, with a flower in the centre and leaves inside and outside the arch. This decorative style goes back to Abbasid stuccoes and wood carvings in Iraq. The panel was possibly part of Tulunid architectural decoration.
24c4d60c-f039-586c-b878-b41f99dc6b12.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
24c4d60c-f039-586c-b878-b41f99dc6b12.owner: National Museum of Fine Arts, Stockholm. In order to reorganise the expanding collections, the main part of the Islamic collection has been on permanent loan to the Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities since 1982.
24c4d60c-f039-586c-b878-b41f99dc6b12.dates: Hegira late 3rd century / AD late 9th century.
24c4d60c-f039-586c-b878-b41f99dc6b12.method_for_datation: The architectural decoration of the mosque of Ahmad ibn Tulun in al-Qata'i, completed in 266 / 879, is close to the style of this panel.
24c4d60c-f039-586c-b878-b41f99dc6b12.method_for_provenance: The object was found during excavations in Egypt.
24c4d60c-f039-586c-b878-b41f99dc6b12.obtention: Purchased by the Crown Prince of Sweden in December 1934 in Cairo.

25fd225a-8425-5648-a345-5ebb03d005da.name: Gate of ash-Shibak Fort
25fd225a-8425-5648-a345-5ebb03d005da.short_description:
This magnificent gate once guarded the entrance to ash-Shibak Fort. Also known as *al-Bait al-Kabir* (literally “the Big House”), ash-Shibak Fort was built by Sheikh Ahmad bin Rabia’a al-Ismaili al-Himyari, a leading figure of the Yaruba Imamate under the rule of Imam Sultan bin Saif II al-Yarubi.  
The gate carvings features calligraphic, floral and animal motifs including the Royal Coat of Arms of the United Kingdom and an Arabic inscription that reads:  
  
*To the Great Lord \[al-Sayyid\] Made in Surat  
Ahmad al-Ismaili In Muharram  
al-Himyari \[may he\] consolidate Islam in the year 1126*  
  
Today, the gate stands as a unique example of defensive artistry and bears witness to the strong commercial and political ties that existed between Oman and India during the time of the al-Yaruba Imams, the Mughal Empire and the British East India Company.

268cfa7c-8dd4-56db-8479-fc02d03a57e6.name: Door
268cfa7c-8dd4-56db-8479-fc02d03a57e6.short_description: One part from a wooden door panel laid out in strap work following the structural lines of an infinite-repetition geometric star pattern (square plan of repetition, eight-pointed stars and other polygons), all compartments with panels carved with palmette and half-palmette designs.
268cfa7c-8dd4-56db-8479-fc02d03a57e6.dates: Hegira late 8th century / AD late 14th century
keywords: Door; geometric patterns; Wood

26fd8fdd-9bc0-5670-be93-f86c07c23383.name: Dresser
26fd8fdd-9bc0-5670-be93-f86c07c23383.short_description: This wooden dresser contains four large drawers and one thin upper drawer. It is topped with a marble slab and rectangular mirror in a wooden frame, decorated with a wooden crest and carved with floral patterns. The wood is covered in a mosaic of bone or ceramic pieces, organised in a floral design. Each drawer has a keyhole and is opened by two individually painted knobs.

keywords: Woodwork; Furniture; Mosaic; Wood

2761dfdd-179f-5f5e-bc92-ae41bdd8bcc2.name: Door of the ante-chamber of the *maqsura*.
2761dfdd-179f-5f5e-bc92-ae41bdd8bcc2.description:
This huge rectangular door is made up of a main-door framework containing two pass-doors. The door is divided into panels separated by uprights and cross-pieces which stand out in relief, carved with rich floral decoration. This decoration also covers the main surrounding framework, on which alternating relief panels (long hexagons and diamond shapes) make a base for even more striking carving. These panels are filled with furled tri-lobed fleurons all connected to a curving stem, which, according to some mysterious symmetry, seems to weave in and out in ever more fantastical convolutions. The top centre panel of the frame is a 16-sided star polygon, even more boldly and exuberantly decorated with pine cones and chalices, palm leaves and stalks, some carved with certain symmetry. One feels that this is the beginning of a break-away from the decorative repertoire of the *minbar* of the Great Mosque of Kairouan (built AH 248 / AD 866) towards the Fatimid art of Egypt, which itself had absorbed some Abbasid themes.  
The simpler decoration of the internal panels of the door and of the pass-doors is confined to a few geometric motifs. Some of these panels seem to have been restored during the Hafsid period.
2761dfdd-179f-5f5e-bc92-ae41bdd8bcc2.short_description: The decoration and manufacturing technique of this door are identical to those used for the *maqsura* (recess) at the Great Mosque of Kairouan. The framing and decoration of the panels that make up the two halves are simple and limited to geometric motifs, presenting similarities with Egyptian Fatimid art.
2761dfdd-179f-5f5e-bc92-ae41bdd8bcc2.initial_owner: The Zirid prince, al-Mu‘izz ibn Badis.
2761dfdd-179f-5f5e-bc92-ae41bdd8bcc2.dates: Hegira, second quarter of the 5th century / AD 11th century.
2761dfdd-179f-5f5e-bc92-ae41bdd8bcc2.method_for_datation: The decoration and structure of this door are absolutely identical to those of the *maqsura* built by the Zirid prince, al-Mu'izz ibn Badis. In fact, some believe it to be the door of the *maqsura* itself. But taking into consideration the differing dimensions of the two objects in question, especially the height, and the absence of any calligraphic inscription, some studies have concluded that this door was the entrance to a room adjacent to the *maqsura* and which is now the imam's audience-chamber. It is likely to have been the room from which the prince and his attendants entered the *maqsura* to join in prayers. This would date the door from the same period as the *maqsura* of al-Mu'izz (second quarter of the 5th / 11th century).
2761dfdd-179f-5f5e-bc92-ae41bdd8bcc2.method_for_provenance: The decoration leaves no doubt that the door is Kairouanese. The cedarwood used in its construction probably came from the forests of northwest Tunisia or from Sicily.
2761dfdd-179f-5f5e-bc92-ae41bdd8bcc2.obtention: Until the mid-1960s, this door was part of the relics of the Great Mosque of Kairouan and was kept in one of its storage rooms. As from 1978, it was displayed in the museum of the Great Mosque and then, in 1992, transferred to the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada. It will be on display in the second section, which is now undergoing refurbishment (2005).
2761dfdd-179f-5f5e-bc92-ae41bdd8bcc2.bibliography: *Ifriqiya: Thirteen Centuries of Art and Architecture in Tunisia*, pp.159–62.
2761dfdd-179f-5f5e-bc92-ae41bdd8bcc2.author: Mourad Rammah
keywords: Carving; floral decoration

2a413532-70d8-5c80-baa6-741f9adf4403.name: Turban stand in Ottoman rococo style
2a413532-70d8-5c80-baa6-741f9adf4403.short_description: The Ottoman tombs of the 17th and 18th centuries are a testimony to the great symbolic power of the turban. While the tombstones of women are characterised by depictions of fruit and flowers, a stone turban symbolising rank crowns the tomb stele of a man. In the Ottoman Empire, court officials and members of the elite classes wore elaborately shaped turbans, the form, colour, and decoration of which signal the social position and status of the wearer. The profession of the turban winder, the *sarıkçı*, ensures that the turban corresponds to and complies precisely with clothing regulations. After being worn, the turbans were placed for their protection on turban stands (*kavukluk*). In 1829, Sultan Mahmud II abolished the turban and introduced the fez, a red felt headdress with a black tassel, as the national headwear. From this time on, the wearing of a turban is restricted to religious dignitaries. In 1925, both fez and turban were prohibited in secular Turkey.
2a413532-70d8-5c80-baa6-741f9adf4403.method_for_datation: Entry in the general inventory and archival documents.
2a413532-70d8-5c80-baa6-741f9adf4403.method_for_provenance: Entry in the general inventory book.

2a8f3f10-1a76-54cb-bfe6-0ccb6a3700bd.name: Picture frame with photograph of James Camille Samson
2a8f3f10-1a76-54cb-bfe6-0ccb6a3700bd.short_description: Part of the decorum of upper class houses in the late 19th century was the convivial circle of gentlemen who retired to the smoking room after dinner to enjoy cognac, cigars and conversation while the hostess entertained her female guests with tea in the ladies’ salon. In the period of the World’s Fair and modern tourism, a tremendous stylistic diversity was available for decorating the smoking room. Moorish-Oriental styles were fashionable: heavy Persian carpets on the floors, Anatolian kilims on the walls, furniture plushily upholstered, side tables with mother-of-pearl inlays, palm plants and hookahs and Caucasian daggers. Trophies and souvenirs of journeys, including picture frames with ﬁnely turned *mashrabiya* latticework were mostly mass-produced in Europe and purchased in specialised furniture shops.
2a8f3f10-1a76-54cb-bfe6-0ccb6a3700bd.method_for_datation: Entry in the general inventory and archival documents.
2a8f3f10-1a76-54cb-bfe6-0ccb6a3700bd.method_for_provenance: Entry in the general inventory book.
2a8f3f10-1a76-54cb-bfe6-0ccb6a3700bd.obtention: Catalog entry: "Estate James Camille Samson, imperial and royal Secretary of Legation, 1908, inventorized addenda, 1926."
2a8f3f10-1a76-54cb-bfe6-0ccb6a3700bd.bibliography: Steinmann, Axel, "Wanderlust", in Christian Schicklgruber (ed), *Weltmuseum Wien, exhibition catalogue*, Vienna: Weltmuseum Wien, 2017: 90-93.
materials: Wood, mother of pearl, bone, glass; albumen print

2e9bb9ef-0628-53b2-88c7-0bb1e2984d88.name: Mint-mould for six coins
2e9bb9ef-0628-53b2-88c7-0bb1e2984d88.description: A bronze mint-mould holding six coins, in use at the mint in Fez during the reign of Sultan Mulay al-Hasan I (r. 1873-94). It should be noted that, compared to earlier periods, coinage was evolving quickly in relation to industry at this time.

2fa0159c-28bf-57b7-b310-d0bf0b2180c6.name: Wooden panel.
2fa0159c-28bf-57b7-b310-d0bf0b2180c6.description: A wooden panel with inlaid decoration of bone, ivory and ebony in the manner of a mosaic. The ornamentation is composed of semi-circles, circles, arches, pillars and vegetal decorations that include five-lobed vine-leaves and half-fan palm-leaves. The artistic roots of these motifs lie in Sassanid, Byzantine and Coptic art. Egypt had acquired fame from the Pharonic period onwards for its craftsmanship in wood and inlay work in ivory, bone and ebony. The Copts inherited these skills, mastered them, and became outstanding artisans in this craft, producing doors, door-panels and partition screens. The woodcrafts flourished in Egypt during the Umayyad and Abbasid periods, and production included objects such as doors, windows, *minbars*, inscription bands, dining tables, tribunes and chairs. All of these objects were decorated with small pieces of ivory, bone and ebony which were set to adjoin each other and to create delicate and detailed geometric and vegetal designs, such as on this inlaid panel, believed to have been a side panel for a piece of furniture belonging to a residence or palace.
2fa0159c-28bf-57b7-b310-d0bf0b2180c6.short_description: Early Egyptian woodwork was decorated both by carving and by inlaying with ivory and bone. This piece is a good example of the second method.
2fa0159c-28bf-57b7-b310-d0bf0b2180c6.method_for_datation: The panel is dated based on an analysis of its geometric and vegetal decorative motifs; the style indicates a date during the Tulunid period of the 3rd / 9th century.
2fa0159c-28bf-57b7-b310-d0bf0b2180c6.method_for_provenance: Wooden inlayed panels such as this were used to furnish mosques and residences. Fustat in particular was famous for the production of such panels in the early Islamic period, and production flourished during the Fatimid and Mamluk periods. Many of these panels were discovered in Fustat.
2fa0159c-28bf-57b7-b310-d0bf0b2180c6.obtention: This panel was uncovered during the course of archaeological excavations carried out at Fustat.

305f4585-8d17-53d5-a7d9-3ce3b3fa0f2c.name: Cupola from Torrijos.
305f4585-8d17-53d5-a7d9-3ce3b3fa0f2c.description: Nailed-board, octagonal cupola ceiling supported on smooth walls covered with tapestries or silks with ornamental drawings. Above the level of these fabrics, in the four corners, sit the squinches, decorated with honeycomb work, that give the ceiling its circular shape from the octagonal base section, where the noble coats of arms of the owners can be seen. A second, lower band bears chequered strips on all four sides, alongside others decorated with Gothic plasterwork, and in their centre large pilgrim shells and the heraldic 'S's of Don Gutierre de Cárdenas, who played an important role in the celebration of the marriage of the Catholic Kings. These two are alluded to in the inscription 'D Ferdinandus I D Isabel' that can be read on a frieze also from the Cardenas Palace, which is held at the National Archaeological Museum. The ceiling sections converge radially on the centre and are delicately decorated with knotwork based on a twelve-star or *sinos* pattern that develops around structures of various different forms known as *almendrillas*, *azafates*, *candilejos* and *costadillos*. The plasterwork is decorated in relief with palmettes, apexes and engravings. The cupola originally covered the room in the northeast corner of the palace of the Torrijos and the Dukes of Maqueda. This ceiling, like the other ones from the palace, currently outside Spain, were commissioned from the decorative painters García del Barco and Juan Rodríguez.
305f4585-8d17-53d5-a7d9-3ce3b3fa0f2c.short_description: An example of Mudéjar excellence in carpentry and the adoption of Muslim models by the Christian aristocracy in their search for luxurious and welcoming spaces. The huge number of separate parts in this hemispherical cupola overlap and interlink to form a great geometric design.
305f4585-8d17-53d5-a7d9-3ce3b3fa0f2c.method_for_datation: From documentation of the Cardenas, friends of the Catholic Kings.
305f4585-8d17-53d5-a7d9-3ce3b3fa0f2c.obtention: The piece was purchased for the National Archaeological Museum from Adela and Elisa Páramo on 15 June 1969.
