30cafd37-23c3-561f-9f01-a12c90b5d8b6.name: Base for a tray (*sinija*)
30cafd37-23c3-561f-9f01-a12c90b5d8b6.description: The *Sinija* (Tr. *sini*) is a large, round tray made of copper or brass. It was used for serving food or as a floor dining table – a *sofra* (Tr. *sofra*). tTherefore it had an important place in the shared living culture of the Ottoman Balkans among urban populations of different confessional and ethnic backgrounds. The diameter of *sinijas* sometimes reached 1–2 meters or more. When used as a floor dining table, the *sinija* was placed on a wooden or iron base. Valued for their craftsmanship, locally produced or imported *sinijas* have also found a place in the interiors of the modern age as wall decor or top parts of decorative side tables placed on custom-made bases of different styles.
30cafd37-23c3-561f-9f01-a12c90b5d8b6.dates: Hegira late 13th–early 14th century / AD late 19th–early 20th century
30cafd37-23c3-561f-9f01-a12c90b5d8b6.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis, material, technique, and analogy with other similar examples
30cafd37-23c3-561f-9f01-a12c90b5d8b6.author: Ana Samardžić
keywords: floor dining table; carving; Ottoman Balkans.

310da155-3663-5beb-b8de-caa608f5aade.name: *Dhiil*
310da155-3663-5beb-b8de-caa608f5aade.description: The *dhiil* is a traditional Somali milk container, both practical and finely crafted, used mainly to collect and store milk from different livestock, and sometimes water. Traditionally made by Somali nomad women, the *dhiil* can be woven from the thorny *qabo* (a plant from the *Euphorbia* genus), as featured, or crafted from wood. Its construction involves peeling and softening the spiny *qabo* stems into long strips, which are then coiled and bound in a basketlike technique. The vessel has a hemispherical base that widens to a central ridge (*kelli*) before narrowing toward the top, capped with a fitted lid (*bugul*). Once woven, the *dhiil* is treated with *asal*, a dye and sealant made from red acacia bark (*qaroon*), giving it a rich colour and protective finish. The interior is traditionally smoked over *shilin* (wood) and cleaned carefully, a process that imparts a distinct smoky flavour to the milk. Milk is shared from the cup of the *dhiil*, called *harrubi*, in a tradition known as *waddagid* ("sharing").
310da155-3663-5beb-b8de-caa608f5aade.method_for_datation: Date not precisely known; established as at least three generations old based on family oral history.
310da155-3663-5beb-b8de-caa608f5aade.method_for_provenance: Provenance established through oral history provided by the lender, supported by family inheritance records.
310da155-3663-5beb-b8de-caa608f5aade.provenance: Belonged to Mohamed family in Somalia; passed down through generations before being inherited by Salim Mohamed.
310da155-3663-5beb-b8de-caa608f5aade.obtention: Loaned to the museum by the owner who inherited it from his grandmother.
keywords: Dhiil, milk container, haroub

3145dc39-d491-535e-aaa2-6545cc31f4e7.name: Chair of Krste Petkov Misirkov
3145dc39-d491-535e-aaa2-6545cc31f4e7.short_description: Misirkov’s book “On Macedonian Matters” lays the foundations of the modern Macedonian language and grammar. Being one of the central figures of the “Slav-Macedonian Scientific Literary Society" in St. Petersburg, he largely contributed to issuing the periodical Macedonian and Russian-language publication, “Makedonski Golos” (“Macedonian Voice").
3145dc39-d491-535e-aaa2-6545cc31f4e7.author: Nada Andonovska (author), Dragan Georgiev, historian (consultant)
keywords: Bi-lingual publication

3281a778-30ea-57b8-8d73-b1b6ddf74613.name: Wooden panel.
3281a778-30ea-57b8-8d73-b1b6ddf74613.description: A rectangular wooden panel decorated with two narrow borders flanking a broad central band. The two narrow borders are ornamented with an epigraphic inscription in *kufic* script, which consists of the *bismillah (In the Name of God)* and the 'Throne' verse (2: 255) as well as the expression '*Hasbi Allah*' ('Allah is sufficient for me'). The broad central band is ornamented with geometric motifs, which divide it into seven square-shaped sections. All sections are decorated with vegetal decorations, winged motifs, oval forms and tri-lobed leaf designs. The third and fifth squares hold a lobed arch, within which is vegetal decoration and, flanking the triangular areas between the outer curvature of the arch and the corners of the square-shaped section, are further vegetal motifs. Both the decorative style and the carving of this piece portray a Hellenic stamp, seen in the relief carving of decorative motifs, the oval shapes, the tri-lobed leaves and the vegetal stems. The panel also displays Sassanid influences seen in the winged motifs and lobed arches.
3281a778-30ea-57b8-8d73-b1b6ddf74613.short_description: Islamic art came into being on the shoulders of Hellenistic and Sassanid arts and then developed its own Islamic character. This piece demonstrates the blending of the three artistic styles.
3281a778-30ea-57b8-8d73-b1b6ddf74613.method_for_datation: This panel was dated based on study into the development of *kufic* script, the origins of the decorative motifs, and the technique of manufacture, which included high relief, decorative motifs, winged designs, oval forms and vegetal motifs. Furthermore, during the Abbasid period, entire texts were used as inscriptions on objects; it is possible, therefore, to date this piece to the early part of the Abbasid era.
3281a778-30ea-57b8-8d73-b1b6ddf74613.method_for_provenance: Wooden panels were used to furnish mosques and residences, and embellished tribunes and chairs. Egypt, Fustat in particular, was famous for the production of such panels in the early Islamic period, and production flourished during the Fatimid and Mamluk periods. Many of these panels were discovered in Fustat where they were used to protect the walls of small tombs from the dust and dirt that might fall from the grave onto the deceased.
3281a778-30ea-57b8-8d73-b1b6ddf74613.obtention: The object was discovered during the course of archaeological excavations at Fustat.

33a6c84f-b10f-5856-b654-7f8c5f9a715b.name: Rectangular piece of wood.
33a6c84f-b10f-5856-b654-7f8c5f9a715b.description:
A rectangular piece of wood decorated with low-relief carvings, which was probably once part of a high frieze. The decorations are arranged along two narrow bands, which hem-in a wider band lying in between them. Both of the narrow bands are embellished with vegetal decorative motifs, such as branches, surrounded by tri-lobed rosettes and fan-leaf palmettes. The central band is embellished with scenes of naturalistic human and animal activity, such as a hunting scene; a bird with a human face is also present. The scene is played out against a background of vegetal decoration, and surrounded by geometric compositions. The decorative components were originally painted which would have highlighted the detail. Symmetry and alternation were the twin dynamics that helped harmonise and defuse the decorative components.  
This panel was unearthed together with some other rectangular wooden pieces in the tomb of the Mamluk Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun, and in the Bimaristan (hospital) Qalawun where they were used to cover the upper frieze. The decorative mode of this panel bears no relationship to the Mamluk period, but is exclusively in the Fatimid style. It is likely, therefore, that this wooden panel once graced a Fatimid palace, specifically the Fatimid Western Palace, which was built by Caliph al-Aziz bi-Allah and completed by al-Mustansir bi-Allah. However, it was on the ruins of the Fatimid Western Palace that the Bimaristan Qalawun was later built and it is, therefore, likely that these wooden frieze components were later re-used to embellish the hospital walls.  
These decorative panels are considered an important source for the study of Fatimid painting for they include scenes of hunting, music, entertainment, battle and excursions, as well as depictions of birds and other animals and reveal the life of opulence led by the Fatimid elite.
33a6c84f-b10f-5856-b654-7f8c5f9a715b.short_description: This item is an example of carving on wood from the Fatimid period, influenced by Abbasid styles from Samarra that spread all over the Islamic world. Decoration is based on hunting scenes and animal shapes on a background of vegetation.
33a6c84f-b10f-5856-b654-7f8c5f9a715b.method_for_datation: This piece was dated through study of the decorative components that appear on it, the style of representation, and by comparison with other analogous decorative pieces.
33a6c84f-b10f-5856-b654-7f8c5f9a715b.method_for_provenance: In view of the fact that the panel was almost certainly made for the Fatimid Western Palace, it is likely that it was made by craftsmen employed in the atelier of Caliph al-Aziz bi-Allah and produced especially to furnish the palace.
33a6c84f-b10f-5856-b654-7f8c5f9a715b.obtention: The object was transferred from the Mausoleum of Qalawun in the *Nahassien* (coppersmith's) district, and received by the Museum in 1909.

366a9ff1-e485-57a9-ad1c-a5eb7cf07698.name: Chest of drawers
366a9ff1-e485-57a9-ad1c-a5eb7cf07698.short_description: This chest has a European shape and the decoration is near to Indian or Near-Eastern motifs. It has an Arab inscription, but only the date could be read it. This chest was probably made in India or in Egypt for the European customers who lived there.

36773e08-5d5d-510b-9eaf-d6bc145e39d8.name: Cigarette case
36773e08-5d5d-510b-9eaf-d6bc145e39d8.description: The Orientalism or Neo-Mudéjar style gave new light to old motifs as decoration in ivory or bone, with flowers and interlaces, as in this cigarette case. The decoration is strongly influenced by Arab pieces.

36adfe60-d1bb-5d20-835e-c6987c2d3ca0.name: Coffee group
36adfe60-d1bb-5d20-835e-c6987c2d3ca0.description: Coffee is always served at the beginning of a visit and is repeatedly offered until guests politely signal that they have had enough by rocking their cup from side to side. In order to keep coffee hot and fresh for unexpected guests it goes through many stages. After roasting and grinding the coffee beans the grains are added to boiling water inside a large *dallah* (coffee pot) called a *khamra*. Next, the liquid is poured into a medium-sized coffee pot called a *taljeemah*. At this stage cardamom seeds, saffron and rose water may be added for flavour. From this jug, the coffee is poured into a serving *dallah* referred to as a *mezallah*, where the coffee is refined and filtered. The server must hold the *mezallah* with their left hand and distribute the *fanayeel* (coffee cups) using the right hand. The coffee should fill less than half of the cup.
36adfe60-d1bb-5d20-835e-c6987c2d3ca0.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab
keywords: coffee; beans; coffee beans

373ae550-80af-546a-8e29-6fd330505a98.name: Qajar lacquer Casket
373ae550-80af-546a-8e29-6fd330505a98.short_description: This lacquer casket depicts the second ruler of the 19th-century Qajar dynasty, Fath’Ali Shah. Seated on the legendary Mughal Peacock Throne, he is flanked by three of his sons, ministers, and other important figures. The side panels, decorated with raised medallions on a *gul-ol-bulbul* (rose and bulbul bird) background, show courtiers in Western clothing, landscapes, and hunting scenes. The caskets are mentioned in William Ouseley’s *Travels into Various Countries of the East; More Particularly Persia* (1823), based on his visits to Iran. Ouseley claims these caskets—made of paper and a serish glue—were mass produced in Isfahan; there are now a number of similar objects in various museums and collections. He also mentions beautifully painted, varnished boxes similar to the Fath’Ali Shah caskets. Common subjects included battle scenes and hunting parties as well as depictions of popular romances.
373ae550-80af-546a-8e29-6fd330505a98.method_for_datation: By comparison with similar objects from the Qajar period.

38e58977-4147-5180-845f-11ffcd1daba9.name: Pulley
38e58977-4147-5180-845f-11ffcd1daba9.description: A wooden pulley in the form of a circular wheel with a recessed rim, around which the rope was wound to facilitate drawing a water bucket from the well. At its center is a round wooden piece fitted with various wooden boards arranged in a circular manner. Animals were used to pull the rope passing through the pulley.

3b494886-dcbc-53f0-858a-e56bcd9a8635.name: Sculpturally conceived emblem
3b494886-dcbc-53f0-858a-e56bcd9a8635.short_description:
This work of art belongs to a group of emblems which is an artistic interpretation of an Arabic letter or word that brings the Sufi farther along his path to God when he remembers or repeats it in his devotions (*dhikr*).  
This emblem is a symmetrical composition with the word *al-shafi* (the Healer), one of Allah’s many names.
keywords: Calligraphy; Sufism; Symmetry; inscription; blazon; standard; procession

3de78d7d-0ff4-5d07-a1ac-c4173aa7e91e.name: *Peškun*
3de78d7d-0ff4-5d07-a1ac-c4173aa7e91e.description:
Hexagonal *peškun* (Tr. *peşkun*) is made of carved walnut wood. It is divided into a bottom middle part with a hexagonal plate in the form of a shelf, making two stories for storing – an upper and a lower plate. Both plates are richly decorated with interlacing floral motifs. In the center of the upper plate, there is a motif of the six-pointed star, while beneath its edges a frieze of trefoil elements is formed. Each of the six vertical sides is divided by a plate into two zones with three openings in the shape of the oriental arch each.  
*Peškun* is the name of a traditional piece of Ottoman furniture in the shape of a table or stool. It was originally meant for sitting, although it had different purposes throughout history, especially as a decorative table in Balkan oriental interiors of the 19th and of the first half of the 20th century. Over time, the larger table (in the set of usually three pieces,) began to be used as a coffee table, while the smaller ones were used as stools. *Peškun* were ordinarily made of walnut wood, ornamented with incrusted floral and geometric motifs made of mother of pearl and bone.
3de78d7d-0ff4-5d07-a1ac-c4173aa7e91e.dates: Hegira late 13th–early 14th century / AD late 19th–early 20th century
3de78d7d-0ff4-5d07-a1ac-c4173aa7e91e.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis, material, technique, and analogy with other similar examples.
3de78d7d-0ff4-5d07-a1ac-c4173aa7e91e.author: Ana Samardžić
keywords: peškun; stool; side table; carving; Ottoman Balkans

3e6397b4-d839-55fb-83c0-463d120d0c76.name: Tray stand
3e6397b4-d839-55fb-83c0-463d120d0c76.short_description: This spectacular tray stand, made of sheet brass inlaid with silver, has a decorative scheme devoted entirely to glorifying the (unnamed) ruler for whom it was made. On the body, among other scenes, is that of the monarch between two pairs of servants, seated on a throne with lions below and winged angels above. Above and below this are astrological symbols, thus showing the ruler not only as an earthly but also a heavenly power.
3e6397b4-d839-55fb-83c0-463d120d0c76.provenance: Northern Syria or Northern Iraq (probably Mosul)

3ea5c496-cc96-57ae-a6e7-f47f064d36cb.name: Teak Panel.
3ea5c496-cc96-57ae-a6e7-f47f064d36cb.description: A wooden panel of dark-brown teak wood. The surface is carved with an abstract design, known as the 'bevelled' style, a pattern of repeated curved shapes with bevelled edges, usually moulded rather than carved, probably derived from stylised vegetal forms. This type of design is typical of the Abbasid period and can also be found on stucco wall panels. This piece would have been part of a larger panel of carved wood used for furniture or doors. It is close in style to wood panels and stucco found at Samarra, capital of the Abbasid dynasty (AH 177–655 / AD 749–1258). Wood, particularly teak, was highly valued in Iraq and was probably imported from South East Asia.
3ea5c496-cc96-57ae-a6e7-f47f064d36cb.short_description: A teak panel, carved with an abstract design in the technique known as the ‘bevelled style’. This stylised design was typical of the Abbasid period and was employed on stucco wall panels as well as on carved wood on walls and ceilings.
3ea5c496-cc96-57ae-a6e7-f47f064d36cb.method_for_datation: Through stylistic analysis: the 'bevelled' style was found on AH 3rd- / AD 9th-century architectural decoration from Samarra that was built in AH 221 / AD 836, and which was the Abbasid capital for only 37 years before the caliphate returned to Baghdad.
3ea5c496-cc96-57ae-a6e7-f47f064d36cb.method_for_provenance: The style of the carving resembles architectural decoration found at Samarra in Iraq.
3ea5c496-cc96-57ae-a6e7-f47f064d36cb.obtention: Acquired by the British Museum in 1944, from the Collection of Sir Sydney Bernard Burney, through the National Art Collections fund.

3f812372-02bd-5235-89dd-a89ca9e526fd.name: Desk
3f812372-02bd-5235-89dd-a89ca9e526fd.short_description: This desk, an important object with great symbolic value, was offered by the Tunisian people to the great reforming minister, Khaireddine (Khayr al-Din) Pacha. The wooden desk is painted white, and a floral pattern decorates its drawers.

3fcb079f-6a10-569e-97e4-f341d5df2eca.name: Ceiling, custom-made for Shangri La's living room
3fcb079f-6a10-569e-97e4-f341d5df2eca.short_description: The living room ceiling at Shangri La was custom-made by Moroccan artisans working under the supervision of the Rabat-based firm S.A.L.A.M. René Martin. It is carved, painted, and gilded throughout. The central field features recessed octagrams in interlocking, knotted niches, predominantly orange and brown in tone. The bottommost border consists of a moulded plaster frieze of floral motifs in an arcade repeated throughout.

410982f8-b847-57f8-9f76-389d106adfca.name: Door jamb.
410982f8-b847-57f8-9f76-389d106adfca.description: The jambs and lintel of the door to the Casa Maturano bear a fairly complex decorative frieze, unlike the other significant wooden example from more or less the same period in Palermo, which is still *in situ* on the main door of the Church of Santa Maria dell'Ammiraglio dating back to 1143, the year the church was founded by Admiral Giorgio of Antioch. It is characterised by traditional decorative rectangular panels similar to Egyptian examples dating back to the 11th and 12th centuries. The central decorative band, framed by two lateral borders characterised by half-palmette plant motifs tightly intertwined, consists of a sequence of opposed double pentagons linked by a pair of semi-circles filled with vegetal spirals, interposed with 16-sided stars. The geometric elements have a beaded edge and are filled with tightly carved intertwined half-palmettes. According to Scerrato (1979), this type of decoration appears to derive from the Samarra stuccoes (Iraq), and presents notable similarities with the wooden ceilings of the Ibn Tulun mosque in Cairo.
410982f8-b847-57f8-9f76-389d106adfca.short_description: These wooden remains were the jambs and lintel of a door from the Casa Maturano in Palermo. Their decoration is reminiscent of the decorative motifs used in the Samarra stuccoes (Iraq), as well as the decoration on the wooden ceilings in the Ibn Tulun Mosque in Cairo.

42831546-e0c3-549c-9fd9-f6b1d2f06488.short_description: Islamic art is often thought to be devoid of figural representation, yet many works of art made in the Islamic world do depict figures. Their presence is particularly notable in applied arts, or objects made for daily life, such as these doors showing idealized scenes of leisure and court life in Iran. The activities of the courtiers – including relaxation, entertainment, and the hunt – as well as their appearance are derived from paintings made during the seventeenth century.

4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.name: Hexagonal dinner stand.
4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.description:
This piece assumes the shape of a hexagonal (six-sided) pedestal upon which dinner trays would be placed; it is therefore known as a dinner stand. Its top surface, which is also hexagonal in shape, has a central circular decoration comprising a radiating inscription in a plaited *kufic* script. The radiating form of the inscription increases its decorative impact as it appears to simulate the rays of the sun coming from a central medallion, in which the artist has inscribed the name of Sultan al-Nasir Hasan ibn al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun, for whom this table was probably made. Framing the surface of this piece, is an inscription in Mamluk *thuluth* script which includes the name of the sultan and a number of his titles, it reads: 'Glory to our lord the Sultan al-Malik al-Nasir al-'Alam, al-'Adil, al-Mujahid, al-Murabit, al-Muthaghir, al-Mu'ayyad, al-Mansur, the Sultan of Islam and the Muslims, the Destroyer of Apostates and Infidels, the Reviver of Justice to all, the Protector of the oppressed against the oppressors, the Protector of the Muslim community, the Protector of worldly and spiritual matters, ibn al-Sultan al-Malik al-Mansur Qalawun Al-Salihi'. And surrounding these inscriptions along the interior are a series of lobed semi-circles decorated with flying ducks that are distinguished by their vitality and movement.  
Each of the six sides of the pedestal's surfaces is comprised of four decorated panels arranged vertically one on top of the other. In the centre of one of these panels is a small door with two arched leafs which open to reveal an internal shelf. The panels are ornamented with openwork arabesque designs, composed of intertwining vegetal leaves and stems, lotus blossoms, and epigraphic inscriptions in *thuluth* script, on a background of openwork decorative motifs. The table has six short 'supports', posts that rest on the legs. A series of inscriptions are recorded on them, which indicate the name of the craftsman and his titles the English translation of which reads: 'Made by the poor slave hopeful of his God's forgiveness, known as the son of the teacher professor Muhammad, son Sunqur al Baghdadi al-Sanqari, in the year AH 728 \[1327\] in the days of our lord al-Malik al-Nasir, glory to his triumph'.  
Such objects, although used extensively as stands for food trays, were also used to carry the Qur'an or torches at night in mosques or palaces, as well as to carry drinks, vases and incense burners. It is possible that this pedestal, which belonged to al-Nasir Muhammad, had been used to carry these types of items in his private palace or in his *madrasa* which was built on the street of the coppersmiths *(Shari' Nahhāsin)* in Cairo. This supposition is made more likely in view of the fact that the object was recovered from the Bimaristan (hospital) of al-Mansur Qalawun, which is adjacent to the Madrasa of al-Nasir Muhammad.  
The dinner stand is one of the most valuable acquisitions in the collections of the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo for it demonstrates the prolific production of metalwork in the Mamluk period. The importance of this particular piece stems from its having been crafted specifically for Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun, not to mention the fact that it contains the name of the craftsman who made it along with the date of manufacture. Its exceptional quality is magnified when its splendour and size are considered.
4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.short_description: This type of table, made from metal or wood, was extensively produced during the Mamluk period in Cairo. It was used to hold food or items that need to be elevated from the floor. This table is made of brass inlaid with silver on which the name and titles of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad and the maker's name were inscribed.
4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.initial_owner: Sultan al-Nasir Hasan ibn al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun who reigned three times: AH 693–4 / AD 1294–5; AH 698–708 / AD 1299–1309; AH 709–41 / AD 1309–40.
4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.method_for_datation: This piece can be dated based on the inscription it carries, which includes the name of the craftsman who made it and the date it was manufactured. This is in addition to the inscriptions on the piece which specifically name Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun.
4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.method_for_provenance:
It is highly probable that the piece was crafted in Cairo, especially in view of the fact that it is decorated with epigraphic inscriptions in Mamluk *thuluth* script, a style prevalent in Mamluk pieces attributed to Egypt. Additionally, the design technique used in its manufacture and the decoration, closely resemble those used in a number of other objects known to have been made in Egypt, including a box (for a Qur'an manuscript) made of copper and inlaid with gold and silver, currently housed in the library of al-Azhar Mosque, which bears the name of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun and is dated 723 (1322). There is an almost identical box in the collections at the Museum of Islamic Art in Berlin, known to have been taken from a mosque in Cairo; this is inscribed with the name of the same craftsman as the pedestal under discussion here: Muhammad ibn Sunqur al-Baghdadi. There is also a silver inlaid candlestick currently in the collections of the Islamic Art Museum in Cairo (reg. no. 15080) which bears the name of Sultan al-Nasir ibn Muhammad ibn Qalawun.  
Furthermore, in Cairo during the Mamluk period there was a *suq* dedicated to the manufacture and sale of inlaid metalwork. The author and historian al-Maqrizi refers to the market in his work *al-Khitat* (1853) as 'the *suq* of the inlay craftsmen' (Suq al-Koftiyin), which was located in a street that in present-day Cairo lies between al-Ghuriyya Street and al-Azhar Street. The market's documented presence further supports the supposition that this piece was crafted in Cairo.
4312ed57-80a5-53ca-a579-d77d2e79388d.obtention: This piece was transferred from the Bimaristan of Sultan al-Mansur Qalawun to the Museum of Islamic Art. It was one of the first pieces to enter the collections at the time of the inauguration of the Museum in 1903.

453d31a1-ac06-52d0-a282-f160b88b5219.name: Wooden screen in two parts.
453d31a1-ac06-52d0-a282-f160b88b5219.description:
A wooden screen that represents a masterpiece of woodcarving and which illustrates the “pivotal position” held by Syria in the field of Islamic woodwork. The screen is in two parts. The top, smaller, section of the screen is a wooden rectangular partition with various frames that divide the surface into rectangular fields. One frame is decorated with carved stylised vegetal motifs, its central field carved with the “Basmala” (“in the name of God the Compassionate the Merciful”), executed in geometric *kufic* script and openwork carving. The upper part of this partition also includes a *kufic* inscription, carved within a field of leafy vegetal patterns, which may be translated as follows: “Abu Ja'far Muhammad bin al-Hasan bin al-Ali, sincere friend of the Commander of the faithful \[the caliph\], God accepts this work from him in the months of the year 497 \[AD 1103\].” The text also includes Qur'anic verses: "Your (real) friends are (no less than) God, His messenger, and the believers, those who establish regular prayers and pay alms and bow down humbly (in worship). As to those who turn (for friendship) to God, His Messenger, and the believers, it is the party of God that must certainly triumph," (5:55-56). On the other side of this panel is the expression “… God is Islam” centrally oriented and executed in *kufic* script and openwork carving. It indicates the final words of the Qur'anic verses (3:18-19) that are inscribed around the frame. The middle panel is decorated with vegetal motifs that spring from a small carved vase.  
The bottom section of the screen is much larger in size than the top. Rectangular and divided into three horizontal sections: the lowest is a row of lathed double columns with rectangular bases and capitals; the middle is a row of lathed single columns with vase-like bases and capitals; the top, a carved screen that is divided into various decorative fields set in polygonal frames consisting of geometric patterns made of carved and pierced pieces of wood and bone inlay.
453d31a1-ac06-52d0-a282-f160b88b5219.short_description: Furnishings of mosques and holy places are often executed in a highly developed style of woodcarving. This *maqsura* screen from an AH 5th- / AD 11th-century royal tomb in Damascus, is a prime example of the important role Syria played in the woodcarving tradition.
453d31a1-ac06-52d0-a282-f160b88b5219.initial_owner: According to the inscribed date, the screen probably originally belonged to the mausoleum of the Seljuq Sultan Duqaq (r. AH 488–97 / AD 1095–1104), located in the Maydan, southwest of old Damascus. During the Atabeg period, nearly 100 years later, it was reworked and moved to the nearby Musalla al-Idain Mosque, built by Amir Ja'far Muhammad bin al-Hasan bin al-Ali.
453d31a1-ac06-52d0-a282-f160b88b5219.dimensions: Top: height 0.79 m, width 2.46 m, bottom: height 2.13 m, width 2.46 m.
453d31a1-ac06-52d0-a282-f160b88b5219.method_for_datation: The year Hegira 497 (AD 1104) it is inscribed on the object.
453d31a1-ac06-52d0-a282-f160b88b5219.method_for_provenance: The distinguished archaeologist Michael Meinecke argued that the original location of the screen was next to the mausoleum of the Seljuq Sultan Duqaq (r. 488–97 / 1095–1104), and that it was moved afterwards to the Musalla al-Idayn Mosque, because the mosque was constructed about a century after the date inscribed on the object.
453d31a1-ac06-52d0-a282-f160b88b5219.obtention: The object was expropriated by the General Directorate of Antiquities in 1927.

4708ea66-8ef0-527a-910d-4a3afc383d49.short_description: This panel may originally have formed the side of a cenotaph. 486b00c2-21f3-53e2-a770-a7f64b267074.name: Door (one of a pair)
486b00c2-21f3-53e2-a770-a7f64b267074.short_description: Tiny, geometric inlay patterns of hexagons and stars cover the surface of this large door. To create the intricate designs, long, narrow strips of green-painted bone, ivory, and wood were glued together in the form of hexagons or stars. The long strips were then cut in thin, widthwise segments, each sliver of which was adhered to the wood base of the object. The final step was to sand and seal the surface with a varnish.

49103ef0-90f2-547a-8043-173577467243.name: Dates group
49103ef0-90f2-547a-8043-173577467243.description:
As a sign of hospitality guests are given *fuala* (light refreshments). Coffee, dates, *betheetha* (a sweet made of dates and fired flour), *khabees* (a sweet made of saffron, ghee and fried flour), leavened bread, and *dibs* (date molasses) were served on a *saroud* (palm mat) and covered with a *mechabeh* (palm food cover) to protect the food from dirt and insects.  
When guest finished eating they were offered a *ghasool* (a bowl of water) or a *maghsal al yad* (pitcher and vessel) to wash their hands. At the end of a visit, guests were perfumed with a *merash* (perfume sprinkler) filled with rose water and other fragrances. Guest were also perfumed with '*oud* incense'.
49103ef0-90f2-547a-8043-173577467243.author: Amanda Snyder, Mona Mukhashab

4a08eb73-aef2-5e58-9066-f1c85dd23da4.name: Bracket Clock
4a08eb73-aef2-5e58-9066-f1c85dd23da4.description:
The case, made of gilt wood, has rich Rococo decoration. Its outline is composed of elongated C-scrolls primarily. The clock has a brass chapter ring with incised Roman numerals for the hours and Arabic numerals for minutes (at five-minute intervals). Semi-precious stones are applied at the outer edge of the chapter ring, at the centre of which is a small movable disc with alarm-setting marks from 1 to 12, and above it an aperture showing the control pendulum. All gaps as well as the arch of the dial have applied ornaments – C-scrolls, *rocaille* and leaves – made of silvered brass.  
The movement between plates is spring-driven with a verge escapement and a short pendulum. The hours, half and quarter hours are struck on bells. It has a separate alarm movement with a verge escapement and short pendulum.  
This clock is unusual for having above its main movement another, smaller one also with a verge escapement and pendulum. This served to drive the alarm and connected to the centre of the lower movement with a lever. It is wound up through the opening in the arch of the dial.  
The clock was in use in the Maruševec Manor near Varaždin. At the beginning of the 18th century Count Krsto Vragović owned the manor, he died in 1717 in a battle against the Turks. After that, Maruševec belonged to the Paszthory and Patačić families. In the 19th century, its owners were count Artur Schlippenbach and Oskar Pongratz.  
After the Second World War, the state confiscated the manor.
4a08eb73-aef2-5e58-9066-f1c85dd23da4.short_description: A richly decorated bracket clock from Maruševec Manor near Varaždin the case, made of gilt wood, has Rococo decoration.

4c16a8ad-8dfc-54dd-bc70-ac76e6862585.name: Decorative wooden panel.
4c16a8ad-8dfc-54dd-bc70-ac76e6862585.description:
A cedarwood panel comprising wood imported mainly from Lebanon that was part of a wider scale procurement process which took place during the implementation of the grand Umayyad project to erect the Haram al-Sharif. The development of the Haram included the construction of the Dome of the Rock, al-Aqsa Mosque and other buildings. The panel presented here is one of a collection of pieces similar in size and carving technique, although different with regard to the decorative program. The Islamic Museum has acquired 16 of these panels, while the Palestinian Museum (Rockefeller Museum) holds some pieces from the collection. In addition to these decorative cedarwood panels, the Islamic Museum holds a large collection of undecorated pieces, including undecorated wooden beams, some of which extend to more than 10 m in length, and date back to the Umayyad period. These panels and beams were retrieved during restoration works at al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock, and form a basic resource for the study of woodworking techniques used in Umayyad constructions. Additionally, the Islamic Museum has acquired other collections of woodwork dating to the Abbasid, Fatimid, Ayyubid, Mamluk and Ottoman periods. The comprehensive woodwork collection at the Museum is considered to be a rare resource for the study of Islamic woodworking throughout the ages.  
This panel has been carved in low relief, which has led to a notable projection of the decoration. The decoration consists of whirling vegetal motifs and various geometric forms. The decorative style is not dissimilar to that of the Umayyad period, which combined several different styles including Byzantine, Sassanid, Coptic, and local Syrian.  
The piece under discussion is adorned with decoration. Central to the overall scheme is a vase in the form of a goblet out which emerges a whirling plant in the shape of three pairs of branching and intertwining leaves that lengthen along the extent of the panel. The decoration is contained within a rectangular frame that is contained on the outside by vegetal motifs; these aim towards connecting this panel with its neighbours, thereby facilitating the transfer from one decorative theme to the next.
4c16a8ad-8dfc-54dd-bc70-ac76e6862585.short_description: This piece of woodwork was used in the building of the Dome of the Rock. Its is thought to be the oldest Islamic woodwork still extant in its original location. The wood is decorated with very beautiful geometric and vegetal motifs and is a reflection of Umayyad decorative arts whose sources derived from different pre-Islamic arts.
4c16a8ad-8dfc-54dd-bc70-ac76e6862585.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
4c16a8ad-8dfc-54dd-bc70-ac76e6862585.initial_owner: Caliph 'Abd al-Malik bin Marwan (r. AH 65–86 / AD 685–705) or Caliph al-Walid bin 'Abd al-Malik (r. AH 86–96 / AD 705–15).
4c16a8ad-8dfc-54dd-bc70-ac76e6862585.dimensions: Height 193 cm, width 55 cm, depth: 8–10 cm.
4c16a8ad-8dfc-54dd-bc70-ac76e6862585.method_for_datation: The date for this panel has been established by comparison with other related pieces: for example, the decoration and technique used to carve this piece were compared with similar woodwork at Khirbat al-Mafjar (Hisham's Palace) in Jericho. Comparisons have also been drawn with other Umayyad pieces.
4c16a8ad-8dfc-54dd-bc70-ac76e6862585.method_for_provenance: Jerusalem was narrowed down as the place of production by means of documents pertaining to the restoration of al-Aqsa Mosque, which have been preserved by al-Aqsa Mosque Restoration Committee.
4c16a8ad-8dfc-54dd-bc70-ac76e6862585.obtention: The piece was initially placed in the al-Aqsa Mosque following construction, by order of 'Abd al-Malik or his son al-Walid, and subsequently transferred from al-Aqsa Mosque to the Islamic Museum in 1938.

4c67ed2f-ee8b-5b76-827e-611ac07238ea.name: Pearl Trader’s Scales Box
4c67ed2f-ee8b-5b76-827e-611ac07238ea.short_description: This wooden box was designed to contain a sophisticated scales set, which incorporated both a large balance and bowls for weighing quantities of pearls and a smaller version, with several, graded weighing bowls for smaller quantities. The weighing systems for pearls was complex and highly sophisticated to allow for the accurate assessment of mixed batches of pearls of varying sizes and quality. The largest and most valuable pearls were separated and assessed individually. The other pearls would be passed through graded sieves and separated into three batches of specific size.  Apart from the very best items, pearls from these batches were sold by weight.

4c71acf9-d06b-5c50-b777-26a1cf2db6b5.name: Door panel with carved decoration
4c71acf9-d06b-5c50-b777-26a1cf2db6b5.short_description: A single door panel with three identical inset decorative panels each carved with a combination of different vegetal motifs in the bevelled style. The carving is characteristic of the Samarra style as it was developed in the building of the homonymous city in the ninth century. Marble wall revetments from the caliph’s palace in the same city contain identical ornamentation.
keywords: Door panel; Bevelled style; Wood; carving

4c9b3c73-f021-537b-b1bc-a5a3c53c31bf.name: Frieze.
4c9b3c73-f021-537b-b1bc-a5a3c53c31bf.description:
The upper part of this long panel is decorated with a traditional Marinid ribbon of eight-petal rosettes between two fillets. The main section sits below this band and is divided into two decorative areas.  
The lower area consists of plant motifs in low relief: noduled foliage and smooth double palms.  
The upper area consists of alternating high-relief arcatures in two different sizes. They consist of two superposed arches separated by a groove: the upper arch is undulated and the lower arch consists of double-palm lobes and is rendered in *cavetto*.  
The large arcatures are crowned with fleurons that cut into the rosette band. They contain an inscription in twisted pseudo-*kufic* characters with floral upstrokes and bear a mirror image of the word '*yumn*' (prosperity), similar to the motifs used in Marinid architectural decoration.  
The smaller ones are stamped with a ribbed six-lobe palmette and crowned with plant decoration surrounded by two bound lobes and flanked by adventitious floral upstrokes that extend beyond the sides of the large arcatures.  
The movement of the floral motifs, which is harmoniously adapted to the shape of the epigraphic decoration, and the spacing of the spandrels of the arches, as well as their large and rigorous rendering, make this well-made Marinid piece particularly interesting.
4c9b3c73-f021-537b-b1bc-a5a3c53c31bf.short_description: The decorative elements of this panel (rosette frame, arches, pseudo-epigraphic inscriptions, palmette and floral motifs) along with their layout and execution are reminiscent of the decorated friezes found at the top of gallery walls in Fez's Marinid *madrasas*.
4c9b3c73-f021-537b-b1bc-a5a3c53c31bf.dimensions: Height 31.5 cm, length 244.5 cm, depth 5 cm.
4c9b3c73-f021-537b-b1bc-a5a3c53c31bf.method_for_datation: From comparative analysis. The decorative elements of this panel, rosette frame, arches, pseudo-epigraphic inscription, palmettes and floral motifs, as well as their layout and execution are reminiscent of the ornamentation found on friezes on top of the walls in the galleries of Marinid *madrasas* in Fez, in particular the Buinaniya.

4cdf29ad-f45a-562e-8ea4-fa190cc10ab3.name: Wooden panel with epigraphic blazon.
4cdf29ad-f45a-562e-8ea4-fa190cc10ab3.description: A wooden panel with a central field and narrow border. Within the central field a round tripartite, epigraphic blazon is set against an arabesque ground. The titles of Sultan Quaytbay (r. AH 872–901 /AD 1468–96) occupy the centre ground, his name is given above and his victory evoked below. The three inscriptions, rendered in *thuluth* script read: ‘al-sultan al-malik al-ashraf’ (centre) ‘Qaytbay’ (above) ‘izz nasrihi’ (below). The central field is surrounded by a stylised split-palmette scroll. Qai’tbay was a prolific patron of both the arts and architecture, he commissioned a large number of mosques, public fountains (*sabil)* religious schools (*madrasa*) and inns (*wikala*). It has been suggested that this panel originally came from the *Wikala* of Sultan Qa’itbay in Cairo, but without further details it is difficult to assign this piece with certainty to that particular complex.
4cdf29ad-f45a-562e-8ea4-fa190cc10ab3.short_description: This wooden panel carries the composite blazon of the Mamluk sultan Qaytbay. Qaytbay was an outstanding patron of the arts and of architecture. He commissioned a large number of mosques, public fountains, religious schools and inns (*wikalas*). This panel is said to come from his *wikala* in Cairo.
4cdf29ad-f45a-562e-8ea4-fa190cc10ab3.method_for_datation: The epigraphic blazon in the centre of the panel gives the titles and the name of the Mamluk Sultan Qaytbay (r. 872–901 / 1468–96).
4cdf29ad-f45a-562e-8ea4-fa190cc10ab3.method_for_provenance: The epigraphic blazon in the centre of the panel gives the titles and name of the Mamluk Sultan Qaytbay; it is possible that this panel was commissioned for the *Wikala* of Sultan Qaytbay in Cairo.
4cdf29ad-f45a-562e-8ea4-fa190cc10ab3.provenance: Possibly from the Wikala of Sultan Qaytbay in Cairo, Egypt.
4cdf29ad-f45a-562e-8ea4-fa190cc10ab3.obtention: Purchased by the NMS from the Maurice Collection in 1884.

4e79bace-bc0e-55dc-9c99-de21e6fc0f6b.name: *Kelek* raft
4e79bace-bc0e-55dc-9c99-de21e6fc0f6b.description:
The Iraqi word for raft is *kelek*, a name that can be traced from Sumerian (*ka-la*) via Akkadian (*kalakku*). Most *keleks* were made on banks of the Tigris in mountainous areas of what is now Iraqi Kurdistan and southern Turkey. *keleks* were traditionally constructed using a grid of long, straight poles made from tree saplings – an important export from the northern highlands to Mosul and Baghdad since ancient times, used in construction and for a wide range of purposes after the rafts had been dismantled.  
  
The *kelek* differs from log rafts as its poles are supported on floats to increase buoyancy: traditionally these were made from inflated animal skins (more recent versions have been known to use tyre inner tubes). The poles and floats are tied together with cordage made from leather, goat-hair, or other materials sourced from further afield.  
  
Some *keleks* were used simply to transport the wooden poles that made up the raft; others carried additional heavy cargoes, including giant millstones and the raw stone used to build ancient Mesopotamian cities. *Keleks* from the northern highlands generally made only one downstream journey before being dismantled and used for their materials. *Keleks* were photographed on the Tigris in the early AH 14th / AD 20th century and were used by archaeologist A. H. Layard to transport statues from Nineveh downstream to Baghdad in the AH mid 13th / AD mid-19th century.  
  
*Keleks* are depicted on at least two Assyrian reliefs from the reign of Sennacherib (705-681 BC): in one scene the raft carries passengers and a fisherman, while another shows it carrying two large stone blocks. Both rafts are propelled by oarsmen seated at the front of the raft. One is guided by a swimmer on an animal skin float.  
  
The *kelek* in the collection of the Open Museum for Water Culture is a reconstruction made in AH 1446/ AD 2024 by a craftsman from Sulaymaniyah, Iraqi Kurdistan.

50c3aa93-d400-5d9f-824f-b394e33b63a6.short_description: This beylical salon is furnished with carved wood from the beylik era, and consists of three large double-seater benches and four smaller benches with full armrests and topped with a pediment. 51c01d82-0b4a-5399-8607-c519021252c0.name: Switchboard (*Telefon Santrali*)
51c01d82-0b4a-5399-8607-c519021252c0.short_description: In 1840, the Ministry of Post made an announcement describing the postal service, declaring it necessary in order to facilitate communication among people. The first regulations about the postal organisation were taken from French Law in 1840. Ottoman Postal Code included 44 specific headlines. In 1855 the first telegraph service and in 1909 the first telephone service were put into common use as a demonstration of modern communication. In order to improve the technology of the telegraph systems, Ottoman authorities imported well-known machines with trademarks such as Siemens & Halske and Western Electric. As a result of this technological improvement, Ottoman officials decided to establish a telegraph factory. Between 1869 and 1915 this factory produced many devices and accessories.
keywords: architecture; Vedat Tek; postal service; communication

521d6cfc-68ec-53af-a60c-48b720b5bbf7.name: Armchairs
521d6cfc-68ec-53af-a60c-48b720b5bbf7.short_description: The armchairs are veneered with ivory, engraved with flowers and leaves as well as mythical beasts and birds. Featuring a central mirror framed with studded tortoiseshell above various openwork rails, the back embellished with metal jewel-like cartouches. The seat on flutes solid ivory front legs and swept forward back legs are supported by engraved gilt brass and gold peacocks with mechanical springs that make the wings flap when weight is applied to their backs. The association of peacocks with thrones, however, goes back to Shah Jahan's famous peacock throne, built in AD 1635.

530f0310-0111-5a9b-bcd8-d43868876a42.name: Panel with abstract decoration
530f0310-0111-5a9b-bcd8-d43868876a42.short_description: This carved panel comes from Egypt, where wood, on account of its rarity and cost, was decorated with care and used in contexts generally reserved for luxury materials. Although it is impossible to say how this wood panel was used originally, it is possible to assign it to the late 3rd/late 9th century on the basis of its distinctive decoration. Decorated in the bevelled style, the panel depicts highly stylised leaves that have been transformed into abstract motifs. As is typical of this style, it is impossible to distinguish between background and foreground or between natural and abstract forms. The bevelled style may have first been developed at Samarra, in northern Iraq, which replaced Baghdad as the Abbasid capital, from Hegira 221–279 / AD 836 to 892. This style was quickly adopted in other parts of the Islamic empire including Egypt, as exemplified by the decoration in the Mosque of Ibn Tulun, Cairo.
530f0310-0111-5a9b-bcd8-d43868876a42.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)

530f0310-0111-5a9b-bcd8-d43868876a42.method_for_datation: It is datable on the basis of its distinctive decoration in the so-called bevelled style as in the mosque of Ibn Tulun and can likewise be ascribed to Egypt.
530f0310-0111-5a9b-bcd8-d43868876a42.method_for_provenance: The style of the panel relates to the architectural decoration of the mosque of Ibn Tulun in Cairo, completed in Hegira 265 / AD 879.

53178417-31fa-543d-866e-9ede2d175694.name: Door Panel
53178417-31fa-543d-866e-9ede2d175694.short_description: Ivory inlays were frequently combined with wood in the production of furniture and architectural fittings in late medieval Egypt. This elaborate method of fabrication, which used costly ivory and rare woods like ebony, required that individual elements, often of minute size, be cut, carved with intricate motifs, and then carefully constructed like a mosaic to form a larger unit of generally geometric design. Accuracy in cutting and assembling was essential since every piece affects the whole. It is difficult to say exactly how the present door functioned, but most likely it was one of a pair, perhaps for a cupboard set into a wall of either a religious or a secular building.

53178417-31fa-543d-866e-9ede2d175694.method_for_datation: The ornamentation and technique suggest a date in the early Mamluk period.

550798b2-2ff6-5c87-b3f5-df183a1a2b89.name: Bridal cushions (background: Maan section of Hijaz Railroad, Jordan)
550798b2-2ff6-5c87-b3f5-df183a1a2b89.description: Bridal cushions from Ma’an, Jordan, traditionally prepared by a bride as part of her trousseau for her new home, are among the most distinctive examples of Jordanian domestic textiles. Their fabrics and techniques reflect connections with textile traditions from the Caucasus, Syria, Turkey, and Central Asia, shaped through centuries of travel, trade, pilgrimage, and cultural exchange. These influences reached Ma’an through its position as an important crossroads on regional routes, particularly as a key stop along the Hejaz Railway, built during the Ottoman period to facilitate travel between Damascus and the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. The background image is from the G. Eric and Edith Matson Photograph Collection at the Library of Congress, showing the Hejaz Railway, which connected communities across the Ottoman Empire and facilitated movement for travellers, pilgrims, and merchants between the Levant and the Hijaz.
550798b2-2ff6-5c87-b3f5-df183a1a2b89.holder: Tiraz: Widad Kawar Home for Arab Dress
550798b2-2ff6-5c87-b3f5-df183a1a2b89.author: Laila Mushahwar
keywords: Furniture; Marriage; Wedding; Ceremony; Textile

55e346ff-6f0e-5e17-90fe-1d309d2d7056.name: Painted chest
55e346ff-6f0e-5e17-90fe-1d309d2d7056.short_description: The main façade of the chest is adorned with a composition of flowers, branches and fruits in curvilinear compartments, while the corners depict female figures flanked by columns. The interior of the lid shows a landscape with five male figures: a man with a European garment sitting on the ground observing another figure dressed in European clothes, two figures on horseback with Ottoman costumes and a European traveller. The panels in the style of rocailles that adorn both the main and the side views of the chest, the compositions of fruit and flowers and the soft colours refer to the prevailing influence of the rococo style that is dominant in the frescos of the mansions of Lesvos the late 18th century. Both the structure of the mansions and the decorative repertoire follow Ottoman aesthetic as these were by influenced by European art but blending baroque, rococo and neoclassical styles.
55e346ff-6f0e-5e17-90fe-1d309d2d7056.author: Xenia Politou
keywords: furniture; rococo; baroque

56669d0c-f1dc-5ef6-92fc-a676c2150aa7.name: Wooden shelving unit
56669d0c-f1dc-5ef6-92fc-a676c2150aa7.short_description: This shelf belonged to a traditional house in the town of Ksar Hellal. It would been hung from a wall as decoration, holding vases and perfume sprinklers, as well as weapons. It is characterized by its floral patterns with birds, flowers and leaves painted in stylised colours on a pale green background, all surrounding a multicolour fish.

58752dc4-a710-5e08-bb58-f1e52b715cb4.name: Axe
58752dc4-a710-5e08-bb58-f1e52b715cb4.description: The traditional hand-forged axe is a simple but highly functional implement which dates back to antiquity in Oman. It is used to shape, chop and split wood, with its steel head serving as a wedge to force wood fibres apart and its wooden handle acting as a lever to increase force at the cutting edge.

58d8569e-9dce-5ab4-bed2-63c6b0b22bb0.name: Cabinet on stand
58d8569e-9dce-5ab4-bed2-63c6b0b22bb0.description: The Neo-Mudéjar style gave new light to different workshops and techniques. As a consequence of this revival woodwork technique for furniture, such as the inlay in Granada style, was recreated in different pieces of furniture such as this cabinet. The decoration of stars and interlacing arabesques at the front of the cabinet shows the influence of the Mudéjar art.
58d8569e-9dce-5ab4-bed2-63c6b0b22bb0.author: Ana Cabrera
keywords: Neo-mudejar style; Applied ArtsProduction of applied arts in Europe in the Islamic mode

5bd0b400-e2a7-5040-8e6d-9c15256ea7f9.name: Wooden panel.
5bd0b400-e2a7-5040-8e6d-9c15256ea7f9.description:
This long decorative panel, carved in low relief and with slightly damaged ends, consists of five well-balanced sections arranged symmetrically along a longitudinal axis. These sections and the panel sides are framed with grooved and cabled borders.  
The lower section is delimited with a lobed arcature containing an arch supported on floral capitals and twisted columns rendered in relief on a dense floral background. This consists of bouquets of palmettes and finely veined single and double palms on either side of ascending stems reminiscent of the tree of life theme.  
The second section is decorated with circular foliage bearing, at regular intervals, veined nodules, single veined calyx palms, double digitate palms and concave coil palms.  
The third section is decorated with geometric ornamentation: an octagonal braid in relief embellished with pearls crowns a composition of mixtilinear knotwork that radiates from an eight-pointed star. A longitudinal groove cuts across this strip.  
The fourth section is similar to the second. The fifth consists of grooved knotwork combining squares and four-lobed curvilinear stars. These polygonal figures created by the knotwork lines are filled at different levels with floral motifs that soften the geometric composition: veined symmetrical calyx palms inserted between two asymmetrical palms with intertwined stems and six-petal rosettes.  
All of these well ordered and finely executed decorative themes, inspired by flora, geometry and architecture, are found in different Almoravid buildings and objects.
5bd0b400-e2a7-5040-8e6d-9c15256ea7f9.short_description: This long ornate panel, carved in low relief, is decorated with finely executed and hierarchically arranged plant, geometric and architectural motifs, as found in different Almoravid buildings and objects known today.
5bd0b400-e2a7-5040-8e6d-9c15256ea7f9.method_for_datation: Through comparative study. Several of the motifs chosen to decorate this piece and their relief, ornamental composition and abundance are also found in other dated Almoravid pieces, such as the *minbar* of the Great Mosque of Algiers, the decoration on the domes of the Qarawiyyin and the Marrakesh *qubba*. This enables us to date this panel to the Almoravid period and specifically to the reign of 'Ali ibn Yusuf (500–37 / 1106–42).
5bd0b400-e2a7-5040-8e6d-9c15256ea7f9.obtention: Salvaged along with other ancient wooden pieces.

5e718b75-a6e3-5eae-9b65-a96062887c90.name: *Dlu*
5e718b75-a6e3-5eae-9b65-a96062887c90.description: The *dlu* is a traditional leather bucket used in Moroccan oases to draw water from deep wells. Typically crafted from thick goat leather treated with natural oils, it was strong enough to withstand constant immersion while remaining flexible. Attached to a rope and pulley system, the *dlu* was lowered into wells to collect water, then hoisted up for domestic, agricultural, and animal use. Its design reflects both simplicity and efficiency, adapted to arid environments where groundwater was the primary source of survival. In Tafilalet, where *khettaras* and wells structured daily life, the *dlu* was indispensable to communities before mechanised pumps. It represents the resilience of rural craftsmanship and the crucial role of traditional tools in sustaining livelihoods in desert societies.

5eacbf30-4e9e-5c27-a757-04efcf633b45.name: Wooden frieze.
5eacbf30-4e9e-5c27-a757-04efcf633b45.description:
An almost complete frieze that would undoubtedly have come from a religious monument. Its surface is decorated with a flowery and twisted *kufic* inscription repeating the end of Qur'anic verse 73 of Sura 22 ('Pilgrimage'). The *kufic* characters are embellished with vegetal elements in the form of tri-lobed demi-fleurons and five-lobed fleurons that prolong the angle of the bevel.  
The text is carved on a plant background consisting of a dense floral composition with absolutely no empty spaces. This decorative element uses pinecones and palms carried by foliage or decorating the involutions: asymmetric smooth palms with calyxes and branches stretching into loops and veined double palms with acanthus leaves whose offshoot, which separates the veins into twos, assumes an oval shape reminiscent of a pinecone scale.  
This frieze, with its low-relief decoration covering the entire surface and where a taste for abundance and ornamental opulence has supplanted Almohad rigour and simplicity, well illustrates the aesthetic choices of Marinid art, which adopts some elements of Almoravid art.
5eacbf30-4e9e-5c27-a757-04efcf633b45.short_description: This incomplete frieze would almost certainly have come from a religious monument. It is decorated with a Qur'anic inscription in flowery, twisted *kufic* characters on an unbroken background of plant decoration in low relief, a good illustration of aesthetic choices in Marinid art.
5eacbf30-4e9e-5c27-a757-04efcf633b45.dimensions: Height 21.6 cm, length 107 cm, depth 3.5 cm.
5eacbf30-4e9e-5c27-a757-04efcf633b45.method_for_datation: From stylistic analysis. The rendering of the letters and the floral forms, which can also be seen in the decoration of the Bab Mrissa gateway in Salé dating from the second half of the 7th / 13th century, as well as its decoration suggests the style of the beginning of the Marinid era.

63191935-a807-58a4-b11e-292c88a654f7.name: Dawud Pasha’s living room
63191935-a807-58a4-b11e-292c88a654f7.short_description: This bedroom belonged to the first *mutasarrif* (ruler) of the Mount Lebanon *mutasarrifiyya*, Dawud Pasha, who governed from 1861–68). The room is furnished with four armchairs and one large sofa. The sofa has a high wooden back, covered with a mosaic of white, beige and brown ceramic and bone pieces, organised in floral and geometric patterns. The seat cushions are covered with navy and beige silk decorated with similar patterns. The sofa was reserved for guests, which Dawud Pasha would receive from his large armchair, a sign of power and authority. The room is lit by two glass lanterns painted with white and golden floral patterns, and a round copper table sits in the centre of the room.
63191935-a807-58a4-b11e-292c88a654f7.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
keywords: Woodwork; Furniture; Floral decoration

64ac8dbf-8dd2-5b1c-a223-2129d475ce2e.name: Case for the crown of Stefan Bocskai
64ac8dbf-8dd2-5b1c-a223-2129d475ce2e.short_description: This decagonal domed case is made of wood and covered with fabric. The clasp at the front and the hinges at the back are silver-gilt. The fabric of the cover is costly Persian silk and is decorated with a figural scene surrounded by flowers. Half sitting, half reclining, a lady is reading a book. Beside her kneels a servant with a wide, sweeping *turban*, offering her a bowl with his right hand and holding a bottle in his left. Between the two figures lies a bowl containing fruit. In the lady's open book can be read the signature of the artist Mu'min, in Arabic script. On the inside of the case, the fabric retains all the freshness of its original colours, and is typical of the refined taste of the court of Shah 'Abbas the Great (AD 1587–1628) at Isfahan. Technically, it can be described as a double-woven lampas of coloured silk. Glued to the floor of the case is an Italian fabric from the early 17th century. Its ground is warp satin in red silk; the pattern, which takes the form of pinnate leaves and blossoms, is yellow silk woven in twill and intervowen with silver.
keywords: Safawid; textile; lampas; satin; floral decoration; figurative decoration; Shah `Abbas the Great; Mu´min; woodwork; court life; women; Italian textiles;

64ec1971-c448-5f70-9a89-e93744796b79.name: Screen.
64ec1971-c448-5f70-9a89-e93744796b79.description: The screen consists of three wooden hinged panels filled with latticework. Each panel is structured in square and rectangular sections of different sizes that show a diversity of geometric designs. Vertical, horizontal and diagonal bars linked by balls with flattened surfaces form the small and large squares, hexagons and abstract flower-like motifs of the latticework. The combination of all these elements in varying density creates the vivid impression of the surfaces. In addition, small hinged apertures and a bay window are integrated in the pattern of the two external panels and the middle panel.
64ec1971-c448-5f70-9a89-e93744796b79.short_description: Screen consisting of three panels filled with latticework. Each panel is structured in square and rectangular sections. They show geometric designs formed of vertical, horizontal and diagonal bars. Small hinged apertures and a bay window are also integrated in the pattern.

65a53b99-07d5-5553-b2ed-33b6de70f6c6.name: Covered Vessel with Relief Design of Arabic Inscription in *Kufic* Script
65a53b99-07d5-5553-b2ed-33b6de70f6c6.short_description:
A circular steatite vessel with a thin, flat lid with a vertical, eared wing handle that has a mushroom-shaped cut-out in the center. Around the exterior of the lid is a band of cross-hatching, and another band of the same width crossing the diameter of the lid. This band is also cross-hatched on one half, up to where it intersects with the handle, then becomes "transparent," filled only with the raised relief inscription beneath that covers the remaining surface of the lid.  
The vessel has straight sides with an upper and lower border of cross-hatching, enclosing a relief band of inscription. The stone is carved to form an Arabic inscription in relief, in an angular script style known as *Kufic*. The tops of the taller letters end in leaves and flowers, a popular calligraphic device in the 10th century. On opposing sides of the vessel are bar-like handles with deep gouges on their outer edges. The area where each handle attaches to the vessel is bordered by cross-hatching.
65a53b99-07d5-5553-b2ed-33b6de70f6c6.dates: Hegira Late 2nd to late 4th / AD 10th century
65a53b99-07d5-5553-b2ed-33b6de70f6c6.dimensions: Height with cover: 14.9cm; Diameter of cover: 21.9cm; Height of vessel without cover: 10.2cm; Diameter of mouth: 22.2cm; Width across handles: 24.8cm; Diameter of base: 22.2cm

65a53b99-07d5-5553-b2ed-33b6de70f6c6.method_for_provenance: Steatite vessels such as this one were used for cooking in the 9th–10th centuries in the northeastern Iranian city of Nishapur. Many small steatite objects have been excavated, but this is the largest complete vessel known.

66b6c62d-5658-5fa6-8f5b-88e0825b6ea8.name: Bureau cabinet for the display of porcelain
66b6c62d-5658-5fa6-8f5b-88e0825b6ea8.description:
A tripartite-body bureau cabinet with varied veneering, it has a chest of drawers at the bottom with three wavy fronted drawers; a bureau with a fall-front in the middle, and a glazed top section with doors that shut onto an interior lined in green silk, with shaped, carved, gilded shelves and consoles to display porcelain.  
While the design for this type of furniture is typical of Venetian production, its purpose reflects contemporary European enthusiasm for the Far East and its art, especially porcelain and lacquer. Although lacquer and porcelain objects were imported into Europe, craftsmen there attempted to master the techniques of lacquer production, and the first European porcelain factories were opened around this time. The popularity of these wares resulted in special porcelain and lacquer display halls in mansions and palaces and the use of bureau cabinets such as this one.
66b6c62d-5658-5fa6-8f5b-88e0825b6ea8.short_description: A tripartite-body bureau cabinet with varied veneering, the top section consists of a carved gilded structure with consoles for displaying porcelain closed by a double glazed door. The bureau’s purpose reflects contemporary European enthusiasm for the Far East and its art, especially porcelain and lacquer, which resulted in special porcelain and lacquer display halls in mansions and palaces and the use of bureau cabinets such as this one.

67c03df2-c806-5779-b549-c93b16f6fdb8.name: Box
67c03df2-c806-5779-b549-c93b16f6fdb8.short_description: From the fifteenth century onward, lacquer objects—including bookbindings, pen cases and boxes such as this one—gained popularity in Iran, peaking in the nineteenth century. Constructed of papier-mâché and sometimes wood, lacquer objects were decorated with small-scale paintings of popular motifs like floral patterns, birds, and royal scenes before a varnish was applied that protected the painting and added a pleasing amber glow. This box is decorated with beautifully painted animal scenes that hark back to earlier Persian manuscript illustrations and the lid depicts Sagittarius, the centaur archer, aiming a bow at his tail, which ends in a dragon head, a long-established image in Iran.

67c03df2-c806-5779-b549-c93b16f6fdb8.method_for_datation: The lacquer medium and the style of painted decoration suggests this box was made in nineteenth-century Iran.
67c03df2-c806-5779-b549-c93b16f6fdb8.method_for_provenance: Lacquer was a particularly popular and established medium in Qajar Iran and the painted decoration relates to an earlier tradition of Persian manuscript illustration.

685a2ad1-af1f-51a1-a4f2-d4dc7fc2a7f0.name: Wooden Sideboard with Mother of Pearl Inlay
685a2ad1-af1f-51a1-a4f2-d4dc7fc2a7f0.short_description: This tall, intricately carved sideboard consists of two parts, the mirror section with intricately carved openwork and mashrabiya ornamentation enhanced with mother-of-pearl inlay, and the narrow table section decorated with similar elements and with its four front legs supporting an elaborate system of lobed arches. the sideboard is further enhanced by religious inscriptions, some of which seem to suggest a Christian context. Sideboards and other European-style furniture were unknown in the Middle East until the second half of the12th/ 18th century. By the 13th/ 19th century, the urban elites in Ottoman cities enthusiastically imported domestic furniture from Italy, France and England or bought locally-made hybrid pieces that combined European and traditional Islamic elements like the item shown here. Many European entrepreneurs like the Italian Furino Brothers, based in Cairo, set up shop in Ottoman cities and specialised in this so-called Arabesque style, especially fashionable for furniture.

68860d9a-5a4b-577c-8584-cef6ff62671a.name: Pair of clogs
68860d9a-5a4b-577c-8584-cef6ff62671a.description:
The high heeled clogs (ar. *qabqab*, tr. *nalın* are an emblematic item of the hamam reflecting the atmosphere of such public baths. They were worn when entering the bath complex to protect the wearer from the dirty water as well as from the hot marble floor. Wearing these shoes meant that the wearer was obliged to walk slowly to avoid falling. This slower pace was in tune with the temporality dictated by the rhythms of the hamam and its cleansing rituals.  
  
This pair of clogs is attributed to Syria. They are made of wood inlaid with silver and multi-coloured triangular pieces of mother-of-pearl. The front and rear parts of the sole are incrusted with repoussé silver bands decorated with floral motifs encircled with two dotted lines. They are embellished with long silver chains ending in trinkets which must have created a gentle tinkling with each step highlighting the sound dimension of the hamam.  
  
The strap holding the foot is made of various layers of leather for comfort. It is topped with a large silver band intricately designed and solidly nailed to the sole.  
  
This pair of clogs is particularly high, suggesting that it might have been the property of the hamam owner who traditionally wore sophisticated clogs with heels higher than those of the clients. Often offered as part of the dowry of the bride in a toiletry trousseau providing her with all the hamam essentials, the clogs were a statement on the social status of their owner and could also bear many symbolic meanings through their decoration.  
  
Although strongly associated with femininity, hamam clogs, with lower heels and different ornamentation, were also worn by men in their own establishments.

68860d9a-5a4b-577c-8584-cef6ff62671a.author: Dounia Handis
keywords: Water; clogs ; Ottomans; hammam, ablutions; qabqab; nalın
materials: Wood with silver and mother-of-pearl overlay

6af5bf51-a5aa-558d-8578-3ac815792a90.name: *Zaima* reed boat
6af5bf51-a5aa-558d-8578-3ac815792a90.description:
The *zaima* is a small reed canoe from the Marshlands of southern Iraq, made of reed bundles of narrow diameter sewn together to form a flat base and sides. Its internal bracing may be made from flexible stems such as cane, palm frond, date bunch stalk (forming the prow), or small branches of trees such as willow, acacia or *gherib*, and it is waterproofed with an outer coating of bitumen. Evidence of these boats' existence in recent decades is sparse, but reports from earlier centuries suggest they were once much more common. Travellers to Mesopotamia in the AH 12th / AD 18th and AH 13th / AD 19th centuries reported that the Marshes were full of canoes made from reeds and cane, tarred on the outside.  
  
During the AH 14th / AD 20th century, especially in the 1970s when the extent of the Marshes and the density of boat traffic reached a peak, the majority of canoes (*meshoufs*) were made of planked wood joined with nails. Images and accounts of reed or cane canoes in this period are exceptional. The only known photographs identified as a *zaima* were taken by the British explorer Wilfred Thesiger in the AH 1370s / AD 1950s. Rashad Salim, during his fieldwork in AH 1438-1441/ AD 2016-19, gathered a handful of oral accounts of reed and cane boats, some known as *zaimas* and some with other names. These were among the simplest and cheapest types of boat made locally by Marsh dwellers.  
  
The boatbuilding community of Huwair, where Safina Projects’ Meshouf-building workshops were held, had no direct experience of constructing *zaimas*, but they agreed to attempt to reconstruct reed and cane canoes, drawing on their familiarity with these widely available local materials (also used in vernacular architecture). They also applied knowledge Rashad Salim had collected in the form of oral history interviews – recorded in both Huwair and Amara – and the photographs and writings of Thesiger. The *zaimas* in the collection of the Open Museum are the result of these experimental workshops.

6b26c1cf-dd38-5093-abf7-2f93ccfd4db3.name: Chair
6b26c1cf-dd38-5093-abf7-2f93ccfd4db3.short_description: This carved wood chair has narrow, curved arms and an elaborate back support. It is extensively inalid with small pieces of ivory, ebony, and other woods. The pieces are predominantly of triangular shape, and have been inset in bands of interlocking hexagons and hexagrams on the exterior surfaces of the chair. The raised seat is upholstered in a William Morris-like print whereby rows of tri-tipped peach floral sprays alternate with white lily sprays, all on a yellow ground.

6b6b4b3d-5bf3-5fad-ab1e-65d67c460f9d.name: Dining room set with bench
6b6b4b3d-5bf3-5fad-ab1e-65d67c460f9d.description:
Displayed in the reception room of Yusuf Al-Sabai's former residence, now part of the FBQ Museum, is a striking dining set comprising a table, chairs, and a bench crafted in the Islamic arabesque style. Renowned for its intricate inlay craftsmanship, this set incorporates mother-of-pearl, ivory, and wood, utilising even the smallest wood chips and other available materials. This approach not only enhances aesthetic appeal but also minimises waste and encourages sustainable practices.  
The set features intricate geometric patterns and architectural elements such as arches and squinches influenced by the Coptic art of Egypt. This piece embodies the essence of Islamic decoration, characterised by unity and meticulous craftsmanship. Its rich ornamentation reflects the concept of *horror vacui* (fear of emptiness), and is evidence of the artist’s desire to fill any available space with intricate details.

6be8c6ea-dc17-5a88-b3da-1b18dceccd50.name: *Namban* Folding Screen (*Namban Byobu*)
6be8c6ea-dc17-5a88-b3da-1b18dceccd50.description:
The *Namban Byobu*, of which there are more than 70 extant, are some of the most impressive visual testimonies to the way Japanese painters perceived the first Europeans to arrive in Japan. The arrival of the Portuguese in 1543 and their expulsion almost a century later in 1639, gave rise to the so called *Namban Bijutsu* artwork, a result of the meeting of the Japanese and European cultures.  
A pair of six-fold painted screens, they both follow the most current theme of the *Namban Byobu*, depicting the arrival of the Portuguese in Japan. On the left, the screen depicts a great ship from Macao, or *kurofune* (“the black ship”), and on the right a procession, or *Namban Gyoretsu*, passing a Japanese street observed by curious inhabitants. Waiting for them are the Jesuits, whose church is built in the Japanese style with interior rooms that largely follow local models, such as the use of *tatami* to cover the floor or of *shoji* to divide the inner space. The daily life of the Jesuit mission is depicted in these *byobu* (*biombo* in Portuguese). The works convey their approach to “accommodation”, according to which special attention was paid to the European priests' and brothers' integration into Japanese society.  
The procession is composed of a Captain-Major, standing underneath a state parasol surrounded by other officers, as well as sailors, African slaves, Indians and Malays. The ornaments worn by the aristocrats and rich merchants are visible and notable: gold chains, crucifixes and daggers. While the majority of the characters wear *bombacha* – large baggy trousers used in the East to protect them from mosquitoes, their doublets have buttons, which were unknown to the Japanese, who called them *botan* from the Portuguese *botão.* This in itself is an interesting example of linguistic appropriation as a result of newly acquired cultural habits.  
These exotic objects, of which much care was taken, included Chinese folding-chairs, lacquered boxes, porcelain, bundles and bales of silk, Persian horses and caged animals. Their different places of origin were the result of Portuguese trade. By the 16th and 17th centuries Portugal had established trade routes along the coastline of the Indian Ocean, the Southern Seas and the China Sea. Some of the traders were born in Asia and many of them were the result of the progressive hybridism that characterised the lives of the Europeans in Asia during the period.
6be8c6ea-dc17-5a88-b3da-1b18dceccd50.short_description: In around 1543, the Portuguese (or *Namban-jin*) arrived in Japan, and so began a period of rich cultural exchange. Similar to several other *Namban* objects, this pair of folding screens – made by artists from Nippon – is a unique visual document that relates to the Portuguese presence in Japan.
6be8c6ea-dc17-5a88-b3da-1b18dceccd50.type: Furnishing that can be included in the *Shoheiga* category, meaning a large painted architectural surface, including folding screens. In this case, it is more specifically *Byobu*, meaning a painted folding screen.
6be8c6ea-dc17-5a88-b3da-1b18dceccd50.initial_owner: Tadao Takamisawa, António da Costa Carneiro, Portuguese ambassador in Japan
6be8c6ea-dc17-5a88-b3da-1b18dceccd50.dimensions: H: 172.8 cm; l: 380.8 cm; depth 2 cm
6be8c6ea-dc17-5a88-b3da-1b18dceccd50.method_for_datation: Tadao Takamisawa attributed the paintings to Kano Domi based on stylistic grounds, and thematic and pictorial parallels with other folding screens and works executed by the Kano school of painting, including Kano Naizen's *Namban Byobu*, also in the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga.
6be8c6ea-dc17-5a88-b3da-1b18dceccd50.obtention: Acquired in the 1930s by Tadao Takamisawa from a *daimyo*'s (Great Lord) castle near Osaka, and later purchased by the Portuguese ambassador –António da Costa Carneiro – in Tokyo. Having belonged to the Ministry of Finance since 1952 it has been on permanent loan to the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga in Lisbon ever since.

6ce9b353-6fa5-545f-8dcd-8780df1109a4.name: Weed cutter (*mahassha*)
6ce9b353-6fa5-545f-8dcd-8780df1109a4.description: This scythe-like agricultural hand tool is traditionally used for cutting weeds in cultivated fields. It also finds use as a reaping tool for crops and animal fodder. The hand-forged steel blade of the cutter is angled for maximum efficiency and attached to a handle made of fig, jujube or lime wood.

6d56bfde-b2d7-5b3d-b418-0b9d3e98d0e8.name: Qur’an Cabinet
6d56bfde-b2d7-5b3d-b418-0b9d3e98d0e8.short_description:
This Qur’an cabinet from Istanbul would embellish rooms in private homes, mosques, *madrasas* (Islamic education centres), and mausoleums. Crafted in the Ottoman style, the box stands on four legs, mother-of-pearl inlaying, geometric patterns and calligraphy.  
  
This rare type of Qur’an cabinet (called *sunduq* or *kursi*) attracts with an unusual form several compartments for religious items and scripts, and the dome-shaped cover. The calligraphy in *Diwani* style reads *Al Fatiha* (the opening chapter of the Qur’an) and *Al Zalzalah* (the 99th chapter).  
  
In the 19th century, the mother-of-pearl style called Damascene became increasingly popular in Ottoman Turkey. Artisans arranged precious materials including mother-of-pearl, tortoiseshell, metals and ivory into interlocking asterisks, octagons and hexagons.
6d56bfde-b2d7-5b3d-b418-0b9d3e98d0e8.owner: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani
6d56bfde-b2d7-5b3d-b418-0b9d3e98d0e8.method_for_datation: The date and origin were established in research-based comparison from an examination of material, calligraphy and style.
6d56bfde-b2d7-5b3d-b418-0b9d3e98d0e8.method_for_provenance: The date and origin were established in research-based comparison from an examination of material, calligraphy and style.
