6da7c160-94fa-5f96-a7c1-9c73200419b5.name: Mihrab.
6da7c160-94fa-5f96-a7c1-9c73200419b5.description:
A wooden *mihrab* with a rectangular section in the centre that is a curved niche. The facade of the *mihrab* is rectangular in form and at the centre it has a rectangular opening, crowned by a pointed arch. The facade is decorated with assembled hexagonal panels, which flank other panels, in the form of six-pointed stars. This design is considered to be the starting point for the use of the decorative component known as 'the star-shaped medallion', which became one of the most important decorative components in wooden objects during the Mamluk period. This *mihrab* is the earliest dated piece on which this decorative component appears. At the top of the facade, are two lines of inscription in floriated *kufic* script that reads: 'One of the things commissioned by the honourable, protected, and great personage, al-Amiriyya, whose service was undertaken by al-Qadi Abu al-Hasan Maknun and who is served now, by al-Amir al-Sadid 'Afif al-Dawla Abu al-Hasan Yumn al-Fa'izi al-Salihi, intended for the shrine of al-Sayyida Ruqayya, the daughter of the Commander of the Faithful, 'Ali'. From the inscription, it is understood that this *mihrab* was made by order of al-Sayyida 'Ulam al-Amiriyya (d. AH 535 / AD 1140), the wife of the caliph, al-Amir bi-Ahkam Allah (r. 495–524 / AD 1101–30), for the tomb of Sayyida Ruqayya. The tomb was built in AH 527 / AD 1133, probably in Cairo. Qur'anic texts written in floriated *kufic* script, from 'al-Baqara' (2: 247), surround the rectangular facade of the *mihrab* and its niche.  
Both sides of the *mihrab,* and the back, are decorated with panels carved with vegetal stems that emerge from vases, and three- and five-lobed vine leaves which surround large clusters of grapes. These decorations indicate the apex of beauty attained in the art of vegetal decoration at the end of the Fatimid period.
6da7c160-94fa-5f96-a7c1-9c73200419b5.short_description: Patronage of religious institutions and providing them with furniture were not confined to men. Many women shared in this practice. This *mihrab* was commissioned by the Caliph's wife for the shrine of Sayyida Ruqayya, the daughter of the Fourth Righteous Caliph, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.
6da7c160-94fa-5f96-a7c1-9c73200419b5.initial_owner: ‘Ulam al-Amiriyya, wife of the caliph, al-Amir bi-Ahkam Allah.
6da7c160-94fa-5f96-a7c1-9c73200419b5.dimensions: Height 210 cm, width 111 cm, depth 45 cm.
6da7c160-94fa-5f96-a7c1-9c73200419b5.method_for_datation: The *mihrab* was dated based on the inscription present in the higher reaches of its façade which state clearly that the *mihrab* was built for the tomb of Sayyida Ruqayya in 527 / 1133
6da7c160-94fa-5f96-a7c1-9c73200419b5.method_for_provenance: The inscription on the *mihrab* states that it was made for the tomb of Sayyida Ruqayya, the patron, who was the wife of the Fatimid Caliph who ruled in Cairo; it is very likely, therefore, that it was commissioned and made in Cairo.
6da7c160-94fa-5f96-a7c1-9c73200419b5.obtention: In 1297 / 1880, the Egyptian government began to collect together artefacts from the country's mosques and historic buildings and preserve them in al-Hakim Mosque. These later became the basis of the collection at the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo. This *mihrab*, which was transferred from the Sayyida Ruqayya Shrine, is considered to be one of the most important of these early acquisitions.

6de30ff8-0fff-5ed3-8984-48abb285b414.name: Double door.
6de30ff8-0fff-5ed3-8984-48abb285b414.description:
Wooden doors, decorated with a braided pattern of stars, were common in Rum-Seljuq mosques, because such complex geometric forms, carved and designed by exceptionally talented wood craftsmen, were much loved. This double door’s decoration is rendered very impressive by the large central panels featuring a geometric design within which individual areas are decorated with arabesque tendrils consisting of individual floral motifs. The geometric design is based on a repeated pattern of small pentagons and hexagons, diamonds and triangles. It is not composed in the usual manner of placing single panels adjacently one after another; instead it consists of a single continuous pattern covering the panel’s entire surface. The wide frieze framing the panels on all sides is decorated with overlapping arabesque tendrils.  
Inscriptions written over a blue background in the upper part of the doors cite Sura 9 verse 18 from the Qur’an: ‘None should come to the mosque of God except those who believe in God and in the Judgement Day’. This inscription was once continued on the door of a neighbouring room to the south. This latter door can also be seen in the Museum of Islamic Art, Berlin. It declares ‘and prayer is said and the poor tax is paid’. Thus, the most important duties of a follower of the Islamic faith were mentioned: confession of faith, prayer and almsgiving. Unlike the double doors that belonged in the front hall and that are decorated over the lower part with plant motifs, these doors are completely covered with decorative geometric patterns. The door from the front hall can be seen today in the Museum in Konya (inventory no. 330).
6de30ff8-0fff-5ed3-8984-48abb285b414.short_description: The inscription from the Qur’an (IX: 18) – ‘None should come to the mosque of God except those who believe in God and in the Judgement Day’ – is appropriate for this wooden door that once led into the Bey Hakim Mosque in Konya, Turkey. The geometric and arabesque patterns are typical of Seljuq art.
6de30ff8-0fff-5ed3-8984-48abb285b414.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
6de30ff8-0fff-5ed3-8984-48abb285b414.method_for_datation: This double door comes from the Bey Hakim mosque in Konya, dated to the mid 7th / 13th century. Stylistic comparison further demonstrates that this double door comes from this period.
6de30ff8-0fff-5ed3-8984-48abb285b414.method_for_provenance: V. Enderlein (see Bibliography) established that this double door comes from the Bey Hakim mosque in Konya. He made this discovery from the inscriptions on both doors, which form a complete text.
6de30ff8-0fff-5ed3-8984-48abb285b414.obtention: Bought from a private owner in 1913.

6ef65a75-a6f9-5d0d-8c90-492c934302b3.name: Window frame.
6ef65a75-a6f9-5d0d-8c90-492c934302b3.description:
A twisted strip and a carved band decorated with a braid of eight-pointed stars runs around the outside of this quadrangular window frame. It consists of three sections: an upper frieze, a balustrade and the gemelled arcature of the opening. All of the wood is covered with a red base and painted in two shades of brown, yellow ochre, ivory white and some green.  
The frieze and the balustrade consist of *mashrabiyya* latticework arranged in a chequered or a diamond pattern. Above this latticework, grooved strips on the balustrade form a knotwork pattern consisting of eight-pointed stars and, on the upper frieze, poly-lobed arches and eight-pointed stars on each side frame a square central medallion bearing the votive inscription 'Mohammed's blessing' in rectangular *kufic* characters.  
The opening, surrounded by two frames, the first in turned wood and the second carved into eight-pointed star knotwork, consists of two gemeled horseshoe arches. These arches are supported on a small column and two small engaged demi-columns in turned wood that are fluted at the base and have simulated capitals. All of the components of this last section are decorated with polychrome plant motifs borrowed both from the Moroccan–Andalusian repertoire and the Ottoman repertoire: foliage, single and double palms, fleurons and carnations.  
With its harmonious polychromy, this external window frame, which looked over the courtyard of a wealthy residence of the 13th / 19th century is a good example of the careful work of the Meknès carpenters who gained renown in this art when their town became the capital of the 'Alawid kingdom under the reign of Mulay Isma'il (AH 1083–1140 / AD 1672–1727).
6ef65a75-a6f9-5d0d-8c90-492c934302b3.short_description: The outer frame of a window overlooking the courtyard of an expensive house is an example of turned, painted wood from Meknès, an art form that flourished in the imperial city from the beginning of the 'Alawid era. The plant decoration is borrowed from Hispano-Maghrebic and Ottoman repertoires.
6ef65a75-a6f9-5d0d-8c90-492c934302b3.method_for_datation: From stylistic and comparative analysis. This type of carpentry, which gives pre-eminence to polychromy and can be found in other museum examples, was first seen in the late 11th / 17th century and became particularly widespread in the 13th / 19th century when middle-class residences, where this sort of work can still be seen, were built in increasing numbers.
6ef65a75-a6f9-5d0d-8c90-492c934302b3.method_for_provenance: From the place it was purchased and its style, which is typical of Meknès.

6f75d3d3-2fb1-5c23-869d-1f05845e0403.name: Writing desk.
6f75d3d3-2fb1-5c23-869d-1f05845e0403.description:
Clerk's chest with a flat lid that fits into the top of the box, making a rectangular prism. It is decorated with different types of wood, mother-of-pearl and bone inlay. The centre of each side of the piece shows a combination of interlinked polygons and eight-pointed stars, while the spaces in between are taken up by four-pointed stars. The whole is framed by a narrow red border followed by other geometrical, smooth and crenellated bands of different widths. The same decorative scheme is repeated on the visible areas of the inside, and the remainder is simply painted.  
The writing desk has retained all of its bronze fixtures: two large hinges that join the lid to the back of the chest, a folded metal sheet riveted to each corner, a keyhole at the front, a handle on the top of the lid fitted with a grip and two handles on the sides for moving it. All of the fixtures are cast and decorated with engravings. The inside of the chest contains a number of compartments intended to store the writing materials.  
The Spanish word *taracea* (marquetry), which is derived from the Arabic word *tarsi* (to insert, inlay), describes a technique that consists of inlaying pieces of wood, bone or mother-of-pearl into a piece of hardwood, such as walnut. This technique of Eastern origin had been perfected in Córdoba in the AH 4th / AD 10th century at the time when al-Hakam II's *minbar* (pulpit), which has not survived,was built. Later, during the Nasrid period, the technique was simplified and the precisely cut pieces were stuck on to a base of paper or parchment, and this was then stuck on to the object.  
This type of desk could be considered to be a precursor of the Spanish *vargueno*.
6f75d3d3-2fb1-5c23-869d-1f05845e0403.short_description: Possibly a writer’s chest that could be carried using the top or side handles. The inside is split into compartments in which writing implements were stored. Inlays of bone, mother-of-pearl and different woods decorated its outer surfaces.
6f75d3d3-2fb1-5c23-869d-1f05845e0403.dimensions: Height 20 cm, width 45 cm, depth 28 cm.
6f75d3d3-2fb1-5c23-869d-1f05845e0403.method_for_datation: Parallels with similar pieces from the National  Archaeological Museum and elsewhere, such as the writing desk of Jaen Cathedral or the chest of the Hispanic Society of America, all dated to the 14th and 15th centuries.
6f75d3d3-2fb1-5c23-869d-1f05845e0403.method_for_provenance: The type of marquetry and decorative design are characteristic of Granada. The insides of the doors of the Nasrid cupboard of the Palace of the Infantas in Granada, which is kept in the National Museum of Hispano-Muslim Art in that city, are decorated with the same stars inscribed in interlinked squares.
6f75d3d3-2fb1-5c23-869d-1f05845e0403.obtention: The piece was purchased for the National Archaeological  Museum on 26 March 1973.

6fdbe124-1e12-5bc3-a524-5bbe4a6ae42f.name: Painted wooden board.
6fdbe124-1e12-5bc3-a524-5bbe4a6ae42f.description:
This cedarwood board comes from the ceilings of the prayer hall of the Great Mosque of Kairouan, where the roof structure is composed of lintels resting on columns and on the walls, following the north–south direction of the nave. The tie-beams, perpendicular to these elements, are supported at each end by carved and painted corbels.  
The oldest part of the ceilings of the Great Mosque of Kairouan dates from the AH 3rd / AD 9th century. It is decorated with foliate scrolls and fleurons.  
The panel has a red background and is composed of four squares with concave sides. Painted green and blue in each of the squares are two intertwining stylised flowers with four petals. They form a sort of octagonal star enclosing a blue or green circle.  
Each petal ends in a bud surrounded by two flared foliate scrolls. Straight out of the Middle Ages, the painted ceilings of the Great Mosque of Kairouan represent an unique collection in Muslim art, which renders any attempt at research into the origin of their decoration quite difficult. In fact, decorated ceilings covered the central nave of the Great Mosque at Córdoba, but the *ante quem* limit of their dating hardly goes back beyond the AH 4th / AD 10th century, and the magnificent ceilings of the Palatine Chapel at Palermo date from the AH 6th / AD 12th century.
6fdbe124-1e12-5bc3-a524-5bbe4a6ae42f.short_description: Originally part of the ceilings of the prayer room in the Great Mosque of Kairouan, this piece is beautifully decorated with foliage and fleurons on a red background. The painted ceilings of the Great Mosque of Kairouan constitute the only collection of its type in Islamic art.
6fdbe124-1e12-5bc3-a524-5bbe4a6ae42f.method_for_datation:
The board's decorative motifs can be found in some of the panels of the carved *minbar* and in the painted wood half-dome of the *mihrab* niche of the Great Mosque of Kairouan, which date from the middle of the 3rd / 9th century. They are certified as being Syrian Umayyad art.  
These indications, as well as comparison with the different types and models of painted wood forming the ceilings collection from the Great Mosque of Kairouan, date this board from the end of the 3rd / 9th century, probably from the time of the restoration work on the doors and ceilings of the prayer hall ordered and funded by the Aghlabid prince, Ibrahim II (r. 261–89 / 875–902). The dating of this panel from the 5th / 11th century is refutable, since the models, boards and beams of this period are not comparable.
6fdbe124-1e12-5bc3-a524-5bbe4a6ae42f.method_for_provenance: These decorative motifs appear in some of the carved panels of the *minbar* and in the painted wood half-dome of the *mihrab* niche of the Great Mosque of Kairouan.
6fdbe124-1e12-5bc3-a524-5bbe4a6ae42f.obtention: After the restoration of the Great Mosque of Kairouan, between 1962 and 1972, some beams, boards and joists were taken out and completely replaced. This piece was placed along with thousands of other fragments in the storerooms of the National Institute of the Patrimony of Kairouan. It was selected for display when the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada was extended.

7045f484-1e6a-55ad-9fd3-497bdc3dd415.name: *Meshouf* (canoe collection)
7045f484-1e6a-55ad-9fd3-497bdc3dd415.description:
The Open Museum for Water Cultures (Basra) holds in its collection 11 *meshoufs* of various types and sizes. *Meshouf* is a generic term for a flat-based canoe made in the region of Iraq's southern marshlands. *meshoufs* range from 3-11m in length and have a narrow form, often with a distinctive crescent-shaped prow.  
  
Variants range from small flat-prowed canoes like the *matour* (a one-man canoe used for hunting waterfowl), to larger types with a prominent curved prow such as the *chilaika*, the prestigious *tarada* (hunting and war canoe of the Marsh Sheikhs), and working vessels like the *barkash*, used for harvesting and transport.  
  
*Meshoufs* became almost extinct from the Iran-Iraq war (1980s) onwards. In Huwair, once a well-known centre for their making, modernised boatbuilding methods and carpentry remained common forms of livelihood. *Meshouf* production was revived with the support of the Safina Projects initiative from AH 1440 / AD 2018 onwards. In addition to the Open Museum’s collection, by AH 1447/ AD 2025 over 70 *meshoufs* were in use across the Iraqi Heritage Boat Clubs Network established by Safina.  
  
Boats of a comparable form have been recorded since the Sumerian period (from around 2500 BC), although in the modern-day *meshouf* the prow is typically much taller than the stern, whereas in the Sumerian version prow and stern are of equal height.  
  
Rashad Salim’s research with Safina Projects has concluded that the AH 14th/ AD 20th century *meshouf* was strongly influenced by the availability of industrially manufactured nails and tools and imported wood. In the pre-industrial period, wood was scarcer, and many marsh dwellers made *meshoufs* from reeds.  
  
The extended family who built the *meshoufs* in this collection are among the most renowned boatbuilders of Huwair. They are part of the Beni Asad tribe, who came to the marshes 300-400 years ago from Arabia, learned boatbuilding methods from the Mandaean-Sabean population, and gradually took over as the main practitioners of the craft.

707017b0-ac19-5968-8e9b-29b8a4f1aeab.name: Weighing armchair
707017b0-ac19-5968-8e9b-29b8a4f1aeab.short_description: Weighing armchairs were used for medical purposes. Early metabolism studies were made by weighing the test subjects before and after eating or any other activities. They were also used to weigh handicapped people and old patients who could not stand up. The chair is made of polished brown walnut wood. There are two rows of metal plates in front of the seating area. There is a decoration made by punched holes on the backside of the armchair. There is a wooden footrest attached with metal bars to the main body of the armchair. On the rear side there is a weighing mechanism.

70e81fc7-992c-56d9-a3b4-5af8b1052c23.name: Prayer pulpit (*minbar*).
70e81fc7-992c-56d9-a3b4-5af8b1052c23.description:
This *minbar* features seven steps that are held up by two pentagonal sides, decorated with triangular, square and trapezium-shaped panels that have been joined through tenons and mortises. An interrupted horseshoe arch is positioned at the foot of the steps on two supports that are ornamented with vegetal decoration. This structure is linked at its sides by two lateral arches of the same height, which are likewise resting on two supports, their upper parts interlinked by a banister. The upper section of this entrance is adorned with candleholders.  
The panels are sculpted in bas-relief, embellished with floral or geometric decoration; the frontal arch features floral decoration, and, embracing the shape of the arch, a *kufic* inscription reads, rising from the right-hand side, 'In the name of Allah, the Merciful Benefactor. This pulpit was created'; sideways: 'The first of the month of Rajab; and rising from the left, 'of the year 490 \[AD 1097\]. The work of Muhammad'.
70e81fc7-992c-56d9-a3b4-5af8b1052c23.short_description: This seven-stepped pulpit with side panels bears geometric and floral motifs, and a *kufic* inscription dating the object and naming its maker. The first step is covered by a pointed horseshoe arch.

711fba2c-8e7a-5558-8785-0e3951b191e0.name: Table
711fba2c-8e7a-5558-8785-0e3951b191e0.description:
In Arab households symbols of hospitality and the embrace of visitors were deeply ingrained in the cultural fabric, taking on multiple forms. Chairs and tables in spaces like reception halls often bore inscriptions extending warm greetings to guests, occasionally integrating profound aphorisms and verses of poetry. These inscriptions served as decorative elements and cultural expression, and reflected philosophical ideals central to the household’s ethos.  
The FBQ museum holds a remarkable 19th-century Syrian wooden table adorned with meticulously carved inscriptions in *thuluth* script featuring mystical verses attributed to Ibn al-Farid. These poetic excerpts, drawn from his renowned poetry “If my position in love with you", epitomise the fusion of artistic refinement and intellectual depth, enhancing the ambiance of hospitality within the domestic sphere. It says:  
أُمْنِيّة ظفِرَتْ روحي بها زَمَناً واليومَ أحسَبُها أضغاثَ أحلام  
ولو علِمْتُ بأَنّ الحُبّ آخِرُهُ هذا الحِمَامُ (الموت ) لَمَا خالَفتُ لُوّامي.  
A wish my soul held onto for a while,  
Today I deem it mere illusions that beguile.  
Had I known love’s end is but a final breath,  
I'd not have shunned the counsel, evading death.  
Ibn al-Farid (1181–1234) was an acclaimed Arab poet born in Cairo to parents originating from Hama, Syria. Revered as the greatest mystic poet among Arabs, his literary compositions are reputed to have been penned during states of spiritual inspiration.  
The table is crafted from wood with intricately-carved inscriptions inlaid with mother-of-pearl. The carving process involves meticulous engraving with overlapping work. This fusion of techniques reflects the cultural sophistication and skilled craftsmanship of 19th-century Syrian artisans.

7543bcd1-8c93-54f6-b8f4-189d3506360e.name: Jewellery casket
7543bcd1-8c93-54f6-b8f4-189d3506360e.short_description: Tamanrasset, home of the Tuareg is a desert oasis surrounded by moonlike landscapes. Situated on the edge of the Ahaggar Mountains it is the last large town in Algeria before the border with Niger and Mali. A travelling smith fabricates a casket from the chipboards of a packing crate which has become useless. He comes from Mali, and is working temporarily in Tahaggart on the edge of the oasis. He decorates the box according to the traditional palette of colours and patterns: green, yellow and red, lozenges, circles, triangles, wavy lines. In addition, he ornaments it on all sides with studs. He signs his work: "I, Bilan, son of Shakany, made this." The casket is intended for storing female jewellery. It can also be used for storing implements for tea. At least that's what it says in the inventory volume. In a shop in Tamanrasset, the female collector acquires industrially produced tea glasses and a bulgy teapot of blue enamel. Cheap imported wares, such as these are used by the Tuareg in daily life.

767d4db4-9712-508d-b378-dd184496be44.name: Door.
767d4db4-9712-508d-b378-dd184496be44.description:
This single leaf of a door shows a geometric ornamentation based on stars and polygons in the main field. These elements are arranged in an all-over repeat pattern composed of a rosette in the middle and quarter sections of the central motif in the four corners. Strips marked with grooves form the strictly geometric structure of the tracery whose openings are filled with small bevelled panels. The strips and panels are connected by tongue and groove joints to achieve an unbroken surface.  
Originally, the door seems to have been of symmetrical composition with a section with two plain rectangular panels in the upper and lower part and a large ornamented area in the middle. Possibly for a different use, the door was lengthened below by the addition of a section of two plain rectangular panels.
767d4db4-9712-508d-b378-dd184496be44.short_description: Single leaf of a door. The geometric ornament is formed of stars and polygons; the rosette in the middle is repeated in the four corners. The door, now lengthened, seems originally to have been of symmetrical composition with two plain rectangular panels above and below.

This door was assigned to the late 9th –early 10th / late 15th–early 16th centuries because of the unornamented polygons. A carved wooden panel from a building of Sultan Qaytbay at Jamaliyya dated 885 / 1481 in the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo shows two small fields with the same geometric organisation.

76f2b2fe-3a46-55c5-9ef0-fc7350403192.name: Pair of Doors with Design of Ten-Pointed Stars and Geometric Motifs
76f2b2fe-3a46-55c5-9ef0-fc7350403192.short_description: Double doors of hollow-core construction. Posterns are centered in the lower section of each door. Decorated overall with elaborate marquetry of small inlaid wood pieces (lazo-work). Each piece is decorated with an arabesque in white and black, painted on an overall red ground in a ten-pointed star motif with an infinite geometric design. The doors and each postern are secured with a iron throw-bolt lock. Each throw-bolt is made of three iron eyelets connected to a hanging lever. The main throw-bolt is large and elaborate, forged with a twisted spiral lever joined at a square panel with a carved crest on the surface. The postern bolts are smaller and plain. Studded iron rivets fasten wide iron strapwork that reinforces the doors horizontally. Some traces of gilding remain on the iron rivets.

79123b79-bd2b-5af1-8898-89d1cb8e5327.name: Throne of Sultan Ahmed I.
79123b79-bd2b-5af1-8898-89d1cb8e5327.description:
The throne of Sultan Ahmed I is one of the best examples of 11th / 17th century Ottoman woodwork. Made in the form of a baldachin, the throne has three low steps that lead up to the one-person seat. The baldachin itself is crowned with a dome.  
  
The throne was made by the important 11th- / 17th-century architect Sedefkâr Mehmed Agha, the head architect of the Ottoman palace; it is dazzlingly beautiful with a mosaic of superb mother-of-pearl and tortoiseshell work side by side with countless precious gems.  
  
The throne is made of walnut wood. Its entire surface is decorated with a mosaic of mother-of-pearl and tortoiseshell. The vegetal decoration includes tulips, carnations, roses and peonies connected to each other by scrolling tendrils and rising from a vase. The vegetal motifs are executed in a naturalistic style in mother-of-pearl, while the remaining area is covered with tortoiseshell.  
  
The inner part of the seat of the throne is decorated with a composition of motifs in a lacquer technique known as *Edirnekari*. Floral motifs in yellow are painted against a red background in the naturalistic style.  
  
The floral motifs which reflect the characteristic style of the Classical Ottoman period are arranged in a most successful composition. The vase and the flowers themselves are further enlivened by the addition of precious gems, including emeralds, jade, turquoise, and diamonds. The use of precious gems in various colours makes the throne even more attractive.  
  
The throne is one of many objects which display the wealth of the Ottoman Palace. It is an important example of the high level of quality attained in vegetal decoration in 11th / 17th century Ottoman art.
79123b79-bd2b-5af1-8898-89d1cb8e5327.short_description: This magnificent throne with superb mother-of-pearl and tortoiseshell inlay work and numerous gems was made for Sultan Ahmed I. The floral motifs reflect the classical Ottoman period and are successfully rendered in very lively compositions.

7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.name: *Tabica* (small board).
7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.description:
The splendid collar-beam framework of Teruel Cathedral, which has been erroneously described as a coffered ceiling, is one of the examples of Mudéjar carpentry most studied by art critics for several reasons, including its extraordinary iconographic and iconological complexity and its significance in the social context, and the interest generated by its style and dating, which has been helped by analysis of the wood. Among other items, the National Archaeological Museum holds two *tabicas* (small wooden boards) from the gables or planking, one of which shows a male figure and the other, the one examined here, a female figure.  
The woman is from the working class, a water bearer dressed in a long-sleeved, corded tunic or dress tied at the waist. The decorative horizontal lines give her a characteristic air. Her hair is short and her head appears to be uncovered, uncommon in figures on ceilings. She is carrying a two-handled jar. The flat colours are dominated by reds, whites and black outlines.  
It is possible to determine the *tabica*'s original position in the eighth section on the left, in the very place where a bomb fell during the war in 1936
7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.short_description: This *tabica* (small wooden board) decorated the planks in the roof of Teruel Cathedral, showing the different classes of Mediaeval society. The figure is a water bearer dressed in contemporary costume: a long-sleeved dress tied around the waist.

7e873aac-dc37-595c-aaf1-3d2a947dd436.name: Hexagonal table
7e873aac-dc37-595c-aaf1-3d2a947dd436.short_description:
Carbon-14 analyses show that the well-preserved table was made in the 11th-12th century. Along with the one in the al-Sabbah Collection, Kuwait, it is the oldest known table of a popular type in the Islamic world. The type was also made in other materials, such as ceramics and metal.  
Its decorative details are elements, also found in slightly older Samanid ceramics.

7f95a1e1-30bf-5b30-abfb-8955cb750a4b.name: *Isbiya* or *Kaiya* barge (model)
7f95a1e1-30bf-5b30-abfb-8955cb750a4b.description:
The *isbiya* (also known locally as the *kaiya*) is a cargo barge traditionally built in the town of Hit on the Western bank of the River Euphrates in Anbar province. It is documented in archival photographs and texts from the AH 13th / AD 19th and AH 14th / AD 20th centuries, and is believed to have existed in a similar form for several millennia, although its organic construction left no known physical remains.  
  
It is built using a technique comparable to wattle-and-daub architecture, with no use of metal (tools or fixings) or planked wood. Like many traditional boats, the *isbiya* is a technology specific to its place of origin, made with locally sourced materials. It is a vertical-sided box, constructed using a framework of branches and sticks, including palm fronds (*isb*) from which it derives its name, mulberry wood and gharb wood. These are bound together with palm leaf cordage, and ringed with thick coils of halfa grass before being waterproofed with several layers of tar. The community are involved in a collective construction process known as *fezaa*.  
  
Archaeological evidence suggests that cargoes of stone, lime and bitumen used to build Ur (3800 – 500 BC) and other ancient cities in southern Mesopotamia were transported using *isbiyas* or similar boats. This trade continued into the AH 14th / AD 20th century to supply tar used to waterproof roofs, boats and as an adhesive. Each *isbiya* made a one-way journey, propelled by the river, and was broken up on arrival, with the materials sold mainly for use as fuel.  
  
Production of the *isbiya* ceased in the late 1950s, when its function was replaced by metal barges, then by road cargo transport. In 2019 a full-sized *isbiya* and its smaller guide-boat, the *delil*, were reconstructed in a workshop organised by Safina Projects with community members in Hit, including elder Haji Noaman, who had assisted in building the last *isbiya* as an apprentice in the late AH 1370s / AD 1950s. In 2024 a scale model *isbiya* was produced for the collection of the Open Museum for Water Culture (Basra).

800c391d-1714-509b-9718-f253f7cec93e.name: *Jendoul* (reconstruction from illustration by al-Wasiti from the Maqamat al-Hariri)
800c391d-1714-509b-9718-f253f7cec93e.description:
The Arabic term *jendoul* here refers to a boat class that exists across many cultures, the Venetian Gondola being the best-known example. Designed as passenger transport for canals, a *jendoul* features a seating area (usually cushioned and sometimes canopied or featuring a cabin) and is typically no longer than 11 metres in length, enabling it to manoeuvre around canal junctions (although similar craft for open waters may be larger). Whether rowing or poling, the boatman or crew usually stands at the back, overlooking the passenger area and steering the boat (sometimes with another crew member at the front).  
  
A *jendoul* typically includes ostentatious ornamentation, representing the status and affluence of its passengers. The materials used are of high quality, and an array of artisan crafts may be exhibited, such as decorative metalwork, wood carving, inlay, lacquerwork, textiles and upholstery, cordage, tassels, and glass lanterns.  
  
Examples of the *jendoul* boat class can be found in historical cultures including Ottoman Turkey, Fatimid Egypt, Kish, Phoenicia, and in South and South-East Asia. A Sumerian boat with the characteristics of a *jendoul* is depicted on a cylinder seal impression (4th millennium BC, Uruk 3 period) found in the wetlands of Uqair in Diyala, Iraq.  
  
A specific type of *jendoul* is depicted by Yahya al-Wasiti in one of his AH 7th / AD 13th century miniatures illustrating the “Maqamat” of al-Hariri: a richly ornamented boat, rowed by three men standing aft. Safina Projects’ work to reconstruct it from this single image was an unusual challenge. The study process included using artist’s impressions and technical drawings, scale modelling, and experimentation with rowing methods to understand how this *jendoul* worked and to calculate its proportions before the first full-sized prototype Abbasid *jendoul* reconstruction was built in AH 1446-7/ AD 2024-25.

8226b2d6-80a1-5f02-b757-05f24715921e.name: Fireplace mirror
8226b2d6-80a1-5f02-b757-05f24715921e.description:
A type of console mirror for use above a fireplace, it has imitation legs in the form of flat scrolls. The mirror itself is octagonal, a richly carved frame of ornate C- and S-scrolls and pierced *rocaille* surround it.  
Two unidentified coats-of-arms, incorporated into the scrollwork, extend into candle stands from which two angels' heads peep out from the crest formed by shell ornaments.  
The mirror furnished the Hütterott family mansion on Crveni otok island, near Rovinj in Istria. A German family of merchants and industrialists from Trieste, their presence in Rovinj began in 1890 when Johann Georg Hütterott opened a climatic health resort there and bought nearby islets, the family playing a major role in the overall advancement of the Rovinj area.
8226b2d6-80a1-5f02-b757-05f24715921e.short_description: The carved gilded frame decorated in a characteristically mid-18th century style, with C- and S-scrolls and pierced *rocaille* belongs to a type of mirror for use above a fireplace. It came from the mansion of the Hütterott family on Crveni otok near Rovinj, which today is a hotel. The merchant and industrialist Hütterott family from Trieste bought several islets near Rovinj in 1890. They advanced the whole Rovinj area, and among other things laid out an exceptional park in Rovinj itself.
8226b2d6-80a1-5f02-b757-05f24715921e.provenance: From the manor of the Hütterott family on Sv. Andrija island, which after 1945, was renamed Crveni otok island near Rovinj, Istria.

82491e9f-24e6-5380-8457-1657289a939a.name: Cabinet on stand
82491e9f-24e6-5380-8457-1657289a939a.description:
A large cabinet of the aedicule type standing on the base that belongs to it. In the shape of a horizontally oriented rectangle, and given frontal emphasis by its architectural appearance, its decoration of paintings on glass are framed by veneers of expensive woods – black ebony and tortoiseshell – materials that are also employed to build up the architectural decoration. Rosewood veneer covers the sides.  
The central aedicule with twisted pillars and gilt bronze fittings bears a fragmented gable, surmounted with painted fields organised to make up a lunette, and, in the lower zone, the decorative painting conceals a drawer for valuables incorporated into the architectural elements. The remainder of the front maintains rhythm and mobility by the recession of the central surface and projection of the architectural elements.  
The decorative repertoire of the glass, painted in tempera on the reverse, consists of figures and mythological scenes with the “*amour* of the gods” prevailing. There are also scenic views treated in the antique manner. Forms and landscapes in fresh colours immersed in silver and blue create refined tints and subtle tonal shading. The painted scenes are in the manner of Luca Giordano and more or less precisely repeat the iconographic motifs of his repertoire.  
The base is of richly carved and gilded wood constructed from luxurious, symmetrically conceived, front-facing vegetation – fleshy acanthus leaves powerfully mobilised in S-curves, and floral festoons enhanced with a central motif of mascarons, and figures of *putti*. Lion's-paw feet support the base.
82491e9f-24e6-5380-8457-1657289a939a.short_description: A cabinet with the appearance of an architectural façade fitted with drawers for valuables. Richly decorated with painted glass panels framed with ebony and tortoiseshell, it stands on its own luxuriously carved and gilt base. The decorative repertoire of the glass compositions consist of figures, mythological scenes and views treated in the antique manner. The painted scenes are in the style of the Baroque painter, Luca Giordano.

82c65c6f-a7c7-5e4d-90e9-d3af98dc437c.name: Chest with painted scenes.
82c65c6f-a7c7-5e4d-90e9-d3af98dc437c.description:
The piece belongs to the genre of chests with a rectangular body and flat lid.  
The decoration, in watercolour black and gilding following the style of Muslim illuminators, covers the entire chest, showing the medley of Christian and Islamic art that can be seen in some well-known examples, including the caskets at Veroli Cathedral and the Bargello Museum in Florence.  
The top of the lid shows an image of Christ between two saints within a medallion, beside which are the images of two cheetahs, one pursuing a gazelle and the other a hare. On the bottom right there is a figure of a giraffe accompanied by two keepers spurring it on, while to the left there is an image of a richly harnessed elephant, which appears to be uprooting a small tree with its trunk.  
The main sides of the casket bear animal scenes characterised by hunters stalking their prey on foot, founding an iconographic type unique among caskets at that time.  
The sides are characterised by a small stylised tree, probably a tree of life around which a pair of peacocks and a pair of birds face each other. This image is also reproduced on the lower decorative bands of the two main sides, with minor variations in the bird species depicted by the tree.  
The motif of the dogs and cheetahs chasing gazelles is repeated rhythmically at the bottom of the four sides. Small birds and peacocks alternate along the top edge of the chest near to the lid.  
In terms of its decoration, the piece can be most readily compared to the mosaics in the Ruggero Hall and in the paintings on the wooden ceiling held by the Regional Gallery of Palermo.
82c65c6f-a7c7-5e4d-90e9-d3af98dc437c.short_description: This chest is an example of the combination of Christian and Islamic art. The animal scenes and some of the birds come from Islamic art, while the images of saints and, in this case, Christ, clearly belong to Christian art.
82c65c6f-a7c7-5e4d-90e9-d3af98dc437c.owner: Ministry of Interior Affairs, General Directorate of Cultural Affairs
82c65c6f-a7c7-5e4d-90e9-d3af98dc437c.dimensions: Height 18 cm, width 48.5 cm, depth 29.5 cm.
82c65c6f-a7c7-5e4d-90e9-d3af98dc437c.method_for_datation: Although the stylistic analogies linking the chest to various well-known examples of Norman art in Sicily, including in particular the mosaics in the Ruggero Hall and the paintings on the wooden ceiling of the Palatine Chapel, seem to be universally accepted by scholars, there are a number of different theories as to the date of the piece. Di Marzo, followed by Scerrato and Pinder Wilson, suggests the 13th century, thus placing the work in the Federican period. Biagi, however, identifies the origins of the decorative type in the Persian miniature and suggests the 12th century. This hypothesis is supported by Cott and Ferrandis. (See Bibliography.)
82c65c6f-a7c7-5e4d-90e9-d3af98dc437c.method_for_provenance: The presence of various examples comparable to this piece has led scholars to believe that there may have been a single centre of production, probably in Sicily or southern Italy, and Amalfi especially. With reference to this chest in particular, the hypothesis put forward by Pinder Wilson and Scerrato, linking the piece to the production of Islamic art in Sicily during the Federican period, seems the most comprehensive. (See Bibliography.)

835a8c7a-4922-5e4a-890f-690762ae7663.name: One side of a double door
835a8c7a-4922-5e4a-890f-690762ae7663.short_description: The door is covered with geometric patterns. The wooden sections on the front contain fine inlays using the *khatamkari* technique, which was probably developed in the 15th-16th century in the form shown here, and was often used to embellish Shiite shrines in Iran and Iraq. The perfection of the patterns has traditionally been a metaphor of the infinity of God.

84dd3553-46ec-5600-8a2a-e99eb0f50285.name: Three choir stalls.
84dd3553-46ec-5600-8a2a-e99eb0f50285.description:
Three surviving seats from the choir stall. The arms, elaborately carved, mimic smooth timber columns with finely worked capital and base. The separators between the seats have been hollowed out and outlined to form mixtilinear arches with a strong Almohad influence. There are wheels in relief on the spandrels. There is now practically no colour left, with the exception of the persistent red and a few other traces from which a painted lion can be made out, already quite deteriorated when the piece was acquired. The dominant decorative elements are plant arabesques and the polychromy of the heraldic motifs relating to the kingdom of León.  
This piece is noteworthy not just for its intrinsic quality, but also because it demonstrates the importance of León in the emergence of Mudéjar carpentry. This low stall, along with the Astudillo stall also held at the National Archaeological Museum, is one of the most exceptional examples of this type of carpentry in this Mudéjar style.
84dd3553-46ec-5600-8a2a-e99eb0f50285.short_description: Mudéjar craftsmen were sometimes used to work on choir stalls in churches and monasteries, and they brought their own techniques and decorative motifs. These stalls from the Monastery of Santa María de Gradefes in León are particularly noteworthy for the excellence of the joinery and their rich decoration of plant arabesques.
84dd3553-46ec-5600-8a2a-e99eb0f50285.method_for_datation: From its typical characteristics. The earliest document on the monastery dates from 1140.
84dd3553-46ec-5600-8a2a-e99eb0f50285.method_for_provenance: From existing documentation. It remained in the monastery until its sale in 1874.
84dd3553-46ec-5600-8a2a-e99eb0f50285.provenance: Monastery of Santa María de Gradefes, León, Spain.
84dd3553-46ec-5600-8a2a-e99eb0f50285.obtention: The piece was purchased for the National Archaeological Museum from José Gil Dorregaray on 13 March 1874.

854a0735-8c8e-5262-ae65-6ccff0a9b37b.name: Pair of Doors
854a0735-8c8e-5262-ae65-6ccff0a9b37b.short_description: Although the building to which this pair of carved wooden doors originally belonged is not precisely known, clues may lie in its Qur’anic inscriptions, carved in the *naskh* script and framing four panels of openwork designs of scrolling vines. Each text quoted from the Qur’an mentions the rewards of Paradise, and those on the right door (2:274) specifically state that wealthy persons who spend their money for pious purposes need not fear what awaits them in the afterlife. Together, this suite of inscriptions suggests that the doors may have once graced a Shi‘ite shrine or a Sufi tomb.
854a0735-8c8e-5262-ae65-6ccff0a9b37b.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
854a0735-8c8e-5262-ae65-6ccff0a9b37b.method_for_datation: The doors are consonant in technique and style to pairs of doors dated to the 15th century from Timurid Iran, as well as other examples of carved wood such as cenotaphs, most of which are associated with the province of Mazandaran. The Qur’anic text of the inscriptions indicates the doors are from a religious edifice.
854a0735-8c8e-5262-ae65-6ccff0a9b37b.method_for_provenance: The LACMA doors are similar in form, size, decorative layout and epigraphic style to other doors from Timurid Iran.

85597a71-d670-530e-8302-7a8eb8d08410.name: Horizontal ground loom
85597a71-d670-530e-8302-7a8eb8d08410.description: This useful tool has been used since the Neolithic age. A horizontal ground loom is a simple arrangement of four pegs tied in place. The warp (vertical) threads are wound onto the sticks and tied in place. The loom has a heddle, batten, jacks, a warp beam and a shed rod. The weaver works the weft (horizontal) threads, by hand, through the stretched out warp. A shuttle is used to pass the wool.

857327b5-d36c-56a4-a959-8c0836d3b51c.name: Spindle
857327b5-d36c-56a4-a959-8c0836d3b51c.description: A spindle is a straight spike made from wood used for spinning and twisting wool fibres into yarn. It is weighted on one end, by a disc or spherical object called a whorl.

85787dd4-f609-5fdf-ad19-38987eb94fa6.name: Carved wood fragment.
85787dd4-f609-5fdf-ad19-38987eb94fa6.description:
This fragment comes from the *minbar* (preacher's chair) of the Great Mosque of Kairouan, which was donated by Prince Abu Ibrahim Ahmad. This is the oldest dated preacher's chair in the Islamic world. Constructed of teak wood, it is made up of an assembly of over 300 carved pieces. Exceptionally rich in ornament, these panels show just how varied were the models from which Ifriqiyan carvers took their repertoire. This fragment was part of the riser forming the top edge of the staircase of the *minbar*.  
The rich floral decoration of the panel consists of alternately arranged foliated scrolls, each one containing a spread vine-leaf and a cluster of grapes. Stylised five-leaf or furled three-leaf vine motifs are the most favoured floral designs of Aghlabid decoration.  
All these Byzantine-influenced decorations have an affinity with those found on sculpted objects and monuments of the Umayyad period. The finesse of the floral decoration, the richness of the work and the high quality of the finish, as well as the nature of the woods used all show how mature Ifriqiyan art was at that time and how well it adopted, developed and took forward the Umayyad tradition.
85787dd4-f609-5fdf-ad19-38987eb94fa6.short_description: This fragment comes from the pulpit of the Great Mosque of Kairouan, which was donated by Prince Abu Ibrahim Ahmad and is the oldest dated pulpit in the Muslim world. Its extremely rich and varied decoration is evidence of the maturity of Ifriqiyan art at that time.
85787dd4-f609-5fdf-ad19-38987eb94fa6.initial_owner: The Aghlabid prince, Abu Ibrahim Ahmad (r. AH 242–9 / AD 856–63).
85787dd4-f609-5fdf-ad19-38987eb94fa6.dimensions: Length 64 cm, width 5.5 cm, thickness 3.5 cm.
85787dd4-f609-5fdf-ad19-38987eb94fa6.method_for_datation: Historical texts reveal that this *minbar* dates from the period of the fifth reigning Aghlabid prince, Abu Ibrahim Ahmad. This is corroborated by the fact that the decoration of the fragment belongs to the Aghlabid repertoire, and by the strong affinity with the carved motifs on the wooden lintels of the Mosque of the Three Doors, dating from the year 252 / 866.
85787dd4-f609-5fdf-ad19-38987eb94fa6.method_for_provenance: Some historical texts suggest that this *minbar* was made in Baghdad, but the information is unclear and not viable. If the teak wood can be shown to originate from the Indian sub-continent, then all the evidence would suggest this is in fact the work of Kairouanese wood-carvers.
85787dd4-f609-5fdf-ad19-38987eb94fa6.obtention: After the restoration of the *minbar* of the Great Mosque of Kairouan around 1920, some pieces were removed and kept with the mosque's relics. When the Great Mosque's museum was created in 1965, this fragment was taken from the relics and displayed at the museum. Since 1986 it has been kept at the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada, where it will be displayed in the second section, which is currently under refurbishment (2005).

85acf1b7-5e53-59d4-aaea-ce86103574d8.name: Painted wooden board.
85acf1b7-5e53-59d4-aaea-ce86103574d8.description:
Painted on this board in *kufic* script is part of the eighteenth verse of *sura* 3. The vertical lines of the letters have a chamfered effect and some are finished off with a bi-lobed fleuron. The background is punched into a simple floral design.  
The angles of the letters *waw* and *mim* develop into scrolls which fill the empty space between them. The characters are carefully designed, precisely drawn, and finished with a chamfered effect. The yellow-ochre outside edging makes the letters stand out from the background. This technique, which substitutes for carving letters in relief, is known to have been used in the ceilings of the Great Mosque of Kairouan since the AH 3rd / AD 9th century.
85acf1b7-5e53-59d4-aaea-ce86103574d8.short_description: This board bears a *kufic* inscription consisting of part of a Qur'anic verse from the *sura* Al-Imran. The inscribed field is decorated with floral motifs. This technique replaced the inscriptions carved in wood in relief and can be seen in the ceilings of the Great Mosque of Kairouan.
85acf1b7-5e53-59d4-aaea-ce86103574d8.initial_owner: Ordered on behalf of the Zirid prince, al-Mu‘izz ibn Badis by his minister, Muhammad ibn Abi al-Arab.
85acf1b7-5e53-59d4-aaea-ce86103574d8.dimensions: Length 141 cm, width 16 cm, thickness 4 cm.

The lettering and the motifs used date this board from the end of the 4th to the beginning of the 5th century (10th–11th century).

8609522c-18c6-5b1c-9149-7c3bb976c5b7.name: Neo-Mamluk, metal-inlaid copper alloy Table
8609522c-18c6-5b1c-9149-7c3bb976c5b7.short_description: In 13th/ 19th- century Egypt, the political, cultural and social climate increasingly encouraged a nationalistic reappraisal of indigenous heritage. The era of the Mamluks, who had ruled Egypt and Syria between the later 7th/13th and the early 10th/ 16th centuries, was particularly celebrated as a golden age in national history. As a result, artisans now turned their efforts to reviving the glories of Mamluk artefacts, and particularly their celebrated, silver- and gold-inlaid metalwork. This stand or table is an exquisite example of such revivalist work. It copies a famous Mamluk Qur’an stand in the Museum of Arab Art in Cairo, inscribed with the name of the Mamluk Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun (r. 1294-1340) and made by Muhammad ibn Sunqur al-Baghdadi.

88c2eecc-1ad6-5b2b-8f02-6efabc4b470c.name: Pediment of a door.
88c2eecc-1ad6-5b2b-8f02-6efabc4b470c.description:
This pediment takes the form of a half-polygon of nine sides, consisting of four panels; the first is ornamented with vegetal decoration; the remaining three are decorated with a nine-line inscription, sculpted in relief and in cursive lettering, except for the last line, which is in quadrangular *kufic*. The final six lines of the inscription are centrally divided by floral and geometric decoration. This inscription features the following text: 'May God protect us from Satan the abuser / In houses that God allowed us to build / in which men invoke his Name and glorify Him, morning and night (Qur'an, XXI, 36–37) / raised house, full of invocations, erected for the worship of God. He will pardon those who find themselves there / and the one who founded and built it, Yahyia ibn Mahdjuba, who offered it to God / Forgive him his past! Protect him from the heat of hell! Enable him to enter paradise where he will experience well-being! / Grant him Your assurance and Your protection against the terrors of the day of resurrection! Offer him a place at the top of paradise! What success for those who are there! / In the year *chin*, *djim*, the construction was finished and completed with the help of God. Oh reader, make wishes in favour of he who built this / Through the forgiveness and indulgence of God, through the intercession of the best of men! Do it so that one can always read the tradition to the people.'  
This inscription is the only one in Algeria that features a date written in the form of a chronogram (in adding together the numeric values of each letter that it consists of, one obtains the date it conceals). This pediment was previously situated above the entrance to a *zawiya* known under the name of Zawiya Ibn Mahdjuba, adjacent to a cemetery. The building was demolished around 1865, during the widening/opening of the rue Nationale.  
The person mentioned is the sheik Abu-Zakariya Yahyia ibn Mahdjuba (d. AH 1017 / AD 1608), who was a *mufti* and who is mentioned in a manuscript contemporary to the era.
88c2eecc-1ad6-5b2b-8f02-6efabc4b470c.short_description: This pediment stood above the entrance to a *zawiya* and consists of four panels. The first is decorated with plant motifs and the other three bear an inscription carved in cursive characters (*kufic* in the last line) that glorify God and the patron of the work. It is dated by a chronogram included in the inscription.
88c2eecc-1ad6-5b2b-8f02-6efabc4b470c.holder: National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Arts
88c2eecc-1ad6-5b2b-8f02-6efabc4b470c.dimensions: Height 85 cm, length of base 127 cm, depth 5.5 cm.
88c2eecc-1ad6-5b2b-8f02-6efabc4b470c.method_for_datation: Via the chronogram included within the inscription; the Arabic letters *djim* and *chin* correspond to numeric values set within the Maghrebi system: *djim* = 1,000, *chin* = 3; 1,000 + 3 = 1003 (AD 1594).
88c2eecc-1ad6-5b2b-8f02-6efabc4b470c.method_for_provenance: Merit is due to E. Bigonet, who was able to track down the person responsible for the demolition of the Zawiya Ibn Mahdjuba. This person authorised him to look through all the heaps that remained of the demolished building. It was thus that he recovered this inscription, which he then offered to the National Museum of Antiquities.
88c2eecc-1ad6-5b2b-8f02-6efabc4b470c.obtention: Gift from E. Bigonet who, in 1878, undertook research in Constantine on the subject of this inscription, already published.

893326f6-9a4d-57db-bdf6-56796de6ef99.name: Fragment from a carved wooden piece.
893326f6-9a4d-57db-bdf6-56796de6ef99.description: In the Raqqa region one can find fragments of wood that once decorated the formal halls of its Abbasid royal palaces. It is possible to classify these fragments into three types according to their techniques of decoration. The first group is adorned with relatively realistic coloured and gilded carved ornamentation that includes floral and calligraphic motifs. The second group is carved in a slanted manner so that the edges of the carved objects appear curved and not sharp. The examples of this group are influenced by the Abbasid Samarra motifs identified as "Samarra Style C". The third group, to which this piece belongs, has decorative motifs carved in a vertical manner so that the panel appears to have an upper surface and a lower background. The decorative carving is flat with sharp edges and the groove to the background is deep, as can be seen in the small deep holes indicating the circular part of the calligraphic letters. The piece is decorated with Arabic *kufic* script that reads “Commander of the Faithful.” It seems to have been partially burned in a fire.
893326f6-9a4d-57db-bdf6-56796de6ef99.short_description: This calligraphic wooden panel with its sharp vertically carved angles and deep circular grooves is one example of the many carving styles that were developed in the Abbasid period and spread throughout the region.
893326f6-9a4d-57db-bdf6-56796de6ef99.method_for_datation: The carving technique used on this wood fragment is distinctly Abbasid-Islamic and was developed during the Abbasid period in Iraq and Syria.
893326f6-9a4d-57db-bdf6-56796de6ef99.method_for_provenance: The wooden piece was discovered in the vicinity of the Abbasid palaces in the Raqqa region, and therefore it is assumed that it was made *in situ*.
893326f6-9a4d-57db-bdf6-56796de6ef99.obtention: The piece was accidentally discovered by a resident of the Raqqa region during the early 1950s. He presented it to the archaeological expedition working there at that time.

8b0ffe7f-502c-57bf-afc8-2a2f22466bfe.name: Console
8b0ffe7f-502c-57bf-afc8-2a2f22466bfe.description: From a base with four round feet springs the console resembling two vine branches, intertwined with vine-leaves and grapes. The carving is powerful as the volumes are full and in the round. The wood is gilded with silver leaf. The table is painted to look like a dark green false marble, with pale green veins. Formerly thought to be a nineteenth-century remake from a Tuscan workshop, today this console is considered an original piece dating to the eighteenth-century. The original provenance is unknown, but it was likely made in Tuscany. The console is part of the furniture of the baroque apartment, on the first floor of the building which was made between 1736 and 1738 for the wedding of Francesco Tozzoni and Carlotta Beroaldi.
8b0ffe7f-502c-57bf-afc8-2a2f22466bfe.short_description: This piece of furniture is very original; the base is made of vine-shoots and grapes realistically intertwined with a strongly naturalistic carving. We don’t know its original provenance. The console is housed in the red living room of the baroque apartment on the first floor of Palazzo Tozzoni, built between 1736 and 1738 for the marriage of Francesco Tozzoni and Carlotta Beroaldi.

8b53557d-3049-52a4-936d-94e2aa610550.name: Panel from a door or *minbar*
8b53557d-3049-52a4-936d-94e2aa610550.short_description: This carved pine panel is composed of two boards flanking alternating square and rectangular panels. The vine scrolls, particularly those carved in high relief in the central panels, exhibit close affinities with their Late Antique prototypes. A nearly identical panel in the Benaki Museum in Athens suggests that together these may have formed a two-panelled door.

8fa09327-47d4-5dce-9649-b4f26818817e.name: Jar
8fa09327-47d4-5dce-9649-b4f26818817e.description: A hollow wooden jar with a rounded base and a large rhomboid-shaped body designed to store a greater quantity of water. It has a slightly protruding circular mouth, while on either side of the body are small recessed areas for fastening a rope to secure it to an animal. The jar is lightweight enough to be carried or transported over short distances. It was used for storing and transporting water in rural or Bedouin settings and was designed to facilitate drawing water from wells or troughs and preserving it for a period of time.

914eb4c5-9b5a-549c-b385-fee293bdb38a.name: Cogged well wheel (*al-manjūr*)
914eb4c5-9b5a-549c-b385-fee293bdb38a.description: The central hub of a cogged well wheel (*al-manjūr*) is made from a single cross-cut section of local hardwood such as the Christ's thorn jujube (Zisiphus spina-christi, locally known as *sidr*). To form the cogs, a double row of hand-shaped wedges, also of hardwood, are fitted into the hub individually. The wheel is then lashed together with shark skin or goat leather.
keywords: Water; Well wheel.

9158959f-5857-53e2-91ec-f0d84c8343d7.name: Rectangular chest with a truncated-pyramid lid.
9158959f-5857-53e2-91ec-f0d84c8343d7.description:
This wooden chest consists of a rectangular structure with a truncated-pyramid lid.  
It has gilded bronze clasps terminating with lance-shaped brackets around the outside and five straps, also lance-shaped, fixed vertically to reinforce the lid and body. Tri-lobed handles, also in gilded bronze, decorate the lid and the smaller sides.  
The edges of the individual faces of the lid are decorated with small painted crosses made up of groups of circles emanating from a central point and painted alternately in red and green ink. On the short sides of the chest, the circles are grouped into triangles with obvious symbolic meaning. There is a fabric lining on the inside that would have originally been red.  
There are a number of similar pieces that can be compared to this one. Specifically, with regard to the decoration, the most comprehensive comparisons are with the oval chest at York Minster in the UK and with two examples with truncated-pyramid lids in Palermo, also in the Palatine Chapel collection. Nonetheless, the most obvious comparisons can be drawn with the chest at the Walters Art Gallery in Baltimore, USA, in which there are similarities not only in the decoration but also in the form and the inclusion of bronze elements.
9158959f-5857-53e2-91ec-f0d84c8343d7.short_description: Caskets similar to this one in shape and materials have been found in Sicily and southern Italy, where they would have been produced by Muslim craftsmen. The insides of these caskets were usually lined with fabric and they may have been used to keep jewellery.
9158959f-5857-53e2-91ec-f0d84c8343d7.dimensions: Height 12.5 cm, width 20.5 cm, depth 14.5 cm.
9158959f-5857-53e2-91ec-f0d84c8343d7.method_for_datation: Despite the lack of specific documentary references, reference may be made to Cott’s work, which mainly attributes carved ivory production to the 12th century. This dating is subsequently taken up by Pinder Wilson with specific reference to the first half of the century, in relation to the chest at York Minster, which he suggests is linked to the trip made by William Fitz Herbert in 1147–8 to Sicily and his cousin Ruggero (Roger) II. (See Bibliography.)
9158959f-5857-53e2-91ec-f0d84c8343d7.method_for_provenance: The existence of various pieces comparable to this one has led scholars to believe that there may have been a single centre of production in Sicily or, according to Pinder Wilson (see Bibliography), southern Italy, specifically Amalfi.

920e1526-6e4c-5336-8f89-0cc695c54cff.name: Ker Porter’s box
920e1526-6e4c-5336-8f89-0cc695c54cff.short_description: In 1814 Ker Porter, British artist and travelller, visited Rich. Together they explored famous sites in Iraq. He mistook the ruins at Aqar Quf for the Tower of Babel. The box contains fragments of a Babylonian mudbrick and bitumen, matching the Biblical description of the Tower.
keywords: Bible; Babel

92830f7a-b5c3-5e7e-9a7f-a0686de50300.name: *Peškun*
92830f7a-b5c3-5e7e-9a7f-a0686de50300.description:
This *Peškun* (Tr. *peşkun*) has a base of ten vertical sides that carry a protruding decagonal plate at the top. The sides are also divided horizontally into three zones, the highest of which has a central flower motif, the middle a honeycomb-like openwork ellipse, and the lowest an opening in the form of a pointed five-leafed arch, below which is a flower with leaves and a rounded three-leafed arch. On the upper panel, there is a star-shaped field with a flower in the center of it, while other floral motifs are in the spaces between the decagon and the arms of the star. All floral and geometric ornaments are made of mother-of-pearl and brass wire using the incrustation technique, while the edge of the decagonal top plate is ornamented with bone.  
*Peškun* is the name of a traditional piece of Ottoman furniture in the shape of a table or stool. It was originally meant for sitting, although it had different purposes throughout history, especially as a decorative table in Balkan oriental interiors of the 19th and of the first half of the 20th century. Over time, the larger table (in the set of usually three pieces) began to be used as a coffee table, while the smaller ones were used as stools. *Peškun* were ordinarily made of walnut wood, ornamented with incrusted floral and geometric motifs made of mother-of-pearl and bone.

keywords: peškun; stool; side table; incrustation; Ottoman Balkans
materials: Walnut, mother of pearl, bone, brass; incrustation

92eac99d-e9e4-5c28-91d6-bd693774ecfb.name: Pair of *minbar* doors
92eac99d-e9e4-5c28-91d6-bd693774ecfb.short_description: A *minbar* consists of a podium that has doors at its base and is reached by stairs. This pair of doors probably comes from the *minbar* of the mosque of the amir Saif al-Din Qawsun in Cairo. Furnishings in Cairo's mosques, especially during the Mamluk period (1250–1517), were decorated with intricately constructed polygons. This pair of doors exhibits a great variety of patterns, most of which are also found in other media, such as stone carvings, marble mosaics, and stucco window grilles. The accurate cutting required to make these patterned objects is remarkable, as every piece affects the whole.

95f0e5c9-0936-55b5-ae88-631dafd406d1.name: *Minbar*.
95f0e5c9-0936-55b5-ae88-631dafd406d1.description:
The *minbar*, a raised wooden pulpit used for delivering the weekly oration, or *khutba*, during Friday communal prayers, is one of the earliest types of Islamic liturgical furnishings, introduced in the time of the Prophet himself. When Nur al-Din (d. AH 569 / AD 1174) came to rule Syria and al-Jazira, he commissioned several important *minbars* as part of his propagation of piety and *jihad*. He assigned the execution of these wooden *minbars* to the renowned carpenters of Aleppo.  
This *minbar*, now located in the Museum of Hama, was commissioned by Nur al-Din as part of a new mosque he constructed in Hama in AH 558 / AD 1163. It consists of a narrow staircase attached to a raised chair with a covered top. Although it has lost its original stairs and flanking walls, the upper structure is entirely original. The raised chair is square with three arched openings and a back rest. A richly engraved and domed entablature crowns the top. Vegetal and geometric arabesques demonstrate a high level of wood carving. It also contains two historical inscriptions along the friezes on either side of the balustrades. The left inscription, which has been removed and hung above the mosque's entrance, speaks of Holy War and Justice. The right inscription, still *in situ*, emphasises Piety and Humility. The cornice also bears a Qur'anic inscription describing the wonder of God's Creation and the Heavens, while the back of the chair is inscribed with the *Shahada*, or declaration of faith, written in two lines of large *thuluth* script within a cartouche.  
Clearly, the *minbar* re-affirms Nur al-Din's political and religious position, a stance which is reiterated on the inscriptions of the mosque as well. The importance of the *minbar* lies in its symbolism of authority. The inscriptions carved upon it and the speeches delivered from its platform are visible and aural manifestations of the community's leadership and vision. In Nur al-Din's case, historical records show that he was meticulous in organising what was said on his behalf in the many mosques built in his name. The image he projected was one of piety as opposed to magnificence, humility as opposed to wealth, and always dedication to Holy War.  
Nur al-Din's dream of liberating Jerusalem is expressed by a similar but more richly ornamented *minbar* he commissioned for the Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem, prior to its reconquest from the Franks by Saladin. Sadly, this *minbar* was destroyed by fire in recent history (1969).
95f0e5c9-0936-55b5-ae88-631dafd406d1.short_description: Nur al-Din's *minbar* of Hama is an important example of Syrian woodcarving. Nur al-Din is known to have employed the most talented Aleppine carpenters to create a number of *minbars* which he distributed throughout the mosques of Syria in order to preach Holy War when the Crusaders took Jerusalem.
95f0e5c9-0936-55b5-ae88-631dafd406d1.initial_owner: Nur al-Din Mahmud bin al-Zangi (r. AH 541–69 / AD 1146–74).
95f0e5c9-0936-55b5-ae88-631dafd406d1.dimensions: Height (at highest point) 430 cm, length 320 cm, width 85 cm.
95f0e5c9-0936-55b5-ae88-631dafd406d1.method_for_datation: The inscription on the back of the chair reads “559” (1164).
95f0e5c9-0936-55b5-ae88-631dafd406d1.method_for_provenance: The pulpit was originally in the Nur al-Din Mosque in Hama which was constructed by Nur al-Din Mahmud bin Zangi in 558 / 1164.
95f0e5c9-0936-55b5-ae88-631dafd406d1.obtention: Although it was originally located in the Nur al-Din Mosque in Hama, the *minbar* is now in the Hama Museum.

96854149-8a79-55f2-9035-739e18d2ab29.name: Door
96854149-8a79-55f2-9035-739e18d2ab29.short_description:
Heavy carvings with remnants of paint accentuate this door which may have graced a mud-brick house to impress guests with rosette, date palm, and frankincense tree patterns symbolizing fertility, life, and wealth. Characteristic of traditional architecture of Oman, Omani doors, frames, and windows would serve as centrepieces to contrast the modest homes, expressing status and hospitality. As symmetry in Islamic art intends to achieve harmony, a mirrored inscription reads, “My success is only by Allah”.  
  
Since meticulous carvings also decorate doors in East Africa, Afghanistan, and Punjab, lands connected to Oman by trade routes, mutual influences question the doors’ origin.

96df24b2-d14d-504f-84ae-d796597c98a1.name: Travel case
96df24b2-d14d-504f-84ae-d796597c98a1.short_description: Travelling became a great cultural and social phenomenon with Romanticism. The “Grand Tour” through the countries of the known world, and particularly around the Mediterranean, became a means of developing cultural and social skills. Travel became refined and even a simple journey to the countryside required such accessories as this travel case for meals.
96df24b2-d14d-504f-84ae-d796597c98a1.author: DGPC
keywords: objects; travel case; silverware

97234026-b759-5b5b-ada5-8fc567b89260.name: Four-poster bed
97234026-b759-5b5b-ada5-8fc567b89260.short_description: This four-poster bed was made for a Muslim market in a pseudo-baroque style and shows evidence of European influences. The metalworkers who made this kind of furniture worked with both copper and iron, and were organised in their own guild, with their workshops located in the lower kasbah.
97234026-b759-5b5b-ada5-8fc567b89260.holder: Musée Public National des Arts et Traditions Populaires

9a94a586-933d-570f-bdba-4376c9fd1357.name: Chests of drawers
9a94a586-933d-570f-bdba-4376c9fd1357.description: Chests of drawers emerged in the early 18th century and displaced chests as storage furniture. Baroque examples were decorated with lavish inlays of differently coloured types of wood. Typical of the French influence are the curved form, the lavish partially gilt brass mountings, and the marble top panel. The art workshop of the Funk brothers in Berne was the most important production site for luxury furniture in the 18th century. The style of the workshop was so unique that the name Funk-Möbel (Funk furniture) became a byword for form and quality.
keywords: Chest of drawers; Furniture; Funk; Berne; Switzerland
materials: Coniferous wood (core), Walnut and exotic wood (veneer)

9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.name: Door wings and a knocker.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.description:
Both of the wooden wings belonging to the door of the Ulu Cami (Great Mosque) in Cizre were clad in sheets of bronze and then decorated with brass strips and plates attached with iron nails. The border band has a decoration of quatrefoils fitted using round-headed nails. Each wing has three medallions, each with a 12-pointed star in the centre. The areas in between are filled with half-medallions that make up two half- and two full-medallions along the join when the wings are shut. The spaces in between the medallions and the geometric motifs are filled with metal plates decorated with arabesque-palmette motifs in openwork. Traces of pigment suggest that the background of these motifs was originally painted in red and blue to make them stand out more boldly. The half- and quarter-medallions along the outer edges of the door wings imply that the composition extends to infinity. Near the centre of the door wings are two loops for mounting the knockers, one of which is now on display in Copenhagen. The cast bronze knocker still on the door is formed of two symmetrical dragons that are engraved and which join at the centre with a lion's head. The dragons, have pointed ears, almond eyes and wings; their scaly bodies loop around in a spiral to form knots, and their tails join and end in eagle's heads.  
  
On the upper portion of the door wings is an inscription frieze with cast bronze letters. As some letters are missing, the inscription cannot be read in full. The legible part reads: 'May Allah give power to Abul Kasım Mahmud Sanjar Shah, our lord'. The person mentioned is the atabeg of Cizre, Mahmud Sanjar Shah, who ruled from AH 605–39 / AD 1208–41.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.short_description: Magnificent portals of monumental mosques symbolise the gates of Paradise. The naming of the sultan, geometric decoration symbolising infinity on the door-wings and the dragon and lion motifs on the doorknockers are an expression not only of the divine power of God but also of the power of the sultan.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.initial_owner: Mahmud Sanjar Shah (AH 605–639 / AD 1208-1241), atabeg of Cizre, from the Artuqid dynasty.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.dimensions: Door wings: each, height 300 cm, width 112 cm (224 cm in total); knocker: height 27.5 cm; width 24 cm, depth 3 cm.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.method_for_datation: The patron was the atabeg of Cizre, Mahmud Sanjar Shah, who ruled from 605–639 / 1208–41. It is likely that the knockers were produced together with the wings for the door of the Ulu Cami (Great Mosque) in Cizre, itself built in 550 / 1155.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.method_for_provenance: The door wings and knockers were specially prepared for the door of the Ulu Cami (Great Mosque) in Cizre. Thus, it is highly likely that they were produced in Cizre or in southeastern Anatolia.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.obtention: The door wings and knocker were transferred to the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts from the Mardin Museum in 1976.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.bibliography:
ölçer, N. *et al*, *Museum of Turkish and Islamic Art*, Istanbul, 2002, pp.95–7.  
  
Roxburgh, D. J. (ed), *Turks: A Journey of a Thousand Years, 600–1600*, London, 2005, pp.399–400.

9c2ac3c9-ddf9-5578-9e26-fad8ec3a615c.name: Dhow collection
9c2ac3c9-ddf9-5578-9e26-fad8ec3a615c.short_description: The National Museum of Qatar holds, in its collection, a fleet comprising of 14 dhows. The growing collection includes a variety of traditional dhows, with several models dating to the early 20th century, as well as more recent replicas of traditional vessels. Originating from Oman, Bahrayn, India and Qatar, among other places traditional dhows represented include *jalbut* (small to medium sized), *shuw\`i* (medium sized, once used for fishing and coastal trade), *sanbuq* (largest type in the Arabian Gulf today) and *baglah* (traditional, deep-sea dhows once used for the long – haul transport of goods.)
keywords: Boat; ship; dhow; pearling; fishing; trade; transportation

9c5728c7-7dd7-5974-a086-b81efa8965fa.name: Sunflowers frame
9c5728c7-7dd7-5974-a086-b81efa8965fa.description:
From an inventory of the properties of Vincenzo Bargellini, these pendant frames made in 1750 were originally made for holding mirrors, today they hold pictures. They were shown at an exhibition in Bologna in 1935 on Bolognese eighteenth-century art. At that time the frame was still holding a mirror.  
No mention is made of these frames in Vincenzo Bargellini's letters to Venice to commission furniture. Therefore, it is believed they were made in Bologna by local craftsmen following Roman and Venetian models.  
The high quality of the work is evident in the rich and naturalistic decoration. The sunflowers are an allusion to a particular destination.  
A frame similar to this pair is held in the Pinacoteca Nazionale di Bologna; the evolution of this same style can be recognised in the frames made for the pictures by Marcantonio Franceschini exhibited in this same museum, made especially for the paintings in 1710–1711.
9c5728c7-7dd7-5974-a086-b81efa8965fa.short_description:
The extraordinary vivacity of this mirror frame testifies at a very early stage (1699) the great skill and the refined taste of Bolognese baroque carvers, who were looking at Rome and Venice for up to date ideas.  
The frame is dated and signed (JACINTO MONTEILTH FECIT1699). Unfortunately, there are no other occurrences of the carver’s name in objects or documents in Bologna. The style of the frame is similar to one in the Pinacoteca Nazionale of Bologna.
9c5728c7-7dd7-5974-a086-b81efa8965fa.holder: Museo di Arte Industriale e Galleria Davia Bargellini
9c5728c7-7dd7-5974-a086-b81efa8965fa.method_for_datation: The frame is dated and signed (JACINTO MONTEILTH FECIT1699). Unfortunately, there are no other occurrences of the carver’s name in objects of documents in Bologna. The style of the frame is similar to that of one in the Pinacoteca Nazionale of Bologna.
9c5728c7-7dd7-5974-a086-b81efa8965fa.obtention: This frame together with its pendant is mentioned in the 1750 inventory of Vincenzo Bargellini, at that time it was holding a mirror. It is exhibited in the museum since 1924, after the convention between the Municipality of Bologna and the Opera pia Davia Bargellini (owner of the picture gallery and of some of the family furniture).
